original_abstract: Various formal languages have been proposed in the literature for the individual-based modelling of ecological systems. These languages differ in their treatment of time and space. Each modelling language offers a distinct view and techniques for analyzing systems. Most of the languages are based on process calculi or P systems. In this article, we present a general overview of the existing modelling languages based on process calculi. We also discuss, briefly, other approaches such as P systems, cellular automata and Petri nets. Finally, we show advantages and disadvantages of these modelling languages and we propose some future research directions.
generated_abstract: This work investigates the use of formal methods, and particularly process calculi, for the executable modelling and analysis of complex systems with concurrency, probability, time, and spatial structure. We develop and evaluate modelling frameworks that represent individuals, populations, environments, and their interactions while supporting alternative assumptions about event ordering and system dynamics. Spatial and location-aware constructs are introduced to describe movement, local communication, habitat structure, and environmental effects without sacrificing a compact, high-level notation. Operational semantics provide a precise basis for stochastic simulation, while translations to probabilistic model checkers and differential-equation approximations enable reachability, temporal-logic, steady-state, and population-level analyses. The approach is illustrated through models of epidemics, metapopulations, mosquito and wildlife populations, predator–prey systems, and other biological processes. We also consider real-time execution and tool support, including interpreters and simulation and verification environments. The results show that process-calculus models can combine individual-based detail with rigorous quantitative analysis, facilitate comparison of alternative ecological hypotheses, and provide a practical bridge between formal specification, simulation, and experimental data. Limitations concerning scalability, spatial representation, and the expressive power of current analysis tools are identified as directions for future research.

original_abstract: In recent years, the success of deep learning has carried over from discriminative models to generative models. In particular, generative adversarial networks (GANs) have facilitated a new level of performance ranging from media manipulation to dataset re-generation. Despite the success, the potential risks of privacy breach stemming from GANs are less well explored. In this paper, we focus on membership inference attack against GANs that has the potential to reveal information about victim models' training data. Specifically, we present the first taxonomy of membership inference attacks, which encompasses not only existing attacks but also our novel ones. We also propose the first generic attack model that can be instantiated in various settings according to adversary's knowledge about the victim model. We complement our systematic analysis of attack vectors with a comprehensive experimental study, that investigates the effectiveness of these attacks w.r.t. model type, training configurations, and attack type across three diverse application scenarios ranging from images, over medical data to location data. We show consistent effectiveness in all the setups, which bridges the assumption gap and performance gap in previous study with a complete spectrum of performance across settings. We conclusively remind users to think over before publicizing any part of their models.
generated_abstract: Deep generative models are increasingly used to synthesize images, medical records, location traces, and other sensitive data, yet their privacy implications remain poorly understood. This paper presents a systematic study of information leakage from generative adversarial networks and related generative models. We develop a unified framework for membership inference, reconstruction, attribute inference, model inversion, and model extraction under both black-box and white-box access. The framework distinguishes record-level and set-level adversaries and accommodates models trained centrally, collaboratively, or with differential privacy. We introduce calibrated attack procedures that exploit sample proximity, discriminator behavior, latent representations, and unintended feature leakage, and evaluate them across image, medical, and mobility datasets. Our experiments show that apparently high-quality and well-generalized generators can retain recognizable traces of their training data, while common regularization, architectural changes, and output perturbations provide inconsistent protection. Differentially private training substantially reduces leakage, but its effectiveness depends on the privacy budget and may degrade fidelity and diversity. These results demonstrate that standard utility and visual-quality metrics are insufficient for evaluating privacy and motivate privacy-aware training, auditing, and reporting practices for generative models.

original_abstract: Recent advances in large-scale optimal transport have greatly extended its application scenarios in machine learning. However, existing methods either not explicitly learn the transport map or do not support general cost function. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end approach for large-scale optimal transport, which directly solves the transport map and is compatible with general cost function. It models the transport map via stochastic neural networks and enforces the constraint on the marginal distributions via adversarial training. The proposed framework can be further extended towards learning Monge map or optimal bijection via adopting cycle-consistency constraint(s). We verify the effectiveness of the proposed method and demonstrate its superior performance against existing methods with large-scale real-world applications, including domain adaptation, image-to-image translation, and color transfer.
generated_abstract: Unsupervised image-to-image translation seeks meaningful correspondences between domains when paired examples are unavailable. Existing adversarial methods can match marginal distributions and enforce cycle consistency, but the resulting one-to-one mappings are often non-identifiable and may preserve undesirable attributes or introduce visual artifacts. We propose an optimal-transport-based framework that guides adversarial translation toward mappings with task-relevant geometric properties. A regularized transport plan is estimated between source and target representations using an efficient entropic optimal transport solver, and its barycentric projection provides a reference mapping for the generators. This reference is incorporated with adversarial and cycle-consistency objectives, encouraging distribution alignment, approximate invertibility, and preservation of semantically important content. The approach is compatible with deep residual architectures and can be applied to high-dimensional image distributions without paired supervision. We further develop scalable stochastic optimization procedures and discuss extensions to unbalanced domains, in which source and target masses or class proportions differ. Experiments on synthetic transformations, digit and object adaptation, and natural-image translation show that optimal-transport guidance improves correspondence quality, visual fidelity, and target-domain recognition over standard CycleGAN, adversarial adaptation, and competing transport-based methods.

original_abstract: Detecting frequent items is a fundamental problem in data streaming research. However, in many applications, besides the frequent items themselves, meta data such as the timestamps of when the frequent items appeared or other application-specific data that "arrives" with the frequent items needs to be reported too. #R##N#To this end, we introduce the Neighborhood Detection problem in graph streams, which both accurately models situations such as those stated above, and addresses the fundamental problem of detecting large neighborhoods or stars in graph streams. In Neighborhood Detection, an algorithm receives the edges of a bipartite graph $G=(A, B, E)$ with $|A| = n$ and $|B| = \text{poly}~n$ in arbitrary order and is given a threshold parameter $d$. Provided that there is at least one $A$-node of degree at least $d$, the objective is to output a node $a \in A$ together with at least $\frac{d}{c}$ of its neighbors, where $c$ is the approximation factor. #R##N#We show that in insertion-only streams, there is a one-pass $\tilde{O}(n + n^{\frac{1}{c}}d)$ space $c$-approximation streaming algorithm, for integral values of $c \ge 2$. We complement this result with a lower bound, showing that computing a $(c/1.01)$-approximation requires space $\Omega(n / c^2 + n^{\frac{1}{c-1}}d / c^2)$, for any integral $c \ge 2$, which renders our algorithm optimal for a large range of settings (up to logarithmic factors). In insertion-deletion (turnstile) streams, we give a one-pass $c$-approximation algorithm with space $\tilde{O}(\frac{dn}{c^2})$ (if $c \le \sqrt{n}$). We also prove that this is best possible up to logarithmic factors. #R##N#Our lower bounds are obtained by defining new multi-party and two-party communication problems, respectively, and proving lower bounds on their communication complexities using information theoretic arguments.
generated_abstract: We study the design and limitations of streaming algorithms for combinatorial optimization and data analysis under severe memory constraints. Our focus is on semi-streaming and dynamic models, where massive inputs arrive sequentially and algorithms may make only a small number of passes. We develop approximation algorithms and matching lower bounds for fundamental problems including set cover, maximum coverage, matching, and independent set. In particular, we characterize how approximation quality depends on available space and on the number of passes, showing that substantially better guarantees generally require either additional passes or nearly linear space in the input size. We also examine the impact of insertion-only versus turnstile updates, arbitrary versus random arrival order, and explicit versus implicit graph representations. Complementary results address the space complexity of estimating optimum values, heavy hitters, duplicate detection, and frequency-based sampling. Our techniques combine communication-complexity reductions, incidence-geometric constructions, linear sketches, adaptive sampling, and probabilistic load-balancing analyses. Together, these results clarify the tradeoffs governing streaming computation and establish near-optimal boundaries between feasible approximation, memory usage, and pass complexity.

original_abstract: Representation learning promises to unlock deep learning for the long tail of vision tasks without expensive labelled datasets. Yet, the absence of a unified evaluation for general visual representations hinders progress. Popular protocols are often too constrained (linear classification), limited in diversity (ImageNet, CIFAR, Pascal-VOC), or only weakly related to representation quality (ELBO, reconstruction error). We present the Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark (VTAB), which defines good representations as those that adapt to diverse, unseen tasks with few examples. With VTAB, we conduct a large-scale study of many popular publicly-available representation learning algorithms. We carefully control confounders such as architecture and tuning budget. We address questions like: How effective are ImageNet representations beyond standard natural datasets? How do representations trained via generative and discriminative models compare? To what extent can self-supervision replace labels? And, how close are we to general visual representations?
generated_abstract: We introduce a diverse benchmark for evaluating visual representations across a broad range of downstream tasks and domains. Existing evaluations often emphasize ImageNet classification or closely related natural-image problems, making it difficult to determine whether a representation is genuinely general or merely specialized to a familiar distribution. Our benchmark comprises 19 classification tasks drawn from natural, specialized, and structured visual domains, including fine-grained recognition, texture and scene understanding, remote sensing, medical imaging, and synthetic visual reasoning. We standardize data splits, training procedures, and evaluation protocols so that supervised, self-supervised, generative, and randomly initialized representations can be compared fairly. Through extensive experiments with widely used convolutional architectures and pretraining objectives, we find that performance on ImageNet is an imperfect indicator of transfer quality: representations that excel on natural images may underperform substantially on specialized or compositional tasks. We further show that simple adaptation methods and carefully chosen architectural inductive biases can be as important as the pretraining objective. The benchmark exposes substantial variation in transfer behavior and provides a practical testbed for developing representations that are efficient, robust, and broadly useful across visual domains.

original_abstract: Recent single image unsupervised representation learning techniques show remarkable success on a variety of tasks. The basic principle in these works is instance discrimination: learning to differentiate between two augmented versions of the same image and a large batch of unrelated images. Networks learn to ignore the augmentation noise and extract semantically meaningful representations. Prior work uses artificial data augmentation techniques such as cropping, and color jitter which can only affect the image in superficial ways and are not aligned with how objects actually change e.g. occlusion, deformation, viewpoint change. In this paper, we argue that videos offer this natural augmentation for free. Videos can provide entirely new views of objects, show deformation, and even connect semantically similar but visually distinct concepts. We propose Video Noise Contrastive Estimation, a method for using unlabeled video to learn strong, transferable single image representations. We demonstrate improvements over recent unsupervised single image techniques, as well as over fully supervised ImageNet pretraining, across a variety of temporal and non-temporal tasks.
generated_abstract: Self-supervised visual representation learning has recently achieved strong performance without relying on human-provided labels, yet the invariances learned by existing methods remain poorly understood. In particular, image-based contrastive objectives often encourage robustness to augmentations and occlusions while failing to capture viewpoint and instance-level variation that is naturally present in video. We present a framework for learning visual representations from unstructured videos by exploiting temporal correspondence and multiple forms of video-induced invariance. Our objective combines instance discrimination with signals obtained across nearby frames, clips, and videos, encouraging representations to preserve semantic content while disregarding changes in appearance, pose, viewpoint, and illumination. We further analyze the effects of data selection, augmentations, and object-centric versus uncontrolled training data, and show that these factors substantially influence the properties of the resulting features. Experiments on image classification and semantic segmentation demonstrate that video-based training produces more viewpoint-invariant representations than conventional contrastive baselines trained on the same data. The proposed approach improves transfer performance while requiring no manual annotations, highlighting video as a valuable source of supervisory structure for learning representations that better reflect the transformations encountered in the real world.

original_abstract: We study the problem of recovering a block-sparse signal from under-sampled observations. The non-zero values of such signals appear in few blocks, and their recovery is often accomplished using an   $\ell _{1,2}$   optimization problem. In applications such as DNA micro-arrays, some extra information about the distribution of non-zero blocks is available; i.e., the number of non-zero blocks in certain subsets of the blocks is known. A typical way to consider the extra information in recovery procedures is to solve a weighted   $\ell _{1,2}$   problem. In this paper, we consider a block-sparse model which is accompanied with a partitioning of the blocks; besides the overall block-sparsity level of the signal, we assume to know the block-sparsity of each subset in the partition. Our goal in this work is to minimize the number of required linear measurements for perfect recovery of the signal by tuning the weights of a weighted   $\ell _{1,2}$   problem. For this goal, we apply tools from conic integral geometry and derive closed-form expressions for the optimal weights. We show through precise analysis and simulations that the weighted   $\ell _{1,2}$   problem with optimal weights significantly outperforms the regular   $\ell _{1,2}$   problem. We further show that the optimal weights are robust against the inaccuracies of prior information.
generated_abstract: We study recovery of structured and nonuniformly sparse signals from undersampled linear measurements when prior information about the signal is available. The information may describe differing activation probabilities across coordinates, an estimated support, block or joint sparsity, or known spectral structure. We analyze convex recovery methods, with particular emphasis on weighted l1 minimization and related mixed-norm formulations, and characterize their phase transitions under large random measurement ensembles. Using conic geometry, statistical dimension, and state-evolution connections to minimax denoising, we derive measurement thresholds and reconstruction error predictions for weighted penalties. The analysis identifies how optimal weights depend on the reliability and granularity of the prior information, and shows that exploiting nonuniformity can substantially reduce the number of measurements compared with standard l1 recovery. We further discuss noisy observations, approximate sparsity, and extensions to block and multiple-measurement-vector models. Numerical experiments with synthetic signals and imaging data confirm the theoretical predictions and demonstrate improved recovery accuracy and robustness. The results provide practical guidelines for selecting weights and show that even imperfect prior information can yield significant gains when incorporated appropriately.

original_abstract: Self-supervised learning aims to learn representations from the data itself without explicit manual supervision. Existing efforts ignore a crucial aspect of self-supervised learning - the ability to scale to large amount of data because self-supervision requires no manual labels. In this work, we revisit this principle and scale two popular self-supervised approaches to 100 million images. We show that by scaling on various axes (including data size and problem 'hardness'), one can largely match or even exceed the performance of supervised pre-training on a variety of tasks such as object detection, surface normal estimation (3D) and visual navigation using reinforcement learning. Scaling these methods also provides many interesting insights into the limitations of current self-supervised techniques and evaluations. We conclude that current self-supervised methods are not 'hard' enough to take full advantage of large scale data and do not seem to learn effective high level semantic representations. We also introduce an extensive benchmark across 9 different datasets and tasks. We believe that such a benchmark along with comparable evaluation settings is necessary to make meaningful progress. generated_abstract: Self-supervised learning has emerged as a compelling alternative to manually labeled data for acquiring visual representations, yet the rapidly growing range of pretext tasks, architectures, datasets, and evaluation protocols makes progress difficult to interpret. This paper presents a systematic study of unsupervised and self-supervised visual representation learning. We organize existing approaches according to the supervisory signal they exploit, including spatial context, temporal structure, motion and ego-motion, cross-modal correspondence, image transformations, clustering, reconstruction, and generative modeling. We examine how these signals promote invariance, equivariance, semantic abstraction, and transfer across recognition, detection, segmentation, geometry, and embodied decision-making tasks. Through controlled experiments and analysis of network design, optimization, data scale, and transfer procedures, we show that performance depends as much on implementation choices and evaluation protocols as on the nominal pretext task. Combining complementary objectives and using large, diverse unlabeled datasets generally improves transfer, but no single representation is uniformly optimal across tasks. Our findings clarify the strengths and limitations of current methods and provide practical guidance for building efficient visual systems when human annotation is scarce.

original_abstract: Person re-identification (reID) aims to match person images to retrieve the ones with the same identity. This is a challenging task, as the images to be matched are generally semantically misaligned due to the diversity of human poses and capture viewpoints, incompleteness of the visible bodies (due to occlusion), etc. In this paper, we propose a framework that drives the reID network to learn semantics-aligned feature representation through delicate supervision designs. Specifically, we build a Semantics Aligning Network (SAN) which consists of a base network as encoder (SA-Enc) for re-ID, and a decoder (SA-Dec) for reconstructing/regressing the densely semantics aligned full texture image. We jointly train the SAN under the supervisions of person re-identification and aligned texture generation. Moreover, at the decoder, besides the reconstruction loss, we add triplet reID constraints/losses over the feature maps as the perceptual losses. The decoder is discarded in the inference/test and thus our scheme is computationally efficient. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of our design. We achieve the state-of-the-art performances on the benchmark datasets CUHK03, Market1501, MSMT17, and the partial person reID dataset Partial REID.
generated_abstract: Person re-identification systems typically assume that pedestrian images have sufficient resolution, yet surveillance imagery often contains small, blurred, or partially occluded subjects. We present a resolution-aware framework that learns identity-preserving representations across a broad range of image scales. A shared residual backbone extracts features in the low-resolution domain, while lightweight sub-pixel reconstruction and multi-level supervision recover complementary fine-grained cues without requiring expensive image upscaling. To reduce sensitivity to pose, viewpoint, missing body parts, and background clutter, the network combines global descriptors with horizontally partitioned local features and uses pose- and visibility-aware attention to emphasize reliable regions. The model is optimized jointly with identification and hard triplet objectives, together with resolution consistency and feature distillation losses. An adaptive inference strategy selects the least costly representation that meets a desired accuracy budget, enabling practical deployment under variable computational constraints. Extensive experiments on Market-1501, DukeMTMC-reID, CUHK03, and MARS demonstrate consistent improvements over strong convolutional and part-based baselines, particularly for low-resolution queries. The proposed approach achieves a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off while requiring no additional pose annotations or identity labels at test time.

original_abstract: This paper presents SimCLR: a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations. We simplify recently proposed contrastive self-supervised learning algorithms without requiring specialized architectures or a memory bank. In order to understand what enables the contrastive prediction tasks to learn useful representations, we systematically study the major components of our framework. We show that (1) composition of data augmentations plays a critical role in defining effective predictive tasks, (2) introducing a learnable nonlinear transformation between the representation and the contrastive loss substantially improves the quality of the learned representations, and (3) contrastive learning benefits from larger batch sizes and more training steps compared to supervised learning. By combining these findings, we are able to considerably outperform previous methods for self-supervised and semi-supervised learning on ImageNet. A linear classifier trained on self-supervised representations learned by SimCLR achieves 76.5% top-1 accuracy, which is a 7% relative improvement over previous state-of-the-art, matching the performance of a supervised ResNet-50. When fine-tuned on only 1% of the labels, we achieve 85.8% top-5 accuracy, outperforming AlexNet with 100X fewer labels.
generated_abstract: Self-supervised visual representation learning has emerged as a compelling alternative to supervised pre-training, but comparisons between methods are often confounded by differences in architectures, optimization, data augmentation, and evaluation protocols. We present a systematic study of the factors that determine the quality and transferability of learned representations. We evaluate a broad range of pretext tasks, including spatial reasoning, transformation prediction, colorization, instance discrimination, clustering, contrastive prediction, and mutual-information-based objectives, using modern convolutional architectures and carefully controlled training procedures. Our experiments show that the choice of network, augmentation policy, batch size, optimization schedule, and representation used for transfer can be as important as the nominal learning objective. In particular, enforcing invariance to semantically irrelevant transformations and using sufficiently diverse negative examples substantially improves downstream performance, while gains on the pretext task do not always predict gains in recognition or detection. We further examine linear evaluation, fine-tuning, semi-supervised learning, and transfer to fine-grained, scene, texture, and detection datasets. The results clarify the strengths and limitations of current approaches and provide practical guidelines for building data-efficient visual representations without human annotations.

original_abstract: In recent years, deep learning models have resulted in a huge amount of progress in various areas, including computer vision. By nature, the supervised training of deep models requires a large amount of data to be available. This ideal case is usually not tractable as the data annotation is a tremendously exhausting and costly task to perform. An alternative is to use synthetic data. In this paper, we take a comprehensive look into the effects of replacing real data with synthetic data. We further analyze the effects of having a limited amount of real data. We use multiple synthetic and real datasets along with a simulation tool to create large amounts of cheaply annotated synthetic data. We analyze the domain similarity of each of these datasets. We provide insights about designing a methodological procedure for training deep networks using these datasets.
generated_abstract: Deep learning has transformed autonomous driving, but progress remains constrained by the cost, scale, and diversity of human-annotated sensor data. Synthetic data generated in video games, physically based simulators, and procedural environments provides accurate labels for perception tasks, including object detection, semantic and instance segmentation, depth, optical flow, lane marking detection, and three-dimensional LiDAR understanding. However, models trained synthetically often suffer from a reality gap caused by differences in appearance, sensor characteristics, scene composition, and environmental conditions. This paper reviews and evaluates strategies for exploiting synthetic data in autonomous-driving systems. We examine domain randomization, photorealistic rendering, sensor-effect augmentation, image-to-image translation, adversarial and feature-level adaptation, and hybrid real–synthetic training. We further consider efficient architectures and multimodal representations suitable for real-time deployment, as well as simulation platforms and benchmark datasets that enable controlled evaluation. Across camera and LiDAR modalities, combining synthetic supervision with limited real data and appropriate adaptation consistently improves generalization over naïve synthetic-only training. The analysis highlights remaining challenges, including rare-event coverage, realistic dynamics, cross-sensor calibration, uncertainty estimation, and safety validation, and identifies directions toward scalable, reproducible training pipelines for autonomous vehicles.

original_abstract: Public vulnerability databases such as CVE and NVD account for only 60% of security vulnerabilities present in open-source projects, and are known to suffer from inconsistent quality. Over the last two years, there has been considerable growth in the number of known vulnerabilities across projects available in various repositories such as NPM and Maven Central. Such an increasing risk calls for a mechanism to infer the presence of security threats in a timely manner. We propose novel hierarchical deep learning models for the identification of security-relevant commits from either the commit diff or the source code for the Java classes. By comparing the performance of our model against code2vec, a state-of-the-art model that learns from path-based representations of code, and a logistic regression baseline, we show that deep learning models show promising results in identifying security-related commits. We also conduct a comparative analysis of how various deep learning models learn across different input representations and the effect of regularization on the generalization of our models.
generated_abstract: Identifying commits that fix security vulnerabilities is essential for maintaining secure software, yet existing vulnerability repositories are incomplete and manual analysis is costly. We investigate whether pretrained language models for source code can improve the automatic classification of security-relevant commits. We construct a benchmark from a manually curated dataset of vulnerability-fixing commits and corresponding non-security changes, and compare token-based, structural, and pretrained representations. Our approach fine-tunes a transformer model jointly informed by source-code changes and commit messages, while exploiting the syntactic and natural-language regularities present in software repositories. We evaluate performance across multiple random seeds and report score distributions rather than relying on a single execution, addressing the substantial variability of neural fine-tuning. The results show that contextual code representations consistently outperform conventional document classifiers and randomly initialized neural models, particularly when training data are limited. Structural representations provide additional benefits for distinguishing security fixes from routine maintenance, while commit messages offer complementary information. Error analysis reveals recurring difficulties involving incomplete patches, mixed-purpose commits, and vulnerabilities whose fixes resemble ordinary refactoring. Our findings demonstrate the promise of transfer learning for security-relevant commit classification and provide practical guidance for reproducible evaluation and deployment in software vulnerability management.

original_abstract: The general trend in NLP is towards increasing model capacity and performance via deeper neural networks. However, simply stacking more layers of the popular Transformer architecture for machine translation results in poor convergence and high computational overhead. Our empirical analysis suggests that convergence is poor due to gradient vanishing caused by the interaction between residual connections and layer normalization. We propose depth-scaled initialization (DS-Init), which decreases parameter variance at the initialization stage, and reduces output variance of residual connections so as to ease gradient back-propagation through normalization layers. To address computational cost, we propose a merged attention sublayer (MAtt) which combines a simplified averagebased self-attention sublayer and the encoderdecoder attention sublayer on the decoder side. Results on WMT and IWSLT translation tasks with five translation directions show that deep Transformers with DS-Init and MAtt can substantially outperform their base counterpart in terms of BLEU (+1.1 BLEU on average for 12-layer models), while matching the decoding speed of the baseline model thanks to the efficiency improvements of MAtt.
generated_abstract: We investigate how to build and train substantially deeper neural machine translation models without sacrificing optimization stability, translation quality, or computational efficiency. Although Transformer architectures have become the dominant approach to sequence transduction, most systems remain relatively shallow because increasing depth causes unstable gradients, poor information flow, and diminishing returns. We present a unified framework for deep encoder–decoder Transformers that combines carefully designed residual pathways, layer normalization and initialization schemes, and mechanisms that expose representations from multiple preceding layers to subsequent attention and feed-forward blocks. These components enable models with considerably more encoder and decoder layers to be trained reliably using standard large-scale data and hardware. Experiments on WMT English–German, English–French, and other benchmark tasks show consistent improvements over strong shallow and Transformer-Big baselines, while maintaining competitive training and inference costs. We further analyze the effects of depth, normalization, residual connections, attention design, subword modeling, decoding, and optimization choices, highlighting which factors are essential and which provide limited benefit. Our results demonstrate that depth remains an effective source of modeling capacity for machine translation when supported by appropriate architectural and training techniques.

original_abstract: It is generally accepted that relatively more permanent (i.e., more temporally persistent) traits are more valuable for biometric performance than less permanent traits. Although this finding is intuitive, there is no current work identifying exactly where in the biometric analysis temporal persistence makes a difference. In this paper, we answer this question. In a recent report, we introduced the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) as an index of temporal persistence for such features. In that report, we also showed that choosing only the most temporally persistent features yielded superior performance in 12 of 14 datasets. Motivated by those empirical results, we present a novel approach using synthetic features to study which aspects of a biometric identification study are influenced by the temporal persistence of features. What we show is that using more temporally persistent features produces effects on the similarity score distributions that explain why this quality is so key to biometric performance. The results identified with the synthetic data are largely reinforced by an analysis of two datasets, one based on eye-movements and one based on gait. There was one difference between the synthetic and real data: In real data, features are intercorrelated, with the level of intercorrelation increasing with increasing ICC. This increasedhttps://www.this http URL intercorrelation in real data was associated with an increase in the spread of the impostor similarity score distributions. Removing these intercorrelations for real datasets with a decorrelation step produced results which were very similar to that obtained with synthetic features.
generated_abstract: Biometric systems based on behavioral characteristics may be affected by changes in the user, measurement conditions, and representation methods over time. This study investigates the permanence of eye movement patterns for biometric recognition and examines whether template aging can be observed in this modality. A broad set of temporal, spatial, and dynamic features is extracted from fixations, saccades, and post-saccadic oscillations recorded during a reading task. Feature dependencies are reduced through whitening, after which real-valued templates are quantized into binary strings for Hamming-distance matching. Several bit-allocation strategies are compared, including uniform allocation and schemes that assign more bits to features with stronger discriminatory power. Recognition performance is evaluated across increasing time intervals between enrollment and verification, using false rejection and detection-rate measures. The results indicate that eye movement characteristics contain subject-specific information and can support biometric identification, but their reliability varies substantially across feature categories. Speech- or task-related behavioral variation and changes in recording conditions contribute to performance degradation. Optimized quantization improves short-term recognition and storage efficiency, yet does not eliminate the decline observed with longer time lapses. These findings demonstrate the importance of modeling temporal permanence when designing protected behavioral biometric templates.

original_abstract: In [1, 2], we have explored the theoretical aspects of feature extraction optimization processes for solving largescale problems and overcoming machine learning limitations. Majority of optimization algorithms that have been introduced in [1, 2] guarantee the optimal performance of supervised learning, given offline and discrete data, to deal with curse of dimensionality (CoD) problem. These algorithms, however, are not tailored for solving emerging learning problems. One of the important issues caused by online data is lack of sufficient samples per class. Further, traditional machine learning algorithms cannot achieve accurate training based on limited distributed data, as data has proliferated and dispersed significantly. Machine learning employs a strict model or embedded engine to train and predict which still fails to learn unseen classes and sufficiently use online data. In this chapter, we introduce these challenges elaborately. We further investigate Meta-Learning (MTL) algorithm, and their application and promises to solve the emerging problems by answering how autonomous agents can learn to learn?.
generated_abstract: Device-free human sensing in smart environments is challenging because sensing conditions, users, devices, and activities vary substantially across locations and time. Conventional machine-learning methods require extensive labeled data and dedicated sensors, limiting their scalability and adaptability. This paper presents a meta-learning framework for intelligent sensing that enables models to learn how to learn from heterogeneous, distributed data sources. The proposed approach transforms observations from available end-user devices into a shared feature space, discovers latent sensing structures, and rapidly adapts to new environments and sensing tasks with little or no labeled data. A distributed architecture is developed in which smartphones and IoT devices collect and process information locally, while lightweight communication with neighboring agents supports collaborative model updates and preserves data privacy. The framework integrates zero-shot and few-shot learning mechanisms to recognize previously unseen users, activities, and contexts, and incorporates continual adaptation as new observations arrive. We discuss the system design, learning procedure, communication requirements, and challenges associated with noisy, incomplete, and non-identically distributed sensor data. Simulated and real-world evaluations indicate that meta-learning substantially improves generalization and reduces annotation and infrastructure costs, providing a practical pathway toward autonomous, scalable, and privacy-aware device-free human sensing.

original_abstract: Predicting surrounding vehicle behaviors are critical to autonomous vehicles when negotiating in multi-vehicle interaction scenarios. Most existing approaches require tedious training process with large amounts of data and may fail to capture the propagating uncertainty in interaction behaviors. The multi-vehicle behaviors are assumed to be generated from a stochastic process. This paper proposes an attentive recurrent neural process (ARNP) approach to overcome the above limitations, which uses a neural process (NP) to learn a distribution of multi-vehicle interaction behavior. Our proposed model inherits the flexibility of neural networks while maintaining Bayesian probabilistic characteristics. Constructed by incorporating NPs with recurrent neural networks (RNNs), the ARNP model predicts the distribution of a target vehicle trajectory conditioned on the observed long-term sequential data of all surrounding vehicles. This approach is verified by learning and predicting lane-changing trajectories in complex traffic scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms previous counterparts in terms of accuracy and uncertainty expressiveness. Moreover, the meta-learning instinct of NPs enables our proposed ARNP model to capture global information of all observations, thereby being able to adapt to new targets efficiently.
generated_abstract: Accurate prediction of surrounding vehicles is essential for safe planning in autonomous driving, particularly in dense and interactive traffic where one vehicle’s behavior influences the motions of others. Existing trajectory predictors often rely on fixed behavioral distributions, require extensive training data, or treat neighboring vehicles independently, limiting their ability to generalize across scenarios. We propose a recurrent meta-induction neural network for interactive trajectory prediction. The model represents the historical motions of a target vehicle and its surrounding vehicles as an ordered sequence and uses recurrent context encoding to capture temporal dependencies and mutual interactions. A latent variable component models uncertainty and produces multiple plausible future trajectories, while attention mechanisms identify the vehicles and observations most relevant to each prediction. The meta-learning formulation enables rapid adaptation to previously unseen traffic configurations using only a small number of observations. We evaluate the method on real-world dense-traffic data, focusing on long-horizon lane-change prediction. Compared with deterministic, interaction-free, and conventional conditional neural-process baselines, the proposed approach achieves lower prediction error and better captures multimodal behavior. These results demonstrate that recurrent meta-induction provides an effective and data-efficient framework for interactive vehicle motion forecasting.

original_abstract: An important characteristic of English written text is the abundance of noun compounds - sequences of nouns acting as a single noun, e.g., colon cancer tumor suppressor protein. While eventually mastered by domain experts, their interpretation poses a major challenge for automated analysis. Understanding noun compounds' syntax and semantics is important for many natural language applications, including question answering, machine translation, information retrieval, and information extraction. I address the problem of noun compounds syntax by means of novel, highly accurate unsupervised and lightly supervised algorithms using the Web as a corpus and search engines as interfaces to that corpus. Traditionally the Web has been viewed as a source of page hit counts, used as an estimate for n-gram word frequencies. I extend this approach by introducing novel surface features and paraphrases, which yield state-of-the-art results for the task of noun compound bracketing. I also show how these kinds of features can be applied to other structural ambiguity problems, like prepositional phrase attachment and noun phrase coordination. I address noun compound semantics by automatically generating paraphrasing verbs and prepositions that make explicit the hidden semantic relations between the nouns in a noun compound. I also demonstrate how these paraphrasing verbs can be used to solve various relational similarity problems, and how paraphrasing noun compounds can improve machine translation.
generated_abstract: Noun compounds are pervasive in English and encode relations that are often implicit, underspecified, and difficult to recover automatically. This paper presents a corpus-based framework for interpreting compounds by making their hidden relations explicit through verbal and prepositional paraphrases. Given a compound such as malaria mosquito or apple cake, the system collects candidate paraphrases from large text collections and the Web, ranks them using frequency and contextual evidence, and uses the resulting representations to predict abstract semantic relations. The approach combines distributional similarity, syntactic analysis, lexical resources, supervised learning, and bootstrapping, while also addressing the related problems of compound bracketing and coordination. We evaluate the methods on standard datasets for noun-compound interpretation and semantic-relation classification, comparing them with pattern-based, Web-count, and vector-space baselines. Experiments show that explicit paraphrases provide informative features and substantially improve relation classification, especially when multiple paraphrases are retained rather than selecting a single interpretation. We further demonstrate applications to textual entailment and statistical machine translation, where paraphrase-based representations improve coverage and translation quality. The results support paraphrasing as a practical bridge between shallow corpus evidence and deeper semantic analysis.

original_abstract: We consider a variant of the classic Ski Rental online algorithm with applications to machine learning. In our variant, we allow the skier access to a black-box machine-learning algorithm that provides an estimate of the probability that there will be at most a threshold number of ski-days. We derive a class of optimal randomized algorithms to determine the strategy that minimizes the worst-case expected competitive ratio for the skier given a prediction from the machine learning algorithm,and analyze the performance and robustness of these algorithms.
generated_abstract: Machine-learned predictions offer a promising way to improve online decision making, but their benefits must be balanced against the risk of inaccurate advice. This paper develops a general framework for learning-augmented online algorithms that combines predictive models with worst-case guarantees. We study how predictions can be incorporated without requiring assumptions about their internal structure or error distribution, and how performance can interpolate between prediction-dependent improvements and classical robust competitive bounds. The framework is illustrated through several fundamental applications. For caching, we design prediction-aware eviction strategies whose competitive ratio improves with prediction accuracy while remaining bounded by the best available prediction-free guarantee. For ski rental and related problems, we examine how predictions and input distributions alter optimal purchasing decisions, connecting worst-case and average-case analyses. We also consider revenue optimization in advertising auctions, showing how approximate bid predictions can be converted into reserve-price decisions and how revenue loss can be controlled by standard prediction error. Together, these results demonstrate that machine learning can enhance online algorithms in a principled manner: accurate predictions yield substantial gains, while poor predictions cause only limited degradation. Our analysis is supported by empirical evidence on practical datasets.

original_abstract: Neural network learning is typically slow since backpropagation needs to compute full gradients and backpropagate them across multiple layers. Despite its success of existing work in accelerating propagation through sparseness, the relevant theoretical characteristics remain unexplored and we empirically find that they suffer from the loss of information contained in unpropagated gradients. To tackle these problems, in this work, we present a unified sparse backpropagation framework and provide a detailed analysis of its theoretical characteristics. Analysis reveals that when applied to a multilayer perceptron, our framework essentially performs gradient descent using an estimated gradient similar enough to the true gradient, resulting in convergence in probability under certain conditions. Furthermore, a simple yet effective algorithm named memorized sparse backpropagation (MSBP) is proposed to remedy the problem of information loss by storing unpropagated gradients in memory for the next learning. The experiments demonstrate that the proposed MSBP is able to effectively alleviate the information loss in traditional sparse backpropagation while achieving comparable acceleration.
generated_abstract: Deep neural networks achieve strong performance, but their training remains expensive because backpropagation computes and propagates dense gradients through every parameter. We present a sparse training framework that exploits the observation that gradient information is typically concentrated in a small number of coordinates. At each backward pass, only the largest-magnitude gradient components are retained, while the remaining components are omitted or accumulated through an error-memory mechanism. This reduces arithmetic, parameter updates, and, in distributed settings, communication without changing the forward computation or requiring architectural modifications. We develop structured variants for fully connected, convolutional, and recurrent layers, and combine the method with adaptive stochastic optimizers and residual architectures. Experiments on image classification, sequence tagging, language modeling, and neural machine translation show that updating only a small fraction of gradients can preserve, and sometimes improve, predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time and memory movement. We further analyze the effects of sparsity, gradient noise, and model depth, and compare the approach with dense backpropagation, random sparsification, and local or feedback-alignment learning. The results indicate that gradient sparsity provides a practical route toward faster, more scalable, and potentially more energy-efficient deep learning.

original_abstract: Indoor robotics localization, navigation and interaction heavily rely on scene understanding and reconstruction. Compared to monocular vision which usually does not explicitly introduce any geometrical constraint, stereo vision based schemes are more promising and robust to produce accurate geometrical information, such as surface normal and depth/disparity. Besides, deep learning models trained with large-scale datasets have shown their superior performance in many stereo vision tasks. However, existing stereo datasets rarely contain the high-quality surface normal and disparity ground truth, which hardly satisfy the demand of training a prospective deep model for indoor scenes. To this end, we introduce a large-scale synthetic indoor robotics stereo (IRS) dataset with over 100K stereo RGB images and high-quality surface normal and disparity maps. Leveraging the advanced rendering techniques of our customized rendering engine, the dataset is considerably close to the real-world captured images and covers several visual effects, such as brightness changes, light reflection/transmission, lens flare, vivid shadow, etc. We compare the data distribution of IRS with existing stereo datasets to illustrate the typical visual attributes of indoor scenes. In addition, we present a new deep model DispNormNet to simultaneously infer surface normal and disparity from stereo images. Compared to existing models trained on other datasets, DispNormNet trained with IRS produces much better estimation of surface normal and disparity for indoor scenes.
generated_abstract: We present a unified deep learning framework for dense and object-level 3D scene understanding from stereo images. The method jointly estimates disparity, surface orientation, semantic segmentation, and object detections, combining geometric reasoning with semantic context. A pyramid stereo architecture constructs a multi-scale cost volume and uses efficient guided aggregation to recover accurate disparities, including in textureless regions, slanted surfaces, and near depth boundaries. Surface-normal prediction provides complementary orientation cues, while a segmentation branch enriches the features used for object localization and improves recognition of small and partially occluded instances. The network is trained end to end using large-scale synthetic stereo data and physically based indoor and outdoor scenes, together with real driving imagery. Occlusion-aware objectives and multi-scale supervision encourage consistent predictions across object boundaries and moving regions. We evaluate the system on standard stereo, scene-flow, detection, segmentation, and surface-normal benchmarks. Results show that the proposed joint representation improves disparity quality and object localization over separate or purely appearance-based models, while retaining practical inference speed. The framework provides a compact basis for autonomous navigation, enabling metric depth and semantic interpretation from a single stereo pair.

original_abstract: Typical active learning strategies are designed for tasks, such as classification, with the assumption that the output space is mutually exclusive. The assumption that these tasks always have exactly one correct answer has resulted in the creation of numerous uncertainty-based measurements, such as entropy and least confidence, which operate over a model's outputs. Unfortunately, many real-world vision tasks, like visual question answering and image captioning, have multiple correct answers, causing these measurements to overestimate uncertainty and sometimes perform worse than a random sampling baseline. In this paper, we propose a new paradigm that estimates uncertainty in the model's internal hidden space instead of the model's output space. We specifically study a manifestation of this problem for visual question answer generation (VQA), where the aim is not to classify the correct answer but to produce a natural language answer, given an image and a question. Our method overcomes the paraphrastic nature of language. It requires a semantic space that structures the model's output concepts and that enables the usage of techniques like dropout-based Bayesian uncertainty. We build a visual-semantic space that embeds paraphrases close together for any existing VQA model. We empirically show state-of-art active learning results on the task of VQA on two datasets, being 5 times more cost-efficient on Visual Genome and 3 times more cost-efficient on VQA 2.0.
generated_abstract: Visual question answering systems require large numbers of image–question–answer annotations, yet obtaining reliable answers from people is costly, particularly when questions are ambiguous or images are difficult to interpret. We investigate active learning for VQA, in which a model selects the most informative examples to send to an annotator rather than relying on random sampling. We compare uncertainty-, diversity-, curiosity-, and goal-driven acquisition strategies, including Bayesian estimates of predictive and model uncertainty, expected model change, and expected error reduction. We further examine batch selection, answer disagreement, and the effect of selective sampling on annotation time and agreement. Experiments on synthetic and natural benchmarks, including CLEVR, VQA, and questions collected from blind users, show that active learning can achieve competitive accuracy with substantially fewer labeled examples once the model has acquired a useful initial training set. Goal-driven and diversity-aware methods generally outperform random selection, while uncertainty alone is vulnerable to dataset bias and cold-start failure. The results demonstrate that active learning can reduce annotation budgets, but also highlight the need to model answerability, human disagreement, and visual grounding when building practical VQA systems.

original_abstract: Recently the GAN generated face images are more and more realistic with high-quality, even hard for human eyes to detect. On the other hand, the forensics community keeps on developing methods to detect these generated fake images and try to guarantee the credibility of visual contents. Although researchers have developed some methods to detect generated images, few of them explore the important problem of generalization ability of forensics model. As new types of GANs are emerging fast, the generalization ability of forensics models to detect new types of GAN images is absolutely an essential research topic. In this paper, we explore this problem and propose to use preprocessed images to train a forensic CNN model. By applying similar image level preprocessing to both real and fake training images, the forensics model is forced to learn more intrinsic features to classify the generated and real face images. Our experimental results also prove the effectiveness of the proposed method.
generated_abstract: The rapid development of generative adversarial networks has made it possible to produce highly realistic face images and videos, creating new challenges for digital forensics, media authentication, and public trust. This paper reviews the principal techniques used to generate and detect deepfakes, with emphasis on face-swapping and facial reenactment systems. We examine detection methods based on visual artifacts, color inconsistencies, face warping, head-pose estimation, eye-blinking patterns, facial attributes, and learned spatial or temporal representations. We also discuss compact convolutional networks, recurrent models, forensic embeddings, and steganalysis-inspired approaches, together with the role of large-scale datasets such as FaceForensics in training and evaluation. Particular attention is given to the limited transferability of detectors trained on a single manipulation method and to performance degradation caused by compression, resolution changes, and previously unseen generation techniques. The review highlights the benefits of combining frame-level forensic cues with temporal information and domain-adaptive learning. Finally, it identifies open problems involving generalization, robustness against post-processing and adversarial manipulation, realistic benchmarking, and the development of reliable detection systems for real-world social media video.

original_abstract: In this study, the deep learning method named reading periodic table, which utilizes deep learning to read the periodic table and the laws of the elements, was extended. The method now also learns the periodicity behind the periodic table, that is, the left- and right-most columns are adjacent to one another behind the table with one row shifted at the learning representation level. While the original method handles the table as it is, the extended method treats the periodic table as if its two edges are connected. This is achieved using novel layers named periodic convolution layers, which can handle inputs having periodicity and may be applied to other problems related to computer vision, time series, and so on if the data possesses some periodicity. In the reading periodic table method, no input of any material feature or descriptor is required. We verified that the method is also applicable for estimating the band gap of materials other than superconductors, for which the method was originally applied. We demonstrated two types of deep learning estimation: methods to estimate the existence of a band gap and those to estimate the value of the band gap given that the materials were known to have one. Finally, we discuss the limitations of the dataset and model evaluation method. We may be unable to distinguish good models based on the random train--test split scheme; thus, we must prepare an appropriate dataset where the training and test data are temporally separate.
generated_abstract: The rapid growth of computational materials databases offers new opportunities for discovering materials with targeted electronic and physical properties. However, extracting useful structure–property relationships from heterogeneous chemical and crystallographic data remains challenging because materials are naturally represented by compositions, periodic structures, graphs, and text. Here we develop a data-driven framework that combines materials informatics with modern machine-learning methods, including ensemble models, graph neural networks, and attention-based deep networks. Using open resources such as the Materials Project, the Crystallography Open Database, and experimentally reported superconductors, we construct composition- and structure-aware representations for inorganic compounds. We evaluate the framework on representative prediction tasks, including superconducting transition temperatures, electronic band gaps, and classification of promising candidate materials. Systematic comparisons show how feature engineering, database quality, model architecture, and validation strategy affect predictive accuracy and generalization beyond the training set. Interpretable analyses identify chemically meaningful descriptors and reveal limitations caused by sparse, biased, and inconsistent data. Finally, we demonstrate how the trained models can be integrated into high-throughput screening pipelines to prioritize unexplored compounds for first-principles calculations and experimental synthesis. The results establish a practical route toward accelerated, reproducible, and data-guided materials discovery.

original_abstract: Online dating has become a common occurrence over the last few decades. A key challenge for online dating platforms is to determine suitable matches for their users. A lot of dating services rely on self-reported user traits and preferences for matching. At the same time, some services largely rely on user images and thus initial visual preference. Especially for the latter approach, previous research has attempted to capture users' visual preferences for automatic match recommendation. These approaches are mostly based on the assumption that physical attraction is the key factor for relationship formation and personal preferences, interests, and attitude are largely neglected. Deep learning approaches have shown that a variety of properties can be predicted from human faces to some degree, including age, health and even personality traits. Therefore, we investigate the feasibility of bridging image-based matching and matching with personal interests, preferences, and attitude. We approach the problem in a supervised manner by predicting similarity scores between two users based on images of their faces only. The ground-truth for the similarity matching scores is determined by a test that aims to capture users' preferences, interests, and attitude that are relevant for forming romantic relationships. The images are processed by a Siamese Multi-Task deep learning architecture. We find a statistically significant correlation between predicted and target similarity scores. Thus, our results indicate that learning similarities in terms of interests, preferences, and attitude from face images appears to be feasible to some degree.
generated_abstract: We present a deep multi-task learning framework for personalized analysis and recommendation of faces in online dating. The system combines fast face detection with convolutional representations learned from complementary visual tasks, including landmark localization, age estimation, gender recognition, facial attractiveness, and other appearance-related attributes. Shared and task-specific features are learned jointly through adaptive cross-task connections, enabling the model to exploit common structure while preserving information specific to each prediction. Residual and densely connected architectures, together with Adam optimization and noise-robust gradient visualization, support efficient end-to-end training on large, heterogeneous image collections. Beyond estimating population-level attributes, we incorporate interaction-based collaborative filtering to model the two-sided nature of dating preferences: a recommendation is useful only when both users are likely to respond positively. Visual features therefore provide predictions for users with little or no rating history, while learned interaction models personalize rankings as feedback accumulates. Experiments on dating-site images and established face-analysis benchmarks show that the proposed approach improves attribute prediction and personalized match recommendation over conventional convolutional and collaborative-filtering baselines. The results demonstrate the potential of combining interpretable facial analysis with preference learning for scalable, individualized online dating services.

original_abstract: In recent years, reinforcement learning has been successful in solving video games from Atari to Star Craft II. However, the end-to-end model-free reinforcement learning (RL) is not sample efficient and requires a significant amount of computational resources to achieve superhuman level performance. Model-free RL is also unlikely to produce human-like agents for playtesting and gameplaying AI in the development cycle of complex video games. In this paper, we present a hierarchical approach to training agents with the goal of achieving human-like style and high skill level in team sports games. While this is still work in progress, our preliminary results show that the presented approach holds promise for solving the posed multi-agent learning problem.
generated_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has enabled substantial progress in sequential decision making by combining representation learning with reinforcement learning. This paper reviews the development of modern DRL methods and their application to increasingly complex environments. We organize existing approaches around several central themes: value-based and policy-based learning, experience replay and distributional estimation, exploration, imitation and inverse reinforcement learning, temporal abstraction, and hierarchical control. We then examine the additional difficulties introduced by multiple interacting agents, including non-stationarity, decentralized execution, coordination, and credit assignment, and discuss representative solutions based on centralized critics, value factorization, counterfactual reasoning, and opponent modeling. Applications spanning video games, robotics, simulated characters, and human-like game agents illustrate both the capabilities and limitations of current systems. Particular attention is given to sample efficiency, sparse and delayed rewards, safety, transfer from simulation, demonstrations, and the computational cost of large-scale training. We conclude by identifying open challenges in generalization, interpretability, robust exploration, multi-agent adaptation, and the integration of planning, structured prior knowledge, and learned representations toward reliable agents that can operate beyond narrowly designed benchmarks.

original_abstract: We introduce and study the problem of Online Continual Compression, where one attempts to learn to compress and store a representative dataset from a non i.i.d data stream, while only observing each sample once. This problem is highly relevant for downstream online continual learning tasks, as well as standard learning methods under resource constrained data collection. To address this we propose a new architecture which Stacks Quantization Modules (SQM), consisting of a series of discrete autoencoders, each equipped with their own memory. Every added module is trained to reconstruct the latent space of the previous module using fewer bits, allowing the learned representation to become more compact as training progresses. This modularity has several advantages: 1) moderate compressions are quickly available early in training, which is crucial for remembering the early tasks, 2) as more data needs to be stored, earlier data becomes more compressed, freeing memory, 3) unlike previous methods, our approach does not require pretraining, even on challenging datasets. We show several potential applications of this method. We first replace the episodic memory used in Experience Replay with SQM, leading to significant gains on standard continual learning benchmarks using a fixed memory budget. We then apply our method to online compression of larger images like those from Imagenet, and show that it is also effective with other modalities, such as LiDAR data.
generated_abstract: Continual learning enables intelligent systems to acquire new capabilities over time without losing previously learned knowledge. This paper investigates lifelong learning for generative models under a realistic setting in which data distributions arrive sequentially and previously observed data cannot be stored. We propose a unified framework that combines compact latent representations, generative replay, and knowledge distillation to preserve prior distributions while adapting to new ones. The model uses a learned discrete representation to encode structured observations, allowing replay to occur in a low-dimensional latent space rather than in the original signal domain. This design reduces memory and computational requirements and supports efficient generation and downstream inference. We evaluate the approach on sequential image and LiDAR-generation tasks, including settings with noisy and incomplete observations. Results show that the proposed method substantially mitigates catastrophic forgetting while maintaining competitive sample quality and reconstruction accuracy as new tasks are introduced. Compared with rehearsal, regularization, and fine-tuning baselines, latent generative replay provides a better balance between retention, adaptation, and resource usage. The findings demonstrate that learned compression and generative modeling offer a practical foundation for lifelong perception in autonomous and resource-constrained systems.

original_abstract: Intrusion detection systems (IDSs) play an important role in identifying malicious attacks and threats in networking systems. As fundamental tools of IDSs, learning based classification methods have been widely employed. When it comes to detecting network intrusions in small sample sizes (e.g., emerging intrusions), the limited number and imbalanced proportion of training samples usually cause significant challenges in training supervised and semi-supervised classifiers. In this paper, we propose a general network intrusion detection framework to address the challenges of both \emph{data scarcity} and \emph{data imbalance}. The novelty of the proposed framework focuses on incorporating deep adversarial learning with statistical learning and exploiting learning based data augmentation. Given a small set of network intrusion samples, it first derives a Poisson-Gamma joint probabilistic generative model to generate synthesised intrusion data using Monte Carlo methods. Those synthesised data are then augmented by deep generative neural networks through adversarial learning. Finally, it adopts the augmented intrusion data to train supervised models for detecting network intrusions. Comprehensive experimental validations on KDD Cup 99 dataset show that the proposed framework outperforms the existing learning based IDSs in terms of improved accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.
generated_abstract: Network intrusion detection systems must identify diverse and previously unseen attacks while maintaining a low false-alarm rate in complex and imbalanced traffic environments. This paper presents a deep learning framework for network intrusion detection that combines traffic preprocessing, learned feature extraction, and supervised classification. Network records are transformed into structured representations suitable for convolutional learning, enabling the model to capture local and hierarchical relationships among traffic attributes. A deep residual architecture is employed to improve optimization and support effective representation learning, while adaptive stochastic optimization is used for efficient training. To address class imbalance and limited examples of rare attacks, adversarial generative modeling is investigated as a means of producing additional representative samples. The proposed approach is evaluated on benchmark intrusion-detection traffic, including NSL-KDD, using accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, detection rate, and false-alarm rate. Results show that the deep model provides competitive or improved performance over conventional machine-learning methods, including random forests, and remains effective when traffic contains unfamiliar or sparsely represented attack categories. The findings demonstrate the potential of residual and generative deep learning techniques for robust, flexible, and scalable intrusion detection.

original_abstract: This paper presents an overview of the evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods, followed by a discussion of several benchmarks and papers evaluating such local features. Our investigations are motivated by 3D reconstruction problems, where the precise location of the features is important. As we describe these methods, we highlight and explain the challenges of feature extraction and potential ways to overcome them. We first present handcrafted methods, followed by methods based on classical machine learning and finally we discuss methods based on deep-learning. This largely chronologically-ordered presentation will help the reader to fully understand the topic of image and region description in order to make best use of it in modern computer vision applications. In particular, understanding handcrafted methods and their motivation can help to understand modern approaches and how machine learning is used to improve the results. We also provide references to most of the relevant literature and code.
generated_abstract: We present R2D2, a fully convolutional network that jointly detects repeatable keypoints and computes reliable local descriptors for image matching. Existing learned approaches often optimize detector repeatability or descriptor discriminativeness separately, and may produce many points that are individually ambiguous or unstable under viewpoint and illumination changes. Our method introduces two complementary confidence measures: repeatability, which favors points that can be consistently detected across transformed views, and reliability, which identifies descriptors that are distinctive relative to nearby alternatives. These measures are learned from image pairs using differentiable objectives, while multi-scale feature extraction provides robustness to changes in image resolution and viewpoint. At inference time, the two confidence maps guide the selection of a sparse set of high-quality features, avoiding extensive non-maximum suppression and expensive pairwise evaluation. We evaluate the resulting detector and descriptor on standard local feature benchmarks and downstream geometric matching tasks, including homography estimation and visual localization. Experiments show that R2D2 substantially improves the quality and stability of correspondences over handcrafted and learned alternatives, particularly in challenging wide-baseline conditions, while retaining efficient fully convolutional computation.

original_abstract: Cyberphysical systems (CPS) are ubiquitous in our personal and professional lives, and they promise to dramatically improve micro-communities (e.g., urban farms, hospitals), macro-communities (e.g., cities and metropolises), urban structures (e.g., smart homes and cars), and living structures (e.g., human bodies, synthetic genomes). The question that we address in this article pertains to designing these CPS systems to be resilient-from-the-ground-up, and through progressive learning, resilient-by-reaction. An optimally designed system is resilient to both unique attacks and recurrent attacks, the latter with a lower overhead. Overall, the notion of resilience can be thought of in the light of three main sources of lack of resilience, as follows: exogenous factors, such as natural variations and attack scenarios; mismatch between engineered designs and exogenous factors ranging from DDoS (distributed denial-of-service) attacks or other cybersecurity nightmares, so called "black swan" events, disabling critical services of the municipal electrical grids and other connected infrastructures, data breaches, and network failures; and the fragility of engineered designs themselves encompassing bugs, human-computer interactions (HCI), and the overall complexity of real-world systems. In the paper, our focus is on design and deployment innovations that are broadly applicable across a range of CPS application areas.
generated_abstract: The increasing use of neural networks in autonomous vehicles, cyber-physical systems, distributed infrastructures, and scientific workflows creates an urgent need for methods that are not only accurate, but also safe, robust, efficient, and interpretable. This paper surveys recent approaches for establishing trustworthiness in learning-enabled systems. We organize existing work around four complementary challenges: robustness to adversarial and accidental perturbations, formal verification of neural networks and their closed-loop interaction with dynamical systems, resilience to strategic or Byzantine agents, and efficient deployment on resource-constrained hardware. We compare exact solver-based techniques with scalable over-approximation methods based on intervals, abstract interpretation, convex and semidefinite relaxations, Lipschitz and Jacobian bounds, and set-based reachability.
