We also review simulation-based, stochastic, and data-driven verification, including compositional reasoning for complex hybrid systems. Beyond verification, we discuss platform-aware model adaptation, energy-efficient inference, interpretable modeling, and game-theoretic security. The synthesis identifies persistent trade-offs among soundness, precision, computational cost, and scalability, and highlights opportunities for integrating certification, active testing, adaptive training, and resilient control into unified end-to-end assurance frameworks.

original_abstract: Recent developments in neural language models (LMs) have raised concerns about their potential misuse for automatically spreading misinformation. In light of these concerns, several studies have proposed to detect machine-generated fake news by capturing their stylistic differences from human-written text. These approaches, broadly termed stylometry, have found success in source attribution and misinformation detection in human-written texts. However, in this work, we show that stylometry is limited against machine-generated misinformation. While humans speak differently when trying to deceive, LMs generate stylistically consistent text, regardless of underlying motive. Thus, though stylometry can successfully prevent impersonation by identifying text provenance, it fails to distinguish legitimate LM applications from those that introduce false information. We create two benchmarks demonstrating the stylistic similarity between malicious and legitimate uses of LMs, employed in auto-completion and editing-assistance settings. Our findings highlight the need for non-stylometry approaches in detecting machine-generated misinformation, and open up the discussion on the desired evaluation benchmarks.
generated_abstract: The rapid spread of fabricated news and machine-generated text has created an urgent need for reliable, interpretable detection methods. This paper presents a unified framework for identifying misleading online content by combining textual, stylistic, source, and propagation-based evidence. We evaluate the approach on several publicly available datasets covering short political claims, news articles, social-media posts, rumours, and fact-checking examples. A Transformer-based encoder captures semantic information, while complementary features model linguistic deception, partisan style, source credibility, user interactions, and early propagation patterns. For claims requiring external validation, the system retrieves relevant evidence and jointly estimates stance and veracity, producing explanations based on influential passages and sources. Experiments show that combining heterogeneous signals consistently outperforms text-only and claim-only baselines, particularly for minority classes and emerging claims with limited evidence. We further examine robustness to domain shift, adversarial paraphrasing, and automatically generated text, finding that performance declines when models rely on dataset-specific cues. The results emphasize the importance of evidence-aware evaluation, debiasing, and transparent predictions, and provide practical guidance for developing fact-checking tools that support, rather than replace, human judgment.

original_abstract: Mesh models are a promising approach for encoding the structure of 3D objects. Current mesh reconstruction systems predict uniformly distributed vertex locations of a predetermined graph through a series of graph convolutions, leading to compromises with respect to performance or resolution. In this paper, we argue that the graph representation of geometric objects allows for additional structure, which should be leveraged for enhanced reconstruction. Thus, we propose a system which properly benefits from the advantages of the geometric structure of graph encoded objects by introducing (1) a graph convolutional update preserving vertex information; (2) an adaptive splitting heuristic allowing detail to emerge; and (3) a training objective operating both on the local surfaces defined by vertices as well as the global structure defined by the mesh. Our proposed method is evaluated on the task of 3D object reconstruction from images with the ShapeNet dataset, where we demonstrate state of the art performance, both visually and numerically, while having far smaller space requirements by generating adaptive meshes
generated_abstract: We present Mesh R-CNN, an end-to-end framework for reconstructing three-dimensional object meshes from a single RGB image. Our model extends the successful Mask R-CNN architecture with a 3D shape prediction branch that estimates a coarse voxel representation for each detected object. A graph convolutional mesh refinement network then converts this representation into a compact triangular mesh and progressively improves its geometry. The combination of image features, instance masks, volumetric reasoning, and mesh-based refinement enables the system to recover both object structure and fine surface details while preserving the efficiency of modern two-dimensional detection systems. We train the model using synthetic and real image–shape pairs and evaluate it on ShapeNet and the Pix3D benchmark, which provides pixel-aligned images and CAD models. Experiments demonstrate substantial improvements over voxel- and point-cloud-based approaches in reconstruction quality, particularly at higher resolutions. The resulting meshes are directly usable for downstream graphics and vision applications, including visualization, interaction, pose estimation, and scene understanding. Mesh R-CNN establishes a practical bridge between instance-level image recognition and detailed 3D geometric reconstruction.

original_abstract: Data science is labor-intensive and human experts are scarce but heavily involved in every aspect of it. This makes data science time consuming and restricted to experts with the resulting quality heavily dependent on their experience and skills. To make data science more accessible and scalable, we need its democratization. Automated Data Science (AutoDS) is aimed towards that goal and is emerging as an important research and business topic. We introduce and define the AutoDS challenge, followed by a proposal of a general AutoDS framework that covers existing approaches but also provides guidance for the development of new methods. We categorize and review the existing literature from multiple aspects of the problem setup and employed techniques. Then we provide several views on how AI could succeed in automating end-to-end AutoDS. We hope this survey can serve as insightful guideline for the AutoDS field and provide inspiration for future research.
generated_abstract: We present a general framework for cognitive automation of data science that learns to construct, configure, and improve machine learning workflows with minimal human intervention. The system represents a workflow as a sequence of data preparation, feature engineering, model, architecture, and optimization choices, and uses meta-learning to transfer experience across related tasks. A contextual bandit controller selects actions based on dataset characteristics, historical performance, computational resources, and user-specified constraints. This formulation supports both exploration of unfamiliar workflows and exploitation of previously successful configurations, while accommodating nonstationary feedback and restricted observations. To reduce the cost of evaluation, the framework reuses representations, parameters, and partial training results through function-preserving transformations and multi-fidelity performance estimates. Its objective is multi-objective: predictive quality is balanced against latency, memory, energy consumption, interpretability, and behavioral requirements. We discuss how differentiable, evolutionary, reinforcement-learning, and Bayesian optimization methods can be integrated within this framework, and how learned constraints can guide online decisions without suppressing useful exploration. Experiments across image, language, relational, and online decision tasks show that automated workflow construction can approach or exceed expert-designed solutions while substantially reducing computational effort and manual engineering.

original_abstract: Real-noise denoising is a challenging task because the statistics of real-noise do not follow the normal distribution, and they are also spatially and temporally changing. In order to cope with various and complex real-noise, we propose a well-generalized denoising architecture and a transfer learning scheme. Specifically, we adopt an adaptive instance normalization to build a denoiser, which can regularize the feature map and prevent the network from overfitting to the training set. We also introduce a transfer learning scheme that transfers knowledge learned from synthetic-noise data to the real-noise denoiser. From the proposed transfer learning, the synthetic-noise denoiser can learn general features from various synthetic-noise data, and the real-noise denoiser can learn the real-noise characteristics from real data. From the experiments, we find that the proposed denoising method has great generalization ability, such that our network trained with synthetic-noise achieves the best performance for Darmstadt Noise Dataset (DND) among the methods from published papers. We can also see that the proposed transfer learning scheme robustly works for real-noise images through the learning with a very small number of labeled data.
generated_abstract: Real-world image denoising is challenging because sensor noise depends on illumination, camera characteristics, signal intensity, and in-camera processing, while most learning-based methods are trained using simplified synthetic noise models. We present a deep convolutional network for blind real-image denoising that adapts its feature representations to the input noise characteristics. The proposed architecture combines residual learning with adaptive normalization and attention mechanisms, enabling the network to estimate and exploit spatially varying noise without requiring a separately trained model for each camera or noise level. To improve generalization, we construct realistic training data using signal-dependent noise models, camera pipeline simulation, and real noisy-clean image pairs. The method can operate on raw and processed color images and is designed for efficient inference. Extensive experiments on established real-noise benchmarks, including DND, SIDD, and challenge datasets, show that the proposed approach consistently improves both quantitative measures and perceptual quality over conventional CNN denoisers and representative model-based methods. It recovers fine structures and natural textures while suppressing chromatic noise and avoiding excessive smoothing, demonstrating the effectiveness of adaptive feature modulation for practical photographic restoration.

original_abstract: Fine-tuning a deep network trained with the standard cross-entropy loss is a strong baseline for few-shot learning. When fine-tuned transductively, this outperforms the current state-of-the-art on standard datasets such as Mini-Imagenet, Tiered-Imagenet, CIFAR-FS and FC-100 with the same hyper-parameters. The simplicity of this approach enables us to demonstrate the first few-shot learning results on the Imagenet-21k dataset. We find that using a large number of meta-training classes results in high few-shot accuracies even for a large number of test classes. We do not advocate our approach as the solution for few-shot learning, but simply use the results to highlight limitations of current benchmarks and few-shot protocols. We perform extensive studies on benchmark datasets to propose a metric that quantifies the "hardness" of a test episode. This metric can be used to report the performance of few-shot algorithms in a more systematic way.
generated_abstract: We study few-shot online signature verification, where a verifier must recognize a writer from only a small number of genuine signatures while rejecting skilled and random forgeries. This setting is challenging because signatures vary substantially within a writer, data are highly imbalanced, and new writers are unavailable during training. We formulate verification as episodic task learning and train a deep embedding network to produce writer-discriminative representations that can be adapted rapidly to previously unseen users. We investigate metric-based, prototype-based, and gradient-based adaptation strategies, together with cosine classification, proxy representations, data augmentation, mixup, and semi-supervised consistency regularization. The resulting system compares a query signature with a support set of genuine examples and requires no writer-specific retraining at enrollment. Experiments on an online signature dataset demonstrate that episodic representation learning substantially improves over conventional writer-independent and writer-dependent baselines, particularly in the one- and few-shot regimes. Incorporating multiple enrollment signatures and task-adaptive metrics further improves robustness to intra-writer variation. The results show that modern few-shot learning methods can provide accurate, efficient, and scalable authentication while preserving strong performance when only limited genuine enrollment data are available.

original_abstract: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples - small input perturbations that result in incorrect predictions. We study this problem in the context of models of source code, where we want the network to be robust to source-code modifications that preserve code functionality. We define a natural notion of robustness, $k$-transformation robustness, in which an adversary performs up to $k$ semantics-preserving transformations to an input program. We show how to train robust models using an adversarial training objective inspired by that of Madry et al. (2018) for continuous domains. #R##N#We implement an extensible framework for adversarial training over source code, and conduct a thorough evaluation on a number of datasets and two different architectures. Our results show (1) the increase in robustness following adversarial training, (2) the ability of training on weak adversaries to provide robustness to attacks by stronger adversaries, and (3) the shift in attribution focus of adversarially trained models towards semantic vs. syntactic features.
generated_abstract: Neural models are increasingly used to analyze and generate source code, yet their robustness to small, semantics-preserving changes remains poorly understood. We present a systematic study of adversarial attacks against code-processing models and evaluate how effectively existing defenses improve reliability. Our approach generates program variants through transformations such as identifier renaming, insertion of dead code, statement reordering, and equivalent syntactic rewrites, while preserving compilation and runtime behavior. We investigate both white-box and black-box settings, including gradient-guided manipulation, query-based search, and stochastic sampling, across models for method-name prediction, functionality classification, type inference, and code summarization. Experiments on Java and Python datasets show that models often depend on superficial lexical cues and can be misled by a small number of localized changes, even when their clean accuracy is high. Adversarial training and representation refinement substantially improve resistance, but may reduce performance on unmodified programs and do not generalize uniformly across transformations. We further use attribution analysis and controlled ablations to identify the program features responsible for brittle predictions. Our results motivate robustness benchmarks and demonstrate that semantic preservation, diverse attacks, and evaluation beyond nominal accuracy are essential for trustworthy machine learning on code.

original_abstract: While stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and variants have been surprisingly successful for training deep nets, several aspects of the optimization dynamics and generalization are still not well understood. In this paper, we present new empirical observations and theoretical results on both the optimization dynamics and generalization behavior of SGD for deep nets based on the Hessian of the training loss and associated quantities. We consider three specific research questions: (1) what is the relationship between the Hessian of the loss and the second moment of stochastic gradients (SGs)? (2) how can we characterize the stochastic optimization dynamics of SGD with fixed and adaptive step sizes and diagonal pre-conditioning based on the first and second moments of SGs? and (3) how can we characterize a scale-invariant generalization bound of deep nets based on the Hessian of the loss, which by itself is not scale invariant? We shed light on these three questions using theoretical results supported by extensive empirical observations, with experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10, with different batch sizes, and with different difficulty levels by synthetically adding random labels.
generated_abstract: We investigate how stochastic gradient descent (SGD) interacts with the sharpest directions of the loss landscape in overparameterized neural networks. Although large learning rates and small batches are often associated with flatter, better-generalizing solutions, the dynamics that produce this behavior remain poorly understood. Through experiments on several architectures and datasets, we show that during the initial phase of training SGD moves toward increasingly sharp regions, until the maximum curvature is constrained by the learning rate and batch size. In the leading Hessian eigenspaces, the SGD update is frequently too large to minimize the loss locally, causing the iterates to overshoot along the sharpest directions. This behavior explains why the curvature encountered along the optimization trajectory differs from the curvature at the final solution. We further demonstrate that selectively reducing the learning rate in these directions can accelerate optimization while producing solutions that are both sharper and better generalizing than those obtained with standard SGD. Our results indicate that the sharpest eigenspaces play a central role in determining training speed, the regions visited by SGD, and the eventual generalization properties of deep networks.

original_abstract: Designing a lightweight semantic segmentation network often requires researchers to find a trade-off between performance and speed, which is always empirical due to the limited interpretability of neural networks. In order to release researchers from these tedious mechanical trials, we propose a Graph-guided Architecture Search (GAS) pipeline to automatically search real-time semantic segmentation networks. Unlike previous works that use a simplified search space and stack a repeatable cell to form a network, we introduce a novel search mechanism with new search space where a lightweight model can be effectively explored through the cell-level diversity and latencyoriented constraint. Specifically, to produce the cell-level diversity, the cell-sharing constraint is eliminated through the cell-independent manner. Then a graph convolution network (GCN) is seamlessly integrated as a communication mechanism between cells. Finally, a latency-oriented constraint is endowed into the search process to balance the speed and performance. Extensive experiments on Cityscapes and CamVid datasets demonstrate that GAS achieves new state-of-the-art trade-off between accuracy and speed. In particular, on Cityscapes dataset, GAS achieves the new best performance of 73.3% mIoU with speed of 102 FPS on Titan Xp.
generated_abstract: Semantic segmentation is essential for autonomous driving and mobile vision, yet achieving accurate pixel-level predictions under strict latency and memory constraints remains difficult. Existing architectures typically rely on manually designed encoder–decoder structures, multi-scale fusion schemes, and upsampling modules, while neural architecture search methods developed for image classification do not directly address the high resolution and multi-scale nature of dense prediction. We present an efficient task- and hardware-aware architecture search framework for semantic segmentation. Our method jointly searches the cell operations, feature-resolution pathways, and multi-scale fusion strategy using a differentiable relaxation of discrete architectural decisions. Resource costs, including computation, parameter count, and measured inference latency, are incorporated into the optimization objective, enabling models to be customized for different deployment platforms. To reduce search expense, candidate operations share weights and weak connections are progressively annealed and pruned during training. Experiments on Cityscapes, CamVid, and PASCAL VOC demonstrate that the searched networks achieve competitive or superior mean intersection-over-union while substantially reducing computation and memory use. The resulting models provide real-time inference on high-resolution images, illustrating that automated search can discover compact segmentation architectures that offer a more favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off than both handcrafted and transferred classification networks.

original_abstract: We introduce PlatonicGAN to discover the 3D structure of an object class from an unstructured collection of 2D images, i.e., where no relation between photos is known, except that they are showing instances of the same category. The key idea is to train a deep neural network to generate 3D shapes which, when rendered to images, are indistinguishable from ground truth images (for a discriminator) under various camera poses. Discriminating 2D images instead of 3D shapes allows tapping into unstructured 2D photo collections instead of relying on curated (e.g., aligned, annotated, etc.) 3D data sets. To establish constraints between 2D image observation and their 3D interpretation, we suggest a family of rendering layers that are effectively differentiable. This family includes visual hull, absorption-only (akin to x-ray), and emission-absorption. We can successfully reconstruct 3D shapes from unstructured 2D images and extensively evaluate PlatonicGAN on a range of synthetic and real data sets achieving consistent improvements over baseline methods. We further show that PlatonicGAN can be combined with 3D supervision to improve on and in some cases even surpass the quality of 3D-supervised methods.
generated_abstract: Reconstructing complete three-dimensional objects from a single image is fundamentally ambiguous, yet it is essential for visual understanding, robotics, and interaction. This paper presents a learning-based framework that combines image evidence with category-level shape priors to infer plausible object geometry, viewpoint, and appearance. Rather than relying exclusively on expensive 3D annotations, the model is trained using synthetic shapes and differentiable projections, allowing silhouettes, depth cues, and multi-view consistency to provide supervision from ordinary images. A coarse volumetric representation captures global structure, while a refinement module recovers fine details and produces a compact surface representation suitable for rendering and downstream applications. To address uncertainty caused by occlusion and unknown viewpoints, the framework can generate multiple geometrically consistent reconstructions instead of a single deterministic estimate. We evaluate the approach on ShapeNet and real-world image datasets, comparing voxel, point-cloud, and mesh outputs using reconstruction accuracy, visual consistency, and generalization to unseen categories. Results demonstrate substantial improvements over existing single-view methods, particularly for occluded regions and novel object instances, while qualitative experiments show that the recovered shapes support novel-view synthesis, shape completion, and robotic grasp planning.

original_abstract: State of the art visual relation detection methods have been relying on features extracted from RGB images including objects' 2D positions. In this paper, we argue that the 3D positions of objects in space can provide additional valuable information about object relations. This information helps not only to detect spatial relations, such as "standing behind", but also non-spatial relations, such as "holding". Since 3D information of a scene is not easily accessible, we propose incorporating a pre-trained RGB-to-Depth model within visual relation detection frameworks. We discuss different feature extraction strategies from depth maps and show their critical role in relation detection. Our experiments confirm that the performance of state-of-the-art visual relation detection approaches can significantly be improved by utilizing depth map information.
generated_abstract: Visual relationship detection aims to represent an image as a set of subject–predicate–object triplets, but its performance is limited by ambiguous visual evidence, highly imbalanced relationships, and the combinatorial size of the label space. We present a unified framework that combines visual scene understanding with relational representation learning. A deep object detector first identifies candidate entities, while multimodal features derived from RGB appearance, spatial configuration, and monocular depth estimate the geometry of object pairs. Relations are modeled in a learned embedding space, where translation- and bilinear-style interactions capture semantic compatibility between subjects, predicates, and objects. To improve generalization to rare and unseen triplets, the visual model is regularized with linguistic priors and graph-structured context, including higher-order motifs and information propagated between neighboring objects and relations. The model is trained end to end with adaptive stochastic optimization and evaluated on Visual Relationship and Visual Genome benchmarks. Experiments show consistent improvements over appearance-only and independently classified baselines, particularly for long-tail and zero-shot relations. The results demonstrate that combining depth cues, contextual message passing, and knowledge-graph-inspired embeddings yields more accurate and coherent scene graphs.

original_abstract: Research communications often introduce biases or misrepresentations without providing reliable links to the research they use so readers can check the veracity of the claims being made. We tested the feasibility of a tool that can be used to automatically recommend research articles to research communications. From 207,538 vaccination-related PubMed articles, we selected 3,573 unique links to webpages using Altmetric. We tested a method for ranking research articles relative to each webpage using a canonical correlation analysis (CCA) approach. Outcome measures were the median rank of the correct source article; the percentage of webpages for which the source article was correctly ranked first; and the percentage ranked within the top 50 candidate articles. The best of the baseline approaches ranked the matching source article first for more a quarter of webpages; and within the top 50 for more than half. Augmenting baseline methods with CCA improved results but failed when added to some of the baseline approaches. The best CCA-based approach ranked the matching source articles first for 14%; and in the top 50 for 38%. Tools to help people identify source articles for vaccination-related research communications are potentially feasible and may support the prevention of bias and misrepresentation of research in news and social media.
generated_abstract: Clinical trial registries and bibliographic databases are increasingly used to assess selective reporting, yet many trial registrations remain unlinked to their corresponding publications. We developed and evaluated an automated natural language processing system for identifying likely links between ClinicalTrials.gov registrations and PubMed articles. The system combined distributed word and phrase representations with contextualized language-model embeddings and transfer learning for text classification and document similarity ranking. We trained and evaluated models using reported registration–publication links, supplemented by manually verified unreported links, and compared their performance with conventional term- and concept-based similarity methods. Models using pretrained language representations captured complementary information about trial design, interventions, conditions, and outcomes, and ranked candidate publications more effectively than approaches based solely on exact terminology. In particular, contextual and fine-tuned representations improved retrieval when registrations and articles used different terminology or described the same intervention at different levels of specificity. The resulting system can prioritize a small set of candidate articles for human screening, reducing the effort required to recover missing links. Automated linkage offers a scalable approach for improving registry completeness, supporting evidence synthesis, and monitoring potential reporting biases across large clinical trial corpora.

original_abstract: This work presents a neural network that consists of nodes with heterogeneous sensitivity. Each node in a network is assigned a variable that determines the sensitivity with which it learns to perform a given task. The network is trained by a constrained optimization that maximizes the sparsity of the sensitivity variables while ensuring the network's performance. As a result, the network learns to perform a given task using only a small number of sensitive nodes. Insensitive nodes, the nodes with zero sensitivity, can be removed from a trained network to obtain a computationally efficient network. Removing zero-sensitivity nodes has no effect on the network's performance because the network has already been trained to perform the task without them. The regularization parameter used to solve the optimization problem is found simultaneously during the training of networks. To validate our approach, we design networks with computationally efficient architectures for various tasks such as autoregression, object recognition, facial expression recognition, and object detection using various datasets. In our experiments, the networks designed by the proposed method provide the same or higher performance but with far less computational complexity.
generated_abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks provide strong performance for image recognition and object detection, but their computational and memory requirements limit deployment on embedded and edge devices. We present a practical framework for compressing pretrained networks through structured pruning of redundant filters and channels. The method evaluates feature importance using activation statistics and discriminative information, identifies highly correlated or low-contribution features, and removes corresponding filters together with their dependent feature maps. Principal component analysis is used to characterize feature redundancy, while a reconstruction and fine-tuning stage compensates for the information lost during pruning. Unlike unstructured weight pruning, the resulting compact models retain dense, hardware-friendly layers and can therefore be accelerated using standard deep-learning libraries. We evaluate the approach on representative VGG, residual, and real-time detection architectures using CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and object-detection benchmarks. The experiments show substantial reductions in parameters, floating-point operations, memory consumption, and inference latency, with only minor degradation in recognition accuracy. The results demonstrate that combining redundancy analysis, structured channel removal, and retraining offers an effective route to deploying accurate deep networks on resource-constrained platforms.

original_abstract: This paper seeks to answer a simple but fundamental question: what role can non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) play in massive multi-in multi-out (MIMO)? It is well established that power-domain NOMA schemes can outperform conventional orthogonal multiple access schemes in cellular networks. However, this fact does not imply that NOMA is the most efficient way to communicate in massive MIMO setups, where the base stations have many more antennas than there are users in the cell. These setups are becoming the norm in future networks and are usually studied by assuming spatial multiplexing of the users using linear multi-user beamforming. To answer the above-mentioned question, we analyze and compare the performance achieved by NOMA and multi-user beamforming in both non-line-of-sight and line-of-sight scenarios. We reveal that the latter scheme gives the highest average sum rate in massive MIMO setups. We also identify specific cases where NOMA is the better choice in massive MIMO and explain how NOMA plays an essential role in creating a hybrid of NOMA and multi-user beamforming that is shown to perform better than two standalone schemes do.
generated_abstract: Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) and massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) are promising technologies for supporting the diverse requirements of fifth-generation and beyond wireless networks. This paper investigates their integration and develops a practical massive-MIMO-NOMA transmission framework for multiuser downlink communication. Users are grouped according to channel conditions, while the base station employs matched-filter or zero-forcing processing to create spatial beams and superposes the signals of users within each group. Achievable ergodic-rate expressions are derived under realistic channel conditions, including imperfect channel state information, finite coherence intervals, and the possible absence of strong channel hardening. The analysis also examines the effects of favorable propagation, pilot reuse, power allocation, and successive interference cancellation on system performance. Based on these results, a low-complexity joint user-grouping and power-allocation strategy is proposed, and the need for downlink pilots is discussed through blind effective-channel estimation. Numerical results show that massive MIMO substantially suppresses intergroup interference, enabling NOMA to improve spectral efficiency and user fairness over orthogonal access, particularly when users have markedly different channel gains. The results also identify operating regimes in which conventional multiuser beamforming is preferable to NOMA.

original_abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for robotics is challenging due to the difficulty in hand-engineering a dense cost function, which can lead to unintended behavior, and dynamical uncertainty, which makes it hard to enforce constraints during learning. We address these issues with a new model-based reinforcement learning algorithm, safety augmented value estimation from demonstrations (SAVED), which uses supervision that only identifies task completion and a modest set of suboptimal demonstrations to constrain exploration and learn efficiently while handling complex constraints. We derive iterative improvement guarantees for SAVED under known stochastic nonlinear systems. We then compare SAVED with 3 state-of-the-art model-based and model-free RL algorithms on 6 standard simulation benchmarks involving navigation and manipulation and 2 real-world tasks on the da Vinci surgical robot. Results suggest that SAVED outperforms prior methods in terms of success rate, constraint satisfaction, and sample efficiency, making it feasible to safely learn complex maneuvers directly on a real robot in less than an hour. For tasks on the robot, baselines succeed less than 5% of the time while SAVED has a success rate of over 75% in the first 50 training iterations.
generated_abstract: We present a safe and sample-efficient framework for learning control policies in continuous, safety-critical environments. Prior demonstrations and experience from previous tasks are incorporated to reduce the need for costly trial-and-error, while uncertainty estimates are used to adapt the model online and identify regions in which predictions are reliable. A safe set and terminal value function preserve recursive feasibility and enable performance improvement over repeated executions. The resulting controller can transition from conservative model-based behavior to a higher-performing learned policy through constrained policy updates, without sacrificing safety during training. We evaluate the approach on simulated and real-world robotic manipulation, locomotion, and autonomous driving tasks involving sparse rewards, nonlinear dynamics, and changing operating conditions. Across experiments, the proposed method achieves substantially better sample efficiency than model-free baselines, improves over demonstrations and nominal controllers, and maintains constraint satisfaction throughout learning. These results indicate that combining predictive control, demonstrations, uncertainty-aware modeling, and reinforcement learning provides a practical route toward reliable autonomous skill acquisition.

original_abstract: This paper proposes the first model-free Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework to synthesise policies for unknown, and continuous-state Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), such that a given linear temporal property is satisfied. We convert the given property into a Limit Deterministic Buchi Automaton (LDBA), namely a finite-state machine expressing the property. Exploiting the structure of the LDBA, we shape a synchronous reward function on-the-fly, so that an RL algorithm can synthesise a policy resulting in traces that probabilistically satisfy the linear temporal property. This probability (certificate) is also calculated in parallel with policy learning when the state space of the MDP is finite: as such, the RL algorithm produces a policy that is certified with respect to the property. Under the assumption of finite state space, theoretical guarantees are provided on the convergence of the RL algorithm to an optimal policy, maximising the above probability. We also show that our method produces ''best available'' control policies when the logical property cannot be satisfied. In the general case of a continuous state space, we propose a neural network architecture for RL and we empirically show that the algorithm finds satisfying policies, if there exist such policies. The performance of the proposed framework is evaluated via a set of numerical examples and benchmarks, where we observe an improvement of one order of magnitude in the number of iterations required for the policy synthesis, compared to existing approaches whenever available.
generated_abstract: Reinforcement learning offers a flexible approach to control in complex and partially known environments, but unconstrained exploration can be inefficient and unsafe, especially when objectives are sparse, delayed, or history dependent. We present a formally guided reinforcement learning framework that combines temporal-logic specifications, automata-based reward representations, and model-free deep learning. High-level task and safety requirements are translated into finite-state monitors and synchronized with the environment, transforming non-Markovian objectives into Markovian learning problems while preserving their semantics. A permissive, shielded policy restricts exploration to actions that satisfy safety constraints, whereas reward shaping and temporal abstraction provide informative feedback for progress toward long-horizon goals. The framework supports unknown transition dynamics and can incorporate demonstrations to accelerate exploration without sacrificing policy improvement. We further integrate probabilistic verification to estimate satisfaction guarantees and identify violations during training and deployment. Experiments on navigation, robotic manipulation, and sparse-reward game environments show that the proposed approach learns effective policies with substantially fewer interactions than unconstrained baselines, while maintaining formal or statistical safety guarantees. The results demonstrate that combining symbolic structure with deep reinforcement learning improves sample efficiency, interpretability, and reliability in safety-critical sequential decision-making.

original_abstract: We present faster high-accuracy algorithms for computing $\ell_p$-norm minimizing flows. On a graph with $m$ edges, our algorithm can compute a $(1+1/\text{poly}(m))$-approximate unweighted $\ell_p$-norm minimizing flow with $pm^{1+\frac{1}{p-1}+o(1)}$ operations, for any $p \ge 2,$ giving the best bound for all $p\gtrsim 5.24.$ Combined with the algorithm from the work of Adil et al. (SODA '19), we can now compute such flows for any $2\le p\le m^{o(1)}$ in time at most $O(m^{1.24}).$ In comparison, the previous best running time was $\Omega(m^{1.33})$ for large constant $p.$ For $p\sim\delta^{-1}\log m,$ our algorithm computes a $(1+\delta)$-approximate maximum flow on undirected graphs using $m^{1+o(1)}\delta^{-1}$ operations, matching the current best bound, albeit only for unit-capacity graphs. #R##N#We also give an algorithm for solving general $\ell_{p}$-norm regression problems for large $p.$ Our algorithm makes $pm^{\frac{1}{3}+o(1)}\log^2(1/\varepsilon)$ calls to a linear solver. This gives the first high-accuracy algorithm for computing weighted $\ell_{p}$-norm minimizing flows that runs in time $o(m^{1.5})$ for some $p=m^{\Omega(1)}.$ #R##N#Our key technical contribution is to show that smoothed $\ell_p$-norm problems introduced by Adil et al., are interreducible for different values of $p.$ No such reduction is known for standard $\ell_p$-norm problems.
generated_abstract: We develop a unified algorithmic framework for efficiently solving a broad class of graph-structured convex optimization problems, including approximate maximum flow, minimum-cost and norm-minimizing flows, ℓp regression, matrix scaling, and related balancing problems. Our methods combine iterative refinement and homotopy schemes with adaptive preconditioning, accelerated coordinate descent, and nearly-linear-time solvers for Laplacian and symmetric diagonally dominant systems. A central contribution is a general reduction from nonlinear objectives to sequences of well-conditioned quadratic problems whose structure can be exploited through sparsification, tree routings, electrical flows, and oblivious routing. This yields nearly linear or input-sparsity-time algorithms over wide ranges of parameters, while preserving high accuracy. In particular, we obtain improved running times for undirected maximum flow and concurrent multicommodity flow, including bounds that are nearly linear in the number of edges, as well as faster algorithms for ℓp regression for constant p and for large-p flow objectives approaching ℓ∞ optimization. We also establish supporting tools for random spanning-tree generation, matrix scaling, and graph partitioning. These results demonstrate that techniques originally developed for Laplacian systems extend substantially beyond linear algebra to nonlinear and combinatorial optimization.

original_abstract: Although supervised learning based on a deep neural network has recently achieved substantial improvement on speech enhancement, the existing schemes have either of two critical issues: spectrum or metric mismatches. The spectrum mismatch is a well known issue that any spectrum modification after short-time Fourier transform (STFT), in general, cannot be fully recovered after inverse short-time Fourier transform (ISTFT). The metric mismatch is that a conventional mean square error (MSE) loss function is typically sub-optimal to maximize perceptual speech measure such as signal-to-distortion ratio (SDR), perceptual evaluation of speech quality (PESQ) and short-time objective intelligibility (STOI). This paper presents a new end-to-end denoising framework. First, the network optimization is performed on the time-domain signals after ISTFT to avoid the spectrum mismatch. Second, three loss functions based on SDR, PESQ and STOI are proposed to minimize the metric mismatch. The experimental result showed the proposed denoising scheme significantly improved SDR, PESQ and STOI performance over the existing methods.
generated_abstract: We propose Conv-TasNet, a fully convolutional time-domain audio separation network that directly estimates separated waveforms from a mixture, without relying on spectrograms or hand-designed time-frequency masks. The model consists of a learned encoder and decoder together with a separation module based on stacked temporal convolutional blocks. This architecture captures long-range temporal structure through dilated convolutions while maintaining low computational complexity and permitting highly parallelized training and inference. We investigate waveform-level training objectives and show that optimizing scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio provides an effective criterion for separating speech sources. Unlike conventional approaches that estimate masks in the spectral domain and must address phase reconstruction, Conv-TasNet learns an appropriate representation and synthesis procedure directly from data. Experiments on the WSJ0-2mix benchmark demonstrate substantial improvements over contemporary separation systems in signal quality, with a favorable balance between accuracy, model size, and runtime. The results establish time-domain representation learning as a compelling alternative to magnitude-spectrum processing and suggest that end-to-end waveform modeling can overcome important limitations of traditional supervised speech separation methods.

original_abstract: In this paper we study the problem of correlation clustering under fairness constraints. In the classic correlation clustering problem, we are given a complete graph where each edge is labeled positive or negative. The goal is to obtain a clustering of the vertices that minimizes disagreements -- the number of negative edges trapped inside a cluster plus positive edges between different clusters. #R##N#We consider two variations of fairness constraint for the problem of correlation clustering where each node has a color, and the goal is to form clusters that do not over-represent vertices of any color. #R##N#The first variant aims to generate clusters with minimum disagreements, where the distribution of a feature (e.g. gender) in each cluster is same as the global distribution. For the case of two colors when the desired ratio of the number of colors in each cluster is $1:p$, we get $\mathcal{O}(p^2)$-approximation algorithm. Our algorithm could be extended to the case of multiple colors. We prove this problem is NP-hard. #R##N#The second variant considers relative upper and lower bounds on the number of nodes of any color in a cluster. The goal is to avoid violating upper and lower bounds corresponding to each color in each cluster while minimizing the total number of disagreements. Along with our theoretical results, we show the effectiveness of our algorithm to generate fair clusters by empirical evaluation on real world data sets.
generated_abstract: Algorithmic decisions increasingly shape access to information, resources, and opportunities, motivating the study of fairness across learning, ranking, allocation, and clustering systems. This paper develops a unified perspective on fair clustering and related decision problems. We formalize fairness as a collection of representation, proportionality, privacy, and local-quality constraints, emphasizing that these notions address different harms and can be incompatible with one another. We review algorithmic techniques including fairlets, linear and convex programming, dependent and LP rounding, primal-dual methods, coresets, streaming, and scalable parallel implementations. We compare their guarantees for \(k\)-center, \(k\)-median, \(k\)-means, facility location, and correlation clustering, and characterize the associated approximation and computational barriers. We also connect clustering fairness to individual fairness, ranking exposure, diversity-constrained selection, and fairness under feedback or censored data. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the tradeoff between representation constraints and clustering quality, and show that coreset and fairlet methods can substantially improve scalability with limited objective loss. Our results highlight the importance of choosing fairness definitions that reflect the application, auditing both global and local outcomes, and reporting accuracy, computational cost, and fairness jointly.

original_abstract: Recent years have witnessed a great development of deep learning based video person re-identification (Re-ID). A key factor for video person Re-ID is how to effectively construct discriminative video feature representations for the robustness to many complicated situations like occlusions. Recent part-based approaches employ spatial and temporal attention to extract the representative local features. While the correlations between the parts are ignored in the previous methods, to leverage the relations of different parts, we propose an innovative adaptive graph representation learning scheme for video person Re-ID, which enables the contextual interactions between the relevant regional features. Specifically, we exploit pose alignment connection and feature affinity connection to construct an adaptive structure-aware adjacency graph, which models the intrinsic relations between graph nodes. We perform feature propagation on the adjacency graph to refine the original regional features iteratively, the neighbor nodes information is taken into account for part feature representation. To learn the compact and discriminative representations, we further propose a novel temporal resolution-aware regularization, which enforces the consistency among different temporal resolutions for the same identities. We conduct extensive evaluations on four benchmarks, i.e. iLIDS-VID, PRID2011, MARS, and DukeMTMC-VideoReID, the experimental results achieve the competitive performance which demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed method.
generated_abstract: Video-based person re-identification is challenging because pedestrian sequences contain substantial changes in pose, viewpoint, illumination, occlusion, and image quality. Existing methods commonly aggregate frame-level features independently or rely on fixed spatial partitions, which limits their ability to model relationships among body regions and across time. We propose a graph-based framework that represents a tracklet as a dynamic spatiotemporal graph, where nodes correspond to spatial regions observed in successive frames and edges encode learned appearance and temporal dependencies. A graph attention mechanism adaptively emphasizes reliable regions and informative frame-to-frame interactions, while a hierarchical aggregation module produces compact identity representations from local to global levels. The model is trained end to end with classification and hard-aware metric-learning objectives, encouraging intra-identity compactness and inter-identity separation. It can suppress corrupted observations caused by blur, occlusion, and misalignment without requiring manual part annotations. Extensive experiments on the MARS, iLIDS-VID, and PRID-2011 benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong image- and video-based baselines in rank-1 accuracy and mean average precision. Visualization and ablation studies further confirm that the learned graph captures meaningful body-part and motion relationships.

original_abstract: Abstract   Within the realm of service robotics, researchers have placed a great amount of effort into learning, understanding, and representing motions as manipulations for task execution by robots. The task of robot learning and problem-solving is very broad, as it integrates a variety of tasks such as object detection, activity recognition, task/motion planning, localization, knowledge representation and retrieval, and the intertwining of perception/vision and machine learning techniques. In this paper, we solely focus on knowledge representations and notably how knowledge is typically gathered, represented, and reproduced to solve problems as done by researchers in the past decades. In accordance with the definition of knowledge representations, we discuss the key distinction between such representations and useful learning models that have extensively been introduced and studied in recent years, such as machine learning, deep learning, probabilistic modeling, and semantic graphical structures. Along with an overview of such tools, we discuss the problems which have existed in robot learning and how they have been built and used as solutions, technologies or developments (if any) which have contributed to solving them. Finally, we discuss key principles that should be considered when designing an effective knowledge representation.
generated_abstract: We present a cognitive robotic framework for understanding and executing manipulation tasks in open, human-centered environments. The system integrates deep visual perception with structured, grounded knowledge representations to connect objects, states, affordances, actions, and their physical consequences. RGB-D observations are processed using convolutional networks for object detection, semantic and affordance segmentation, state recognition, and motion estimation, while temporal models anticipate ongoing and future manipulation actions. Perceptual hypotheses are converted into a functional object-oriented representation that captures object–motion relations and supports retrieval, composition, and generalization of manipulation plans across videos, objects, and scenes. A probabilistic reasoning layer combines learned evidence with geometric and physical constraints, enabling the robot to reject unknown objects, select appropriate tools and grasps, and adapt plans through interaction and human guidance. The framework is evaluated on cooking and household manipulation scenarios involving long activities, novel objects, and unseen object parts. Results demonstrate improved activity recognition, affordance understanding, and plan generation compared with purely visual or purely symbolic baselines, while experiments on a robot show successful transfer of knowledge from observed human demonstrations to executable manipulation behaviors.

original_abstract: Mental health problems are on the rise globally and strain national health systems worldwide. Mental disorders are closely associated with fear of stigma, structural barriers such as financial burden, and lack of available services and resources which often prohibit the delivery of frequent clinical advice and monitoring. Technologies for mental well-being exhibit a range of attractive properties which facilitate the delivery of state of the art clinical monitoring. This review article provides an overview of traditional techniques followed by their technological alternatives, sensing devices, behaviour changing tools, and feedback interfaces. The challenges presented by these technologies are then discussed with data collection, privacy and battery life being some of the key issues which need to be carefully considered for the successful deployment of mental health tool-kits. Finally, the opportunities this growing research area presents are discussed including the use of portable tangible interfaces combining sensing and feedback technologies. generated_abstract: Psychological stress is difficult to detect reliably outside the laboratory because physiological responses vary substantially across individuals and collecting labelled data in everyday settings is burdensome. We present an on-device transfer-learning framework for personalised stress modelling using a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN). A base model is first trained on physiological data collected from 20 participants during a controlled stressor experiment. The model is then transferred to an edge-computing platform and adapted to each user with a small amount of personally labelled data acquired in real time through an integrated sensor and labelling interface. Heart rate, heart-rate variability, and electrodermal activity are used as input modalities, allowing the system to operate without continuous cloud connectivity and supporting privacy-preserving inference. We investigate whether personalisation improves performance when the model is applied across domains, from controlled tasks to unconstrained real-world activity. The proposed approach reduces the amount of data and time required to build individual models while addressing the limitations of population-level stress classifiers. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining edge sensing, efficient labelling, transfer learning, and CNN-based inference for adaptive, continuous, and personalised stress monitoring.

original_abstract: Salient object detection models often demand a considerable amount of computation cost to make precise prediction for each pixel, making them hardly applicable on low-power devices. In this paper, we aim to relieve the contradiction between computation cost and model performance by improving the network efficiency to a higher degree. We propose a flexible convolutional module, namely generalized OctConv (gOctConv), to efficiently utilize both in-stage and cross-stages multi-scale features, while reducing the representation redundancy by a novel dynamic weight decay scheme. The effective dynamic weight decay scheme stably boosts the sparsity of parameters during training, supports learnable number of channels for each scale in gOctConv, allowing 80% of parameters reduce with negligible performance drop. Utilizing gOctConv, we build an extremely light-weighted model, namely CSNet, which achieves comparable performance with about 0.2% parameters (100k) of large models on popular salient object detection benchmarks.
generated_abstract: Salient object detection is fundamental to visual understanding, yet existing deep models often require substantial computation and memory, limiting their use in mobile and embedded applications. We present an efficient salient object detection framework that combines compact convolutional design with multi-level semantic and spatial feature learning. A lightweight backbone extracts hierarchical representations, while an attention-guided decoder selectively aggregates contextual information and preserves fine object boundaries. To further reduce redundancy, channel importance is learned during training and uninformative filters are pruned, producing a compact model that can be executed with standard dense operators. The network is optimized with a saliency-aware objective that encourages confident foreground predictions and improves boundary quality without requiring post-processing or carefully tuned thresholds. Extensive experiments on widely used salient object benchmarks show that the proposed method delivers competitive or superior precision, recall, F-measure, and mean absolute error compared with substantially larger models. It also achieves a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off, with reduced parameters, FLOPs, and inference latency. These results demonstrate that accurate salient object detection can be achieved on resource-constrained platforms while retaining robust performance in cluttered scenes and on objects with complex shapes.

original_abstract: Despite their popularity in the chatbot literature, retrieval-based models have had modest impact on task-oriented dialogue systems, with the main obstacle to their application being the low-data regime of most task-oriented dialogue tasks. Inspired by the recent success of pretraining in language modelling, we propose an effective method for deploying response selection in task-oriented dialogue. To train response selection models for task-oriented dialogue tasks, we propose a novel method which: 1) pretrains the response selection model on large general-domain conversational corpora; and then 2) fine-tunes the pretrained model for the target dialogue domain, relying only on the small in-domain dataset to capture the nuances of the given dialogue domain. Our evaluation on six diverse application domains, ranging from e-commerce to banking, demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed training method.
generated_abstract: We present a scalable neural architecture for selecting and generating responses in multi-turn dialogue. The system combines a dense dual-encoder retriever with a context-aware reranker and a lightweight generative model. Utterances, dialogue history, and candidate responses are represented with pretrained contextual sentence encoders, while a sequential matching module preserves dependencies among turns and participant history. Approximate nearest-neighbor search using hierarchical navigable small-world graphs enables retrieval from millions of responses with low latency. A Transformer-based reranker then incorporates the full dialogue context, domain knowledge, and predicted belief state to distinguish relevant responses from semantically similar but inappropriate alternatives. When retrieval is uncertain, the model refines the best candidate or generates a response conditioned on the retrieved text, improving informativeness and reducing generic replies. We evaluate the approach on open-domain response selection benchmarks and multi-domain task-oriented datasets, including Ubuntu Dialogue, MultiWOZ, and Frames. The proposed system consistently outperforms standard sequence-to-sequence, retrieval-only, and separately trained ranking baselines in ranking accuracy and human judgments. Ablation studies show complementary benefits from dense retrieval, contextual reranking, dialogue-state features, and retrieval-conditioned generation, while efficient batching and approximate search make the method suitable for real-time deployment.

original_abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of unsupervised domain adaptation in the semantic segmentation. There are two primary issues in this field, i.e., what and how to transfer domain knowledge across two domains. Existing methods mainly focus on adapting domain-invariant features (what to transfer) through adversarial learning (how to transfer). Context dependency is essential for semantic segmentation, however, its transferability is still not well understood. Furthermore, how to transfer contextual information across two domains remains unexplored. Motivated by this, we propose a cross-attention mechanism based on self-attention to capture context dependencies between two domains and adapt transferable context. To achieve this goal, we design two cross-domain attention modules to adapt context dependencies from both spatial and channel views. Specifically, the spatial attention module captures local feature dependencies between each position in the source and target image. The channel attention module models semantic dependencies between each pair of cross-domain channel maps. To adapt context dependencies, we further selectively aggregate the context information from two domains. The superiority of our method over existing state-of-the-art methods is empirically proved on "GTA5 to Cityscapes" and "SYNTHIA to Cityscapes".
generated_abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation for semantic segmentation aims to transfer models trained with abundant synthetic annotations to real images without requiring target-domain labels. However, the substantial appearance discrepancy between domains, together with differences in class distributions and spatial structure, often leads to inaccurate and poorly localized predictions. We propose a unified adaptation framework that combines pixel-level translation, class-aware feature alignment, and self-supervised prediction consistency. A conditional generator reduces low-level style differences while preserving scene geometry, and an adversarial discriminator aligns representations at both global and category levels. To prevent destructive alignment between unrelated classes, pseudo-label confidence and spatial relationships are used to weight the adaptation objective. We further introduce an attention-based refinement module that captures long-range dependencies and emphasizes informative regions, while consistency constraints across translated and original images improve the reliability of target predictions. The framework is trained using labeled source images and unlabeled target images only, without target-domain annotations or additional manual supervision. Experiments on synthetic-to-real and cross-city benchmarks, including GTA5, SYNTHIA, and Cityscapes, demonstrate consistent improvements over supervised source-only models and representative adaptation methods, confirming the effectiveness of combining appearance, structure, and semantic alignment.

original_abstract: The problem of building a coherent and non-monotonous conversational agent with proper discourse and coverage is still an area of open research. Current architectures only take care of semantic and contextual information for a given query and fail to completely account for syntactic and external knowledge which are crucial for generating responses in a chit-chat system. To overcome this problem, we propose an end to end multi-stream deep learning architecture which learns unified embeddings for query-response pairs by leveraging contextual information from memory networks and syntactic information by incorporating Graph Convolution Networks (GCN) over their dependency parse. A stream of this network also utilizes transfer learning by pre-training a bidirectional transformer to extract semantic representation for each input sentence and incorporates external knowledge through the the neighborhood of the entities from a Knowledge Base (KB). We benchmark these embeddings on next sentence prediction task and significantly improve upon the existing techniques. Furthermore, we use AMUSED to represent query and responses along with its context to develop a retrieval based conversational agent which has been validated by expert linguists to have comprehensive engagement with humans.
generated_abstract: We present a knowledge-grounded neural dialogue system for engaging in coherent, informative, and goal-directed multi-turn conversations. The model jointly represents dialogue history, user and system profiles, and external knowledge organized as a graph. A bidirectional language encoder captures contextual semantics, while graph convolutional layers propagate information among entities, relations, aliases, and syntactically related words. An attention-based retrieval module produces a soft distribution over relevant knowledge-graph substructures, avoiding brittle symbolic queries and allowing the entire system to be trained end to end. A hierarchical decoder then generates responses conditioned on both the conversational state and retrieved facts, with controllable mechanisms for specificity, diversity, and personalization. We train the model using supervised dialogue data and further optimize response relevance, factual consistency, and task success with user-oriented objectives. Experiments on open-domain and goal-oriented dialogue benchmarks show consistent improvements over sequence-to-sequence, memory-network, retrieval, and knowledge-free baselines. Human evaluations find that the proposed system produces responses that are more informative, specific, coherent, and engaging, while reducing generic replies and factual errors. The results demonstrate the value of combining pretrained language representations with structured knowledge and differentiable retrieval for practical conversational agents.

original_abstract: Currently, semantic segmentation shows remarkable efficiency and reliability in standard scenarios such as daytime scenes with favorable illumination conditions. However, in face of adverse conditions such as the nighttime, semantic segmentation loses its accuracy significantly. One of the main causes of the problem is the lack of sufficient annotated segmentation datasets of nighttime scenes. In this paper, we propose a framework to alleviate the accuracy decline when semantic segmentation is taken to adverse conditions by using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). To bridge the daytime and nighttime image domains, we made key observation that compared to datasets in adverse conditions, there are considerable amount of segmentation datasets in standard conditions such as BDD and our collected ZJU datasets. Our GAN-based nighttime semantic segmentation framework includes two methods. In the first method, GANs were used to translate nighttime images to the daytime, thus semantic segmentation can be performed using robust models already trained on daytime datasets. In another method, we use GANs to translate different ratio of daytime images in the dataset to the nighttime but still with their labels. In this sense, synthetic nighttime segmentation datasets can be generated to yield models prepared to operate at nighttime conditions robustly. In our experiment, the later method significantly boosts the performance at the nighttime evidenced by quantitative results using Intersection over Union (IoU) and Pixel Accuracy (Acc). We show that the performance varies with respect to the proportion of synthetic nighttime images in the dataset, where the sweet spot corresponds to most robust performance across the day and night.
generated_abstract: Pixel-wise semantic segmentation is a powerful means of unifying scene perception for autonomous and assisted navigation, but existing methods are generally designed for narrow forward-facing cameras. This limitation prevents reliable understanding of the complete surroundings, particularly in wearable systems. We propose Panoramic Annular Semantic Segmentation (PASS), a framework that combines a compact panoramic annular lens with online panorama unfolding to obtain wide-field environmental awareness. To avoid the substantial cost of collecting densely annotated panoramic data, PASS learns from conventional perspective-view datasets. We adapt a real-time ERF-PSPNet architecture to process multiple unfolded panorama segments, generate semantically meaningful feature maps, and fuse them into smooth, consistent predictions across the full view. We further introduce focal-length-aware and style-transfer-based augmentations to improve robustness to the geometric distortions, blur, and appearance variations caused by panoramic imaging. Extensive experiments on diverse real-world scenes demonstrate that the proposed framework preserves real-time efficiency while delivering accurate and spatially coherent segmentation over an enlarged field of view. The results show that panoramic annular imaging and efficient semantic segmentation can provide practical surrounding perception for navigation and robotic applications.

original_abstract: Maximum Mutual information (MMI), which models the bidirectional dependency between responses ($y$) and contexts ($x$), i.e., the forward probability $\log p(y|x)$ and the backward probability $\log p(x|y)$, has been widely used as the objective in the \sts model to address the dull-response issue in open-domain dialog generation. Unfortunately, under the framework of the \sts model, direct decoding from $\log p(y|x) + \log p(x|y)$ is infeasible since the second part (i.e., $p(x|y)$) requires the completion of target generation before it can be computed, and the search space for $y$ is enormous. Empirically, an N-best list is first generated given $p(y|x)$, and $p(x|y)$ is then used to rerank the N-best list, which inevitably results in non-globally-optimal solutions. In this paper, we propose to use non-autoregressive (non-AR) generation model to address this non-global optimality issue. Since target tokens are generated independently in non-AR generation, $p(x|y)$ for each target word can be computed as soon as it's generated, and does not have to wait for the completion of the whole sequence. This naturally resolves the non-global optimal issue in decoding. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed non-AR strategy produces more diverse, coherent, and appropriate responses, yielding substantive gains in BLEU scores and in human evaluations.
generated_abstract: Neural dialogue generation has advanced rapidly from simple sequence-to-sequence models to systems that incorporate context, personas, topics, external knowledge, latent variables, and controllable decoding. However, progress is difficult to assess because dialogue is open-ended: likelihood-based training favors generic responses, automatic metrics correlate weakly with human judgments, and improvements in fluency may come at the expense of relevance, coherence, diversity, or factuality. This paper provides a systematic review of neural methods for open-domain conversational response generation. We organize existing approaches according to how they represent dialogue context, introduce content and style, model response diversity, and optimize or decode candidate responses. We discuss recurrent, convolutional, and attention-only architectures; hierarchical and variational models; knowledge- and persona-grounded systems; reinforcement and adversarial learning; and deterministic and stochastic decoding strategies. We also examine evaluation practices, including lexical metrics, diversity measures, adversarial tests, and human assessment. Through comparative analysis, we identify recurring limitations such as exposure bias, dull responses, weak long-range discourse modeling, and unreliable evaluation. Finally, we outline promising directions involving controllable generation, structured inference, efficient non-autoregressive decoding, grounded reasoning, and evaluation protocols that better reflect meaningful human interaction.

original_abstract: Human attribute analysis is a challenging task in the field of computer vision, since the data is largely imbalance-distributed. Common techniques such as re-sampling and cost-sensitive learning require prior-knowledge to train the system. To address this problem, we propose a unified framework called Dynamic Curriculum Learning (DCL) to online adaptively adjust the sampling strategy and loss learning in single batch, which resulting in better generalization and discrimination. Inspired by the curriculum learning, DCL consists of two level curriculum schedulers: (1) sampling scheduler not only manages the data distribution from imbalanced to balanced but also from easy to hard; (2) loss scheduler controls the learning importance between classification and metric learning loss. Learning from these two schedulers, we demonstrate our DCL framework with the new state-of-the-art performance on the widely used face attribute dataset CelebA and pedestrian attribute dataset RAP.
generated_abstract: Pedestrian attribute recognition is an important component of visual surveillance and person search, but remains challenging because attributes are multi-label, highly imbalanced, spatially localized, and affected by viewpoint, occlusion, and background clutter. Existing approaches typically address only one of these issues, and models trained on large-scale data are often dominated by frequent attributes while failing on rare ones. We propose an end-to-end framework for deep imbalanced pedestrian attribute recognition that combines attentive feature learning, curriculum-based optimization, and minority-aware classification. The network extracts multi-scale, attribute-sensitive representations from a residual backbone and progressively emphasizes informative regions and difficult examples. To reduce the bias caused by long-tailed labels, we introduce a class-balanced objective with incremental hard mining and effective-sample reweighting. Related attributes are organized into correlated groups and learned through a curriculum, enabling knowledge transfer between tasks while limiting interference among unrelated attributes. View and contextual cues are jointly modeled to improve robustness under unconstrained surveillance conditions. Experiments on challenging pedestrian attribute benchmarks, including RAP, PETA, and WIDER-Attribute, demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, particularly for rare attributes and occluded pedestrians. Ablation studies verify the complementary contributions of attention, curriculum learning, and imbalance-aware optimization.

original_abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel method, aggregation cross-entropy (ACE), for sequence recognition from a brand new perspective. The ACE loss function exhibits competitive performance to CTC and the attention mechanism, with much quicker implementation (as it involves only four fundamental formulas), faster inference\back-propagation (approximately O(1) in parallel), less storage requirement (no parameter and negligible runtime memory), and convenient employment (by replacing CTC with ACE). Furthermore, the proposed ACE loss function exhibits two noteworthy properties: (1) it can be directly applied for 2D prediction by flattening the 2D prediction into 1D prediction as the input and (2) it requires only characters and their numbers in the sequence annotation for supervision, which allows it to advance beyond sequence recognition, e.g., counting problem. The code is publicly available at this https URL.
generated_abstract: Recognizing text in natural images remains challenging because text may appear at arbitrary orientations, along curves, under perspective distortion, and amid complex backgrounds. We present an end-to-end attention-based framework for robust scene text recognition that jointly learns visual representation, geometric alignment, and sequence transcription from word images and their text labels. A fully convolutional backbone extracts multi-scale features, while a flexible rectification module normalizes irregular layouts without requiring character or line annotations. The resulting feature sequence is decoded by an attention-based recurrent recognizer that models character dependencies and dynamically focuses on relevant image regions. To improve training stability and reduce attention drift, we incorporate auxiliary dense character supervision and alignment-aware objectives. The proposed design combines the advantages of convolutional, recurrent, and attention models while avoiding explicit segmentation, lexicons, and hand-crafted preprocessing. Experiments on regular and irregular benchmarks, including IIIT5K, SVT, ICDAR, SVT-Perspective, and CUTE80, demonstrate consistent improvements over conventional recognition pipelines and competitive performance against recent specialized methods. Qualitative analyses further show that the model learns meaningful alignments and generalizes effectively to unseen words and severely distorted text.

original_abstract: Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (cGANs) are finding increasingly widespread use in many application domains.
