Despite outstanding progress, quantitative evaluation of such models often involves multiple distinct metrics to assess different desirable properties, such as image quality, conditional consistency, and intra-conditioning diversity. In this setting, model benchmarking becomes a challenge, as each metric may indicate a different "best" model. In this paper, we propose the Frechet Joint Distance (FJD), which is defined as the Frechet distance between joint distributions of images and conditioning, allowing it to implicitly capture the aforementioned properties in a single metric. We conduct proof-of-concept experiments on a controllable synthetic dataset, which consistently highlight the benefits of FJD when compared to currently established metrics. Moreover, we use the newly introduced metric to compare existing cGAN-based models for a variety of conditioning modalities (e.g. class labels, object masks, bounding boxes, images, and text captions). We show that FJD can be used as a promising single metric for cGAN benchmarking and model selection. Code can be found at https://github.com/facebookresearch/fjd.
generated_abstract: Generative modeling has rapidly advanced from producing simple synthetic samples to supporting controllable synthesis of high-resolution images, video, audio, text, and multimodal content. This paper surveys the development of deep generative models, with emphasis on generative adversarial networks and their applications in conditional image generation. We organize existing methods according to their objectives, conditioning mechanisms, architectural designs, and strategies for improving fidelity, stability, diversity, and spatial or semantic control. We review foundational GAN formulations alongside progressive, hierarchical, attention-based, projection-based, and normalization-based models, as well as variational, autoregressive, and hybrid approaches. Particular attention is given to text-to-image synthesis, layout- and scene-graph-based generation, image-to-image translation, interactive manipulation, and multimodal generation from unpaired data. We also examine methods for mitigating mode collapse and training instability, including latent-space regularization, spectral normalization, progressive growth, and improved optimization procedures. Finally, we critically discuss evaluation through likelihood, perceptual similarity, human judgments, and distributional metrics such as Inception Score, FID, precision and recall, and classification-based measures. The survey identifies persistent challenges and outlines directions toward more reliable, diverse, interpretable, and user-controllable generative systems.

original_abstract: We study a game between two firms in which each provide a service based on machine learning. The firms are presented with the opportunity to purchase a new corpus of data, which will allow them to potentially improve the quality of their products. The firms can decide whether or not they want to buy the data, as well as which learning model to build with that data. We demonstrate a reduction from this potentially complicated action space to a one-shot, two-action game in which each firm only decides whether or not to buy the data. The game admits several regimes which depend on the relative strength of the two firms at the outset and the price at which the data is being offered. We analyze the game's Nash equilibria in all parameter regimes and demonstrate that, in expectation, the outcome of the game is that the initially stronger firm's market position weakens whereas the initially weaker firm's market position becomes stronger. Finally, we consider the perspective of the users of the service and demonstrate that the expected outcome at equilibrium is not the one which maximizes the welfare of the consumers.
generated_abstract: We study the problem of learning strategic behavior when the payoff structure of a game is inferred from data. This setting arises in competing prediction systems, recommendation platforms, wireless-service markets, and other environments in which agents both learn from and influence a shared population. We introduce a distribution-dependent notion of equilibrium generalization: an equilibrium computed on a finite sample should remain approximately stable when evaluated on the underlying population. Our analysis separates errors due to estimation on observed outcomes from errors caused by previously unseen outcomes. Using occupancy counts and missing-mass techniques, we derive finite-sample bounds for the deviation between empirical and population payoffs, including explicit rates for distributions with regular variation and related tail conditions. These results yield sufficient conditions under which empirical pure equilibria, including regression equilibria, are approximate population equilibria, and provide sample-complexity guarantees for learning them. We also discuss how the structure of the game—potential, harmonic, and nonstrategic components—affects stability and convergence of learning dynamics. The framework clarifies when competition promotes reliable learning and when strategic adaptation can amplify the uncertainty created by limited observations.

original_abstract: Deep learning based medical image diagnosis has shown great potential in clinical medicine. However, it often suffers two major difficulties in practice: 1) only limited labeled samples are available due to expensive annotation costs over medical images; 2) labeled images may contain considerable label noises (e.g., mislabeling labels) due to diagnostic difficulties. In this paper, we seek to exploit rich labeled data from relevant domains to help the learning in the target task with unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA). Unlike most existing UDA methods which rely on clean labeled data or assume samples are equally transferable, we propose a novel Collaborative Unsupervised Domain Adaptation algorithm to conduct transferability-aware domain adaptation and conquer label noise in a cooperative way. Promising empirical results verify the superiority of the proposed method.
generated_abstract: Deep learning has shown considerable promise for medical image analysis, but its clinical deployment is hindered by domain shift, limited annotations, class imbalance, and noisy labels. This paper presents a unified framework for robust and transferable medical image classification and segmentation under these practical constraints. The framework combines a lightweight convolutional backbone with domain-invariant representation learning, category-aware adversarial alignment, and classifier discrepancy minimization to adapt knowledge from labeled source data to unlabeled target domains. To reduce negative transfer, transferable regions and source samples are selected through attention and curriculum-based weighting, while private and shared representations preserve domain-specific information. A co-training strategy further identifies reliable target predictions and mitigates annotation noise through loss correction and small-loss sample selection. For highly imbalanced data, focal and cost-sensitive objectives are integrated with an efficient active-learning procedure that prioritizes informative examples under a limited labeling budget. Experiments on medical image benchmarks, including microscopy, radiography, and computed tomography, demonstrate consistent improvements over conventional supervised, domain-adaptive, and noise-robust baselines. The results show that combining efficient architectures, robust optimization, and selective knowledge transfer can substantially improve generalization to new institutions, modalities, and disease populations.

original_abstract: In this paper, we study robust tensor completion by using transformed tensor singular value decomposition (SVD), which employs unitary transform matrices instead of discrete Fourier transform matrix that is used in the traditional tensor SVD. The main motivation is that a lower tubal rank tensor can be obtained by using other unitary transform matrices than that by using discrete Fourier transform matrix. This would be more effective for robust tensor completion. Experimental results for hyperspectral, video and face datasets have shown that the recovery performance for the robust tensor completion problem by using transformed tensor SVD is better in PSNR than that by using Fourier transform and other robust tensor completion methods.
generated_abstract: We study robust recovery of low-rank tensors from incomplete and corrupted observations. Tensor data often possess several forms of structure simultaneously, while conventional matricization-based nuclear-norm models may require excessive samples or fail to represent multilinear correlations. We formulate recovery as the separation of a structured low-rank tensor, a sparse corruption tensor, and, when appropriate, a noise component. To better exploit tensor structure, we consider tensor nuclear norms induced by tensor factorizations and complementary nonconvex rank surrogates, together with entrywise sparsity regularization. We develop efficient alternating direction and proximal algorithms for the resulting constrained and penalized models, including scalable updates for high-dimensional tensors. Under incoherence and sparsity conditions, we establish exact or stable recovery guarantees for noiseless and noisy settings, and prove convergence of the proposed iterative schemes to stationary solutions. The framework includes tensor completion and tensor robust principal component analysis as special cases and is compatible with multiple tensor representations, including t-product, tensor-train, and unfolding-based models. Experiments on synthetic data, color images, hyperspectral imagery, and videos demonstrate improved recovery accuracy and computational efficiency over existing convex and factorization-based methods.

original_abstract: Recently, the deep learning community has given growing attention to neural architectures engineered to learn problems in relational domains. Convolutional Neural Networks employ parameter sharing over the image domain, tying the weights of neural connections on a grid topology and thus enforcing the learning of a number of convolutional kernels. By instantiating trainable neural modules and assembling them in varied configurations (apart from grids), one can enforce parameter sharing over graphs, yielding models which can effectively be fed with relational data. In this context, vertices in a graph can be projected into a hyperdimensional real space and iteratively refined over many message-passing iterations in an end-to-end differentiable architecture. Architectures of this family have been referred to with several definitions in the literature, such as Graph Neural Networks, Message-passing Neural Networks, Relational Networks and Graph Networks. In this paper, we revisit the original Graph Neural Network model and show that it generalises many of the recent models, which in turn benefit from the insight of thinking about vertex \textbf{types}. To illustrate the generality of the original model, we present a Graph Neural Network formalisation, which partitions the vertices of a graph into a number of types. Each type represents an entity in the ontology of the problem one wants to learn. This allows - for instance - one to assign embeddings to edges, hyperedges, and any number of global attributes of the graph. As a companion to this paper we provide a Python/Tensorflow library to facilitate the development of such architectures, with which we instantiate the formalisation to reproduce a number of models proposed in the current literature.
generated_abstract: Graph-structured data provide a natural representation for many problems in science, engineering, and artificial intelligence, yet conventional deep learning architectures often fail to capture the dependencies and symmetries inherent in such data. This paper examines graph neural networks as a framework for learning relational representations and performing iterative reasoning over entities and their interactions. We unify recurrent, gated, interaction, relation, and message-passing architectures, emphasizing their common structure: local information exchange, permutation-invariant aggregation, and task-specific decoding. We review applications spanning molecular property prediction, physical simulation, program verification, network analysis, visual and textual question answering, and combinatorial optimization. Particular attention is given to the ability of these models to learn algorithmic procedures, generalize across graph sizes and distributions, and support multitask prediction through shared node embeddings. We also discuss connections with deep residual networks, reinforcement learning, generative modeling, and search-based decision procedures. The analysis identifies current limitations, including depth-related oversmoothing, weak extrapolation to larger instances, computational cost, and limited interpretability, and outlines research directions for combining relational inductive biases with scalable learning and structured reasoning.

original_abstract: Accurate prediction of others' trajectories is essential for autonomous driving. Trajectory prediction is challenging because it requires reasoning about agents' past movements, social interactions among varying numbers and kinds of agents, constraints from the scene context, and the stochasticity of human behavior. Our approach models these interactions and constraints jointly within a novel Multi-Agent Tensor Fusion (MATF) network. Specifically, the model encodes multiple agents' past trajectories and the scene context into a Multi-Agent Tensor, then applies convolutional fusion to capture multiagent interactions while retaining the spatial structure of agents and the scene context. The model decodes recurrently to multiple agents' future trajectories, using adversarial loss to learn stochastic predictions. Experiments on both highway driving and pedestrian crowd datasets show that the model achieves state-of-the-art prediction accuracy.
generated_abstract: Accurate prediction of surrounding-agent behavior is essential for safe autonomous navigation, yet human motion is inherently multimodal and shaped by both scene context and interactions with neighboring agents. We present a unified framework for forecasting and reproducing vehicle and pedestrian trajectories in dynamic environments. The model represents agents and their relationships as a spatiotemporal graph, encodes motion histories and visual scene information with residual convolutional features, and uses attention to identify the agents and regions most relevant to future behavior. A conditional generative module produces diverse, physically feasible trajectory hypotheses, while an adversarial recurrent discriminator encourages predictions that match the distribution of expert behavior over long horizons. The framework can additionally infer high-level maneuvers and refine candidate futures through interaction-aware scoring. We evaluate the approach on public freeway, pedestrian-crowd, and urban trajectory datasets using displacement, likelihood, collision, diversity, and behavioral realism metrics. Results show consistent improvements over deterministic recurrent predictors, maneuver-based models, and existing generative approaches, particularly for long-term prediction and complex interactions. Qualitative analyses demonstrate that the learned attention patterns are interpretable and that the generated trajectories capture realistic lane changes, collision avoidance, and socially compliant motion.

original_abstract: Contemporary monocular 6D pose estimation methods can only cope with a handful of object instances. This naturally limits possible applications as, for instance, robots need to work with hundreds of different objects in a real environment. In this paper, we propose the first deep learning approach for class-wise monocular 6D pose estimation, coupled with metric shape retrieval. We propose a new loss formulation which directly optimizes over all parameters, i.e. 3D orientation, translation, scale and shape at the same time. Instead of decoupling each parameter, we transform the regressed shape, in the form of a point cloud, to 3D and directly measure its metric misalignment. We experimentally demonstrate that we can retrieve precise metric point clouds from a single image, which can also be further processed for e.g. subsequent rendering. Moreover, we show that our new 3D point cloud loss outperforms all baselines and gives overall good results despite the inherent ambiguity due to monocular data.
generated_abstract: We present an end-to-end framework for estimating the 6D pose, metric dimensions, and complete 3D shape of objects from a single RGB image. The method combines a modern object detector with a category-level geometric representation that decouples image appearance from object pose and supports instances not observed during training. For each detected region, the network predicts pixel-aligned object coordinates, visibility-aware confidence, and a compact continuous representation of the object surface. These predictions are transformed into robust 2D–3D correspondences and used to recover rotation, translation, and scale through a differentiable geometric solver. A render-and-compare objective further enforces consistency between the estimated shape, pose, segmentation, and input image, while uncertainty-based loss weighting balances the heterogeneous learning tasks. Training relies primarily on synthetic CAD renderings with extensive domain randomization and requires only limited real-image supervision. Experiments on standard pose-estimation, category-level reconstruction, and autonomous-driving benchmarks show that the proposed approach is accurate under occlusion, truncation, symmetry, and domain shift. It achieves competitive or superior results to multi-stage RGB and RGB-D systems while maintaining efficient inference suitable for real-time robotic perception.

original_abstract: Manually labelling large collections of text data is a time-consuming, expensive, and laborious task, but one that is necessary to support machine learning based on text datasets. Active learning has been shown to be an effective way to alleviate some of the effort required in utilising large collections of unlabelled data for machine learning tasks without needing to fully label them. The representation mechanism used to represent text documents when performing active learning, however, has a significant influence on how effective the process will be. While simple vector representations such as bag of words have been shown to be an effective way to represent documents during active learning, the emergence of representation mechanisms based on the word embeddings prevalent in neural network research (e.g. word2vec and transformer-based models like BERT) offer a promising, and as yet not fully explored, alternative. This paper describes a large-scale evaluation of the effectiveness of different text representation mechanisms for active learning across 8 datasets from varied domains. This evaluation shows that using representations based on modern word embeddings---especially BERT---, which have not yet been widely used in active learning, achieves a significant improvement over more commonly used vector-based methods like bag of words.
generated_abstract: Screening studies for inclusion in systematic reviews is time-consuming and requires substantial expert effort. Active learning can reduce this burden by prioritizing citations for human assessment, but its effectiveness depends strongly on how documents are represented and which articles are selected. We investigate topic detection and text representation methods for active learning in systematic review screening. We compare conventional bag-of-words features with topic-based representations and distributed representations derived from paragraph vectors, word embeddings, subword models, and contextual language models. We evaluate uncertainty-based, density-aware, batch, and representation-focused acquisition strategies across systematic reviews from clinical and social science domains. Our experiments examine both classification performance and practical screening workload, including the number of relevant studies identified at different annotation budgets. The results show that richer semantic representations generally improve early-stage prioritization, while combining uncertainty with diversity or density reduces redundant selections and avoids overfitting to initially sampled documents. Paragraph-vector and contextual representations are particularly useful when terminology varies across studies. We provide statistical comparisons across reviews and discuss stability, computational cost, and implications for reproducible screening workflows. The findings demonstrate that representation-aware active learning can substantially reduce manual screening without compromising recall.

original_abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for reinforcement learning (RL) have shown distinct advantages, e.g., solving memory-dependent tasks and meta-learning. However, little effort has been spent on improving RNN architectures and on understanding the underlying neural mechanisms for performance gain. In this paper, we propose a novel, multiple-timescale, stochastic RNN for RL. Empirical results show that the network can autonomously learn to abstract sub-goals and can self-develop an action hierarchy using internal dynamics in a challenging continuous control task. Furthermore, we show that the self-developed compositionality of the network enhances faster re-learning when adapting to a new task that is a re-composition of previously learned sub-goals, than when starting from scratch. We also found that improved performance can be achieved when neural activities are subject to stochastic rather than deterministic dynamics.
generated_abstract: We present a recurrent hierarchical reinforcement-learning architecture that learns both what to do and over which timescale to act. The model combines stochastic latent-state dynamics with multiple recurrent timescales, allowing fast layers to encode immediate sensory and motor contingencies while slower layers maintain task context, abstract goals, and long-horizon predictions. Rather than imposing manually designed options or subgoals, temporal abstractions emerge through jointly learned policies, termination mechanisms, and latent representations. A predictive-coding objective trains the model to explain incoming observations and to represent uncertainty, while an actor-critic objective uses these representations for efficient control under partial observability and sparse rewards. During adaptation, inference variables can be updated from prediction errors, enabling rapid adjustment without retraining the entire network. We evaluate the approach on partially observed navigation, continuous motor-control, and sequential imitation tasks, including settings with changing dynamics and delayed feedback. The proposed architecture learns reusable skills, improves exploration and sample efficiency over flat recurrent and model-free baselines, and remains robust when observations are incomplete or task demands change. These results suggest that learned temporal hierarchies and probabilistic predictive representations provide a common mechanism for flexible behavior and continual adaptation.

original_abstract: We study the problem of subspace tracking in the presence of missing data (ST-miss). In recent work, we studied a related problem called robust ST. In this paper, we show that a simple modification of our robust ST solution also provably solves ST-miss and robust ST-miss. To the best of our knowledge, our result is the first “complete” guarantee for ST-miss. This means that we can prove that under assumptions on only the algorithm inputs, the output subspace estimates are close to the true data subspaces at all times. Our guarantees hold under mild and easily interpretable assumptions, and allow the underlying subspace to change with time in a piecewise constant fashion. In contrast, all existing guarantees for ST are partial results and assume a fixed unknown subspace. Extensive numerical experiments are shown to back up our theoretical claims. Finally, our solution can be interpreted as a provably correct mini-batch and memory-efficient solution to low-rank matrix completion.
generated_abstract: We study the problem of tracking a time-varying low-dimensional subspace when each incoming data vector is only partially observed. This setting arises in streaming matrix completion, online principal component analysis, and applications such as video surveillance and network monitoring, where acquiring or storing complete observations is impractical. We propose a simple online algorithm based on the recursive projected compressive sensing framework. At each time instant, the algorithm first estimates the missing entries by exploiting the current subspace estimate, and then updates the subspace using newly recovered data. Unlike previous analyses, our result provides a complete performance guarantee: under mild incoherence, bounded-noise, sufficient-observation, and slow-subspace-change assumptions, the estimated subspace remains uniformly close to the true subspace at all times after initialization. The method accommodates time-varying subspaces and does not require assumptions on unobserved data beyond those needed for identifiability. We establish explicit bounds on tracking error, observation requirements, memory, and computational complexity, and show that the method is fast and memory efficient. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate competitive or improved performance relative to existing online subspace tracking and matrix completion methods.

original_abstract: Intelligent agents gather information and perceive semantics within the environments before taking on given tasks. The agents store the collected information in the form of environment models that compactly represent the surrounding environments. The agents, however, can only conduct limited tasks without an efficient and effective environment model. Thus, such an environment model takes a crucial role for the autonomy systems of intelligent agents. We claim the following characteristics for a versatile environment model: accuracy, applicability, usability, and scalability. Although a number of researchers have attempted to develop such models that represent environments precisely to a certain degree, they lack broad applicability, intuitive usability, and satisfactory scalability. To tackle these limitations, we propose 3-D scene graph as an environment model and the 3-D scene graph construction framework. The concise and widely used graph structure readily guarantees usability as well as scalability for 3-D scene graph. We demonstrate the accuracy and applicability of the 3-D scene graph by exhibiting the deployment of the 3-D scene graph in practical applications. Moreover, we verify the performance of the proposed 3-D scene graph and the framework by conducting a series of comprehensive experiments under various conditions.
generated_abstract: We present a unified framework for semantic understanding and task planning in indoor 3D environments. The system incrementally reconstructs globally consistent scenes from RGB-D video and fuses geometric, visual, and linguistic information into a structured 3D scene graph. Object instances are detected and represented as point-set features, while attributes and spatial relations are inferred using learned object, relation, and language models. The graph links observations across views and supports reasoning about objects, their properties, and interactions, rather than treating the scene as an unstructured collection of detections. Natural-language descriptions and questions can be grounded in the reconstructed environment, enabling the system to answer queries and infer implicit spatial constraints. These symbolic relations are also used by a task planner to generate robot actions in partially known and changing worlds. The planner maintains beliefs about the environment, incorporates new observations, and produces explanations when goals cannot be achieved. Experiments on reconstructed indoor scenes and robot manipulation and navigation tasks demonstrate that joint geometric and semantic reasoning improves object and relation recognition, language grounding, question answering, and planning robustness. The resulting framework provides a practical bridge between 3D perception, natural language interaction, and explainable robot autonomy.

original_abstract: One of the primary challenges faced by deep learning is the degree to which current methods exploit superficial statistics and dataset bias, rather than learning to generalise over the specific representations they have experienced. This is a critical concern because generalisation enables robust reasoning over unseen data, whereas leveraging superficial statistics is fragile to even small changes in data distribution. To illuminate the issue and drive progress towards a solution, we propose a test that explicitly evaluates abstract reasoning over visual data. We introduce a large-scale benchmark of visual questions that involve operations fundamental to many high-level vision tasks, such as comparisons of counts and logical operations on complex visual properties. The benchmark directly measures a method's ability to infer high-level relationships and to generalise them over image-based concepts. It includes multiple training/test splits that require controlled levels of generalization. We evaluate a range of deep learning architectures, and find that existing models, including those popular for vision-and-language tasks, are unable to solve seemingly-simple instances. Models using relational networks fare better but leave substantial room for improvement.
generated_abstract: We introduce Embodied Question Answering (EQA), a task that requires an agent to navigate through a visual environment in order to answer questions about its surroundings. Unlike conventional visual question answering, where the relevant image is provided directly, EQA agents must actively acquire the information needed to respond, coupling language understanding, visual perception, navigation, and reasoning. We present a new dataset of question–answer pairs grounded in procedurally generated 3D environments, together with trajectories that identify the locations required to answer each question. We develop a modular neural architecture comprising a question-conditioned navigation policy and a visual question answering module. The navigator predicts actions from first-person observations and language, while the answerer uses the resulting visual experience to produce an answer. We evaluate both supervised and reinforcement-learning training regimes and analyze performance across question types, navigation difficulty, and answer complexity. Experiments show that agents can learn to reach informative locations and answer questions more accurately than methods that navigate randomly or rely only on their initial view. However, substantial gaps from oracle navigation and human performance remain, highlighting the need for stronger embodied reasoning and exploration.

original_abstract: There is evidence that Russia's Internet Research Agency attempted to interfere with the 2016 U.S. election by running fake accounts on Twitter - often referred to as "Russian trolls". In this work, we: 1) develop machine learning models that predict whether a Twitter account is a Russian troll within a set of 170K control accounts; and, 2) demonstrate that it is possible to use this model to find active accounts on Twitter still likely acting on behalf of the Russian state. Using both behavioral and linguistic features, we show that it is possible to distinguish between a troll and a non-troll with a precision of 78.5% and an AUC of 98.9%, under cross-validation. Applying the model to out-of-sample accounts still active today, we find that up to 2.6% of top journalists' mentions are occupied by Russian trolls. These findings imply that the Russian trolls are very likely still active today. Additional analysis shows that they are not merely software-controlled bots, and manage their online identities in various complex ways. Finally, we argue that if it is possible to discover these accounts using externally - accessible data, then the platforms - with access to a variety of private internal signals - should succeed at similar or better rates.
generated_abstract: This study examines how automated and state-sponsored accounts shaped political discussion on Twitter during the 2016 U.S. presidential election. We combine machine-learning methods, network analysis, linguistic features, activity entropy, and social-network-based geolocation to distinguish likely humans, bots, and Internet Research Agency accounts in a large collection of election-related posts. We characterize the content, timing, ideological positioning, geographic distribution, and interaction patterns of these accounts, and investigate how their messages reached and were amplified by human users. The analysis shows that automated accounts were disproportionately active during the early diffusion of low-credibility and inflammatory content, frequently targeting highly connected users and operating across apparently distinct partisan communities. Russian-linked accounts adopted different personas and issue positions, but their activity was predominantly conservative and pro-Trump in the election context. Exposure was broad, whereas amplification was concentrated among conservative users and users with prior ideological affinities. Geographic and linguistic signals further indicate that account identity and location cannot be inferred reliably from profile information alone. These findings demonstrate that political manipulation relies on coordinated, adaptable mixtures of bots, trolls, and human intermediaries, highlighting the need for cross-platform detection and provenance-aware countermeasures.

original_abstract: We present a method for provably defending any pretrained image classifier against $\ell_p$ adversarial attacks. By prepending a custom-trained denoiser to any off-the-shelf image classifier and using randomized smoothing, we effectively create a new classifier that is guaranteed to be $\ell_p$-robust to adversarial examples, without modifying the pretrained classifier. The approach applies both to the case where we have full access to the pretrained classifier as well as the case where we only have query access. We refer to this defense as black-box smoothing, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through extensive experimentation on ImageNet and CIFAR-10. Finally, we use our method to provably defend the Azure, Google, AWS, and ClarifAI image classification APIs. Our code replicating all the experiments in the paper can be found at this https URL .
generated_abstract: Adversarial examples remain a fundamental obstacle to the reliable deployment of deep neural networks. This paper presents a systematic study of methods for improving and evaluating adversarial robustness in image classification. We organize existing approaches into attack-dependent defenses, input and feature transformation methods, adversarially trained models, and certifiable defenses based on convex relaxation, abstract interpretation, randomized smoothing, and differential privacy. We also examine alternative threat models, including Wasserstein and functional perturbations, and consider white-box, black-box, query-limited, and transfer-based attacks. Through a unified empirical evaluation, we show that many apparent improvements arise from weak attack procedures, gradient masking, nondifferentiable preprocessing, or mismatches between the training and evaluation threat models. Adaptive attacks frequently eliminate the reported benefits of detection, denoising, and ensemble defenses, whereas certified methods provide reliable guarantees but often trade clean accuracy, computational efficiency, or perturbation radius. Our analysis further highlights the promise of scalable verification and randomized smoothing, together with the importance of attack-independent evaluation. We conclude with practical recommendations for robust training, certification, and benchmarking, emphasizing explicit threat models, adaptive attacks, and reporting both empirical and provable guarantees.

original_abstract: Few-shot learning algorithms aim to learn model parameters capable of adapting to unseen classes with the help of only a few labeled examples. A recent regularization technique - Manifold Mixup focuses on learning a general-purpose representation, robust to small changes in the data distribution. Since the goal of few-shot learning is closely linked to robust representation learning, we study Manifold Mixup in this problem setting. Self-supervised learning is another technique that learns semantically meaningful features, using only the inherent structure of the data. This work investigates the role of learning relevant feature manifold for few-shot tasks using self-supervision and regularization techniques. We observe that regularizing the feature manifold, enriched via self-supervised techniques, with Manifold Mixup significantly improves few-shot learning performance. We show that our proposed method S2M2 beats the current state-of-the-art accuracy on standard few-shot learning datasets like CIFAR-FS, CUB, mini-ImageNet and tiered-ImageNet by 3-8 %. Through extensive experimentation, we show that the features learned using our approach generalize to complex few-shot evaluation tasks, cross-domain scenarios and are robust against slight changes to data distribution.
generated_abstract: Few-shot visual recognition aims to classify novel categories from only a handful of labeled examples, but performance is strongly limited by the quality and transferability of learned representations. We present a unified framework that combines self-supervised representation learning with episodic few-shot adaptation. A convolutional encoder is first trained on unlabeled images using complementary pretext objectives that exploit spatial context, geometric transformations, image completion, and cross-modal or temporal consistency. These objectives encourage representations that preserve semantic structure while suppressing nuisance variations. The resulting encoder is then optimized for novel-category recognition using a lightweight metric-based classifier, with prototypes formed from the available support examples. To improve robustness in the extreme low-data regime, we incorporate feature normalization, strong input regularization, and learned augmentation or hallucination of additional support features. Experiments on standard few-shot benchmarks, including cross-domain settings, show consistent improvements over supervised pretraining, conventional meta-learning methods, and individual self-supervised objectives. Ablation studies demonstrate that representation quality, rather than classifier complexity, is the principal determinant of performance, and that combining diverse self-supervised signals yields more transferable features. Our results establish self-supervision as a practical foundation for rapid, data-efficient visual learning.

original_abstract: This paper studies the problem of predicting the distribution over multiple possible future paths of people as they move through various visual scenes. We make two main contributions. The first contribution is a new dataset, created in a realistic 3D simulator, which is based on real world trajectory data, and then extrapolated by human annotators to achieve different latent goals. This provides the first benchmark for quantitative evaluation of the models to predict multi-future trajectories. The second contribution is a new model to generate multiple plausible future trajectories, which contains novel designs of using multi-scale location encodings and convolutional RNNs over graphs. We refer to our model as Multiverse. We show that our model achieves the best results on our dataset, as well as on the real-world VIRAT/ActEV dataset (which just contains one possible future). We will release our data, models and code.
generated_abstract: Accurate prediction of the future motion of surrounding agents is essential for safe autonomous navigation, yet remains difficult because behavior is uncertain, multimodal, and strongly influenced by interactions and scene context. We present a unified framework for forecasting multiple agents from visual observations and their motion histories. The model combines convolutional and recurrent encoders to represent temporal dynamics, a graph-based attention mechanism to exchange information between agents, and spatial attention over semantic scene features to capture lanes, obstacles, and other navigational cues. A latent decision module generates diverse future hypotheses, while an adversarial and likelihood-based objective encourages realistic trajectories and calibrated probabilities without collapsing to a single mode. The framework supports conditional prediction, allowing forecasts to adapt to a planned ego-agent maneuver, and is trained using both real-world data and procedurally generated simulation data. We evaluate the approach on pedestrian and autonomous-driving benchmarks, including crowded scenes and map-rich urban environments. It consistently improves displacement accuracy, diversity, collision avoidance, and long-horizon forecasting over deterministic recurrent, GAN-based, and mixture-density baselines. Qualitative analyses further show that the learned attention maps identify socially and physically relevant regions, providing interpretable evidence for the predicted behavior.

original_abstract: This work explores the large-scale multi-agent communication mechanism under a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) setting. We summarize the general categories of topology for communication structures in MARL literature, which are often manually specified. Then we propose a novel framework termed as Learning Structured Communication (LSC) by using a more flexible and efficient communication topology. Our framework allows for adaptive agent grouping to form different hierarchical formations over episodes, which is generated by an auxiliary task combined with a hierarchical routing protocol. Given each formed topology, a hierarchical graph neural network is learned to enable effective message information generation and propagation among inter- and intra-group communications. In contrast to existing communication mechanisms, our method has an explicit while learnable design for hierarchical communication. Experiments on challenging tasks show the proposed LSC enjoys high communication efficiency, scalability, and global cooperation capability.
generated_abstract: Large-scale multi-agent systems must coordinate under partial observability, changing interaction structures, and severe communication constraints. Existing deep reinforcement learning methods often assume fixed agent populations, centralized information, or unrestricted communication, limiting their applicability to distributed cyber-physical and edge-computing systems. We present a scalable framework for learning decentralized coordination through dynamic, self-organizing regions. Agents construct a permutation-invariant relational representation of their local neighborhood, use attention to identify relevant agents and information, and learn when and with whom to communicate. A hierarchical graph policy separates intra-region coordination from inter-region interactions, while a curriculum progressively increases the population and adapts the policy to changing network sizes. Centralized training with decentralized execution supports efficient value estimation and counterfactual credit assignment without requiring communication at execution time beyond local exchanges. We evaluate the framework in cooperative navigation, resource allocation, pursuit, and heterogeneous distributed coordination tasks with varying numbers, layouts, and connectivity patterns. Compared with independent learners, value-factorization methods, and communication-based actor-critic baselines, the proposed approach achieves higher returns, improved sample efficiency, and substantially better robustness to agent failures and population changes. Learned coordination regions also provide interpretable structures for analyzing emergent collective behavior.

original_abstract: We investigate the combination of actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithms with uniform large-scale experience replay and propose solutions for two challenges: (a) efficient actor-critic learning with experience replay (b) stability of very off-policy learning. We employ those insights to accelerate hyper-parameter sweeps in which all participating agents run concurrently and share their experience via a common replay module. To this end we analyze the bias-variance tradeoffs in V-trace, a form of importance sampling for actor-critic methods. Based on our analysis, we then argue for mixing experience sampled from replay with on-policy experience, and propose a new trust region scheme that scales effectively to data distributions where V-trace becomes unstable. We provide extensive empirical validation of the proposed solution. We further show the benefits of this setup by demonstrating state-of-the-art data efficiency on Atari among agents trained up until 200M environment frames.
generated_abstract: We introduce Agent57, a general reinforcement learning agent that achieves or exceeds human-level performance on all 57 games in the Arcade Learning Environment. The agent addresses the diverse challenges of the Atari benchmark, including sparse rewards, long time horizons, stochastic dynamics, and games requiring either exploration or precise exploitation. Agent57 combines a recurrent value-based architecture with episodic and lifelong novelty bonuses, enabling efficient exploration in unfamiliar states while retaining useful knowledge over extended interactions. A meta-controller selects among policies with different exploration strengths and discount factors, allowing the agent to adapt its behavior to the requirements of each game. The system is trained using a distributed, off-policy learning architecture with prioritized replay and multi-step return estimation, providing high-throughput experience collection and stable learning from diverse behavior policies. We evaluate Agent57 on the full Atari-57 suite using the established human-normalized score and report state-of-the-art performance, including strong results on the previously most difficult games. These findings demonstrate that combining adaptive exploration, memory, temporal abstraction, and scalable off-policy learning can produce a single agent capable of robust performance across a broad range of tasks.

original_abstract: We present a context aware object detection method based on a retrieve-and-transform scene layout model. Given an input image, our approach first retrieves a coarse scene layout from a codebook of typical layout templates. In order to handle large layout variations, we use a variant of the spatial transformer network to transform and refine the retrieved layout, resulting in a set of interpretable and semantically meaningful feature maps of object locations and scales. The above steps are implemented as a Layout Transfer Network which we integrate into Faster RCNN to allow for joint reasoning of object detection and scene layout estimation. Extensive experiments on three public datasets verified that our approach provides consistent performance improvements to the state-of-the-art object detection baselines on a variety of challenging tasks in the traffic surveillance and the autonomous driving domains.
generated_abstract: Accurate and efficient vehicle detection is essential for autonomous driving and intelligent transportation systems, yet remains challenging because vehicles appear at widely varying scales, are frequently occluded, and occur in complex urban environments. We propose a unified deep convolutional detection framework that combines multi-scale feature representations, contextual reasoning, and localization-quality estimation. The detector uses shared features to identify vehicles and regress their bounding boxes in a single forward pass, while scale-aware pooling preserves the structure of small objects. A recurrent context module incorporates information from neighboring regions, improving classification and localization in crowded scenes. During inference, classification confidence is calibrated with an explicit estimate of bounding-box quality, producing more reliable ranking and suppression of overlapping hypotheses. The network is trained end to end and can be initialized from either classification models or detection data, making it applicable across domains. We evaluate the method on challenging traffic benchmarks, including KITTI and MIO-TCD, covering diverse viewpoints, object sizes, weather conditions, and traffic densities. Experiments show consistent improvements over established one-stage and region-based detectors, while maintaining real-time performance suitable for deployment in vehicle and roadside systems.

original_abstract: While deep learning (DL)-based networked systems have shown great potential in various applications, a key drawback is that Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in DL are blackboxes and nontransparent for network operators. The lack of interpretability makes DL-based networked systems challenging to operate and troubleshoot, which further prevents DL-based networked systems from deploying in practice. In this paper, we propose TranSys, a novel framework to explain DL-based networked systems for practical deployment. Transys categorizes current DL-based networked systems and introduces different explanation methods based on decision tree and hypergraph to effectively explain DL-based networked systems. TranSys can explain the DNN policies in the form of decision trees and highlight critical components based on analysis over hypergraph. We evaluate TranSys over several typical DL-based networked systems and demonstrate that Transys can provide human-readable explanations for network operators. We also present three use cases of Transys, which could (i) help network operators troubleshoot DL-based networked systems, (ii) improve the decision latency and resource consumption of DL-based networked systems by ~10x on different metrics, and (iii) provide suggestions on daily operations for network operators when incidences occur.
generated_abstract: Machine learning is increasingly used to automate networking decisions, including packet classification, routing, traffic optimization, resource allocation, and adaptive video streaming. Although learned policies can outperform hand-designed heuristics, their opaque and dynamic behavior makes it difficult to diagnose failures, establish trust, and provide safety guarantees. This paper examines interpretability and verification techniques for machine-learning-driven networked systems. We organize existing approaches into model inspection, post hoc explanation, policy extraction, adversarial robustness analysis, and formal verification, and discuss how each addresses different questions about learned behavior. We highlight the limitations of feature-importance and saliency methods, including instability, lack of fidelity, and susceptibility to adversarial manipulation. We then develop a practical methodology that combines systematic input exploration, interpretable surrogate models, and formal checks against designer-specified properties. Through case studies involving neural adaptive bitrate selection and other networking controllers, we show how these tools can reveal hidden dependencies, undesirable actions, and failures on previously unseen conditions. Our analysis identifies challenges arising from sequential decisions, delayed rewards, changing environments, and scalability. We conclude with design guidelines for building learning-based network systems that are not only effective, but also understandable, robust, and verifiable.

original_abstract: The rapid evolution of the blockchain community has brought together stakeholders from fundamentally different backgrounds: cryptographers, protocol designers, software developers, startup entrepreneurs, corporate executives and investors, academics of various disciplines, and end users. The result is a diverse ecosystem, presently exemplified by the development of a wide range of different blockchain protocols. This raises questions for policy and decision makers: How do different protocols compare? What are their trade-offs? Existing efforts to survey the area reveal a fragmented terminology, and the lack of a unified framework to make the different desirable properties of blockchain protocols explicit. In this paper, we work towards bridging this gap. We evaluate protocols within a five-dimensional design space with the following axes. Optimality: does the protocol achieve its main goals? Stability: are the incentives of its participating agents well-aligned? Efficiency: is its output maximal relative to its use of resources? Robustness: can it cope when its operational assumptions are invalid or perturbed? Persistence: can it recover from catastrophic events? Based on the relevant literature, we organize the properties of existing protocols in subcategories of increasing granularity. The result is a dynamic scheme -- termed the PREStO framework. Its scope is to aid the communication between stakeholders of different backgrounds, including managers and investors, and to identify research challenges and opportunities for blockchain protocols in a systematic way. We illustrate this via use cases and make a first step to understand the blockchain ecosystem through a more comprehensive lens.
generated_abstract: Blockchain systems combine distributed consensus, cryptographic mechanisms, and economic incentives to coordinate mutually distrustful participants. Their security and performance therefore depend not only on protocol correctness, but also on the strategic behavior of miners, validators, pool operators, users, and attackers. This paper presents a systematic analysis of incentive mechanisms and game-theoretic models for blockchain networks. We organize existing approaches across proof-of-work, proof-of-stake, Byzantine-fault-tolerant, and hybrid protocols, and examine how rewards, costs, information propagation, voting power, and network delays shape participation and decentralization. We review major deviations and attacks, including selfish mining, block withholding, pool infiltration, double spending, stake bleeding, and Sybil behavior, together with proposed defenses and alternative reward schemes. Particular attention is given to equilibrium assumptions, coalition formation, mining-pool centralization, wealth compounding, and the limitations of Nash equilibrium in dynamic and bounded-rational environments. We also compare analytical, simulation-based, and empirical evaluation methodologies, highlighting gaps between formal guarantees and deployed systems. Finally, we identify open challenges involving scalability, privacy, energy use, incentive compatibility, robustness, interoperability, and the design of economically sustainable consensus protocols.

original_abstract: The recently proposed Lottery Ticket Hypothesis of Frankle and Carbin (2019) suggests that the performance of over-parameterized deep networks is due to the random initialization seeding the network with a small fraction of favorable weights. These weights retain their dominant status throughout training -- in a very real sense, this sub-network "won the lottery" during initialization. The authors find sub-networks via unstructured magnitude pruning with 85-95% of parameters removed that train to the same accuracy as the original network at a similar speed, which they call winning tickets. In this paper, we extend the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis to a variety of transfer learning tasks. We show that sparse sub-networks with approximately 90-95% of weights removed achieve (and often exceed) the accuracy of the original dense network in several realistic settings. We experimentally validate this by transferring the sparse representation found via pruning on CIFAR-10 to SmallNORB and FashionMNIST for object recognition tasks.
generated_abstract: We investigate how neural networks can be compressed and accelerated while preserving their predictive performance, with particular attention to the roles of architecture, initialization, optimization, and regularization. We compare unstructured connection pruning, structured filter pruning, variational and L0-based sparsification, sensitivity-based pruning at initialization, and automated resource-constrained architecture search. Experiments on Fashion-MNIST and standard convolutional and residual networks show that substantial reductions in parameters and computation are possible, but parameter sparsity does not necessarily translate into practical speedups unless it is expressed through hardware-friendly structures. Across a range of pruning criteria, retraining a compact architecture from a random initialization often matches or outperforms fine-tuning inherited weights, indicating that the discovered architecture can be more important than the weights selected from an overparameterized model. We further examine lottery-ticket and supermask behavior, finding that initialization benefits depend strongly on network depth, sparsity, and training protocol. Residual connections and depth provide optimization advantages, whereas mobile architectures offer an effective accuracy-efficiency tradeoff. These results establish practical guidelines for evaluating sparse models and suggest treating pruning primarily as a resource-aware architecture design problem rather than solely as weight elimination.

original_abstract: It has been widely accepted that Graphics Processing Units (GPU) is one of promising schemes for encryption acceleration, in particular, the support of complex mathematical calculations such as integer and logical operations makes the implementation easier; however, complexes such as parallel granularity, memory allocation still imposes a burden on real world implementations. In this paper, we propose a new approach for Advanced Encryption Standard accelerations, including both encryption and decryption. Specifically, we adapt the Electronic Code Book mode for cryptographic transformation, look up table scheme for fast lookup, and a granularity of one state per thread for thread scheduling. Our experimental results offer researchers a good understanding on GPU architectures and software accelerations. In addition, both our source code and experimental results are freely available.
generated_abstract: Graphics processing units (GPUs) provide substantial acceleration for highly parallel workloads, but achieving high throughput depends critically on matching algorithmic access patterns to the underlying memory hierarchy. This paper investigates the performance implications of GPU memory behavior for representative data-intensive applications, including AES encryption and Cauchy Reed-Solomon erasure coding. We analyze how thread granularity, data placement, shared-memory bank conflicts, cache utilization, and host-device transfers affect throughput across different NVIDIA GPU generations. Based on these observations, we develop and evaluate optimized CUDA implementations that use appropriate on-chip memories, coalesced accesses, parallel workload decomposition, and overlapping of computation with data movement. Experimental results demonstrate that seemingly small choices in allocation strategy and bytes processed per thread can produce substantial performance differences, while architecture-specific memory characteristics strongly influence the best configuration. The optimized AES implementation achieves multi-tens to hundreds of gigabits per second depending on the GPU and workload granularity, and the erasure-coding implementation significantly outperforms existing GPU libraries. Our results provide practical guidelines for designing GPU accelerators and show that careful memory-hierarchy characterization is essential for portable, high-performance cryptographic and storage-processing systems.

original_abstract: We present CoSQL, a corpus for building cross-domain, general-purpose database (DB) querying dialogue systems. It consists of 30k+ turns plus 10k+ annotated SQL queries, obtained from a Wizard-of-Oz (WOZ) collection of 3k dialogues querying 200 complex DBs spanning 138 domains. Each dialogue simulates a real-world DB query scenario with a crowd worker as a user exploring the DB and a SQL expert retrieving answers with SQL, clarifying ambiguous questions, or otherwise informing of unanswerable questions. When user questions are answerable by SQL, the expert describes the SQL and execution results to the user, hence maintaining a natural interaction flow. CoSQL introduces new challenges compared to existing task-oriented dialogue datasets:(1) the dialogue states are grounded in SQL, a domain-independent executable representation, instead of domain-specific slot-value pairs, and (2) because testing is done on unseen databases, success requires generalizing to new domains. CoSQL includes three tasks: SQL-grounded dialogue state tracking, response generation from query results, and user dialogue act prediction. We evaluate a set of strong baselines for each task and show that CoSQL presents significant challenges for future research. The dataset, baselines, and leaderboard will be released at this https URL.
generated_abstract: We study context-dependent semantic parsing for task-oriented interactions, where users ask a sequence of questions about complex databases and later questions refer implicitly to earlier ones. Unlike conventional text-to-SQL systems that generate each query independently, our approach jointly models the current utterance, dialogue history, and database schema. The model encodes questions and schemas with structure-aware representations, explicitly tracks references and state changes across turns, and generates SQL through a constrained, syntax-guided decoder. To exploit the strong correspondence between neighboring queries, it can reuse and edit components of previously generated SQL while retaining the ability to construct new clauses for changed intents. Schema linking and attention over tables, columns, and their relations further support transfer to unseen databases and domains. We evaluate the system on cross-domain contextual text-to-SQL benchmarks, including sequences with nested queries, joins, aggregation, and implicit references. Results show consistent gains over generating queries from scratch and over prior context-independent and editing-based baselines, particularly on later turns and queries requiring history resolution. The findings demonstrate that combining interaction-level memory with explicit schema structure is essential for robust conversational database access.

original_abstract: Coflow scheduling models communication requests in parallel computing frameworks where multiple data flows between shared resources need to be completed before computation can continue. In this paper, we introduce Path-based Coflow Scheduling, a generalized problem variant that considers coflows as collections of flows along fixed paths on general network topologies with node capacity restrictions. For this problem, we minimize the coflows' total weighted completion time. We show that flows on paths in the original network can be interpreted as hyperedges in a hypergraph and transform the path-based scheduling problem into an edge scheduling problem on this hypergraph. We present a $(2\lambda + 1)$-approximation algorithm when node capacities are set to one, where $\lambda$ is the maximum number of nodes in a path. For the special case of simultaneous release times for all flows, our result improves to a $(2\lambda)$-approximation. Furthermore, we generalize the result to arbitrary node constraints and obtain a $(2\lambda\Delta + 1)$- and a $(2\lambda\Delta)$-approximation in the case of general and zero release times, where $\Delta$ captures the capacity disparity between nodes.
generated_abstract: Coflows provide a natural abstraction for communication stages in data-parallel applications: a coflow completes only when all of its constituent transfers have finished. We study the problem of scheduling coflows over a shared network to minimize total weighted completion time, allowing release dates and general network topologies. Unlike approaches that optimize routing, bandwidth allocation, or coflow ordering separately, our framework jointly captures these decisions and exploits the precedence relation induced by coflow completion. We formulate the problem using an interval-indexed linear program and derive a deadline-based scheduling procedure that converts a fractional solution into a feasible integral schedule. The resulting algorithms achieve constant-factor approximation guarantees for fixed-route and packet-based coflows, and provide a logarithmic-factor guarantee when routes must also be selected. For complete bipartite datacenter networks, we obtain improved bounds that remain valid in the presence of release dates. We also develop practical priority and list-scheduling variants suitable for online operation. Experiments on synthetic workloads and real datacenter traces show that the proposed methods substantially reduce weighted completion time compared with existing coflow schedulers, while requiring considerably less computation than joint nonlinear optimization.

original_abstract: There is great potential for damage from adversarial learning (AL) attacks on machine-learning based systems. In this paper, we provide a contemporary survey of AL, focused particularly on defenses against attacks on statistical classifiers. After introducing relevant terminology and the goals and range of possible knowledge of both attackers and defenders, we survey recent work on test-time evasion (TTE), data poisoning (DP), and reverse engineering (RE) attacks and particularly defenses against same. In so doing, we distinguish robust classification from anomaly detection (AD), unsupervised from supervised, and statistical hypothesis-based defenses from ones that do not have an explicit null (no attack) hypothesis; we identify the hyperparameters a particular method requires, its computational complexity, as well as the performance measures on which it was evaluated and the obtained quality. We then dig deeper, providing novel insights that challenge conventional AL wisdom and that target unresolved issues, including: 1) robust classification versus AD as a defense strategy; 2) the belief that attack success increases with attack strength, which ignores susceptibility to AD; 3) small perturbations for test-time evasion attacks: a fallacy or a requirement?; 4) validity of the universal assumption that a TTE attacker knows the ground-truth class for the example to be attacked; 5) black, grey, or white box attacks as the standard for defense evaluation; 6) susceptibility of query-based RE to an AD defense. We also discuss attacks on the privacy of training data. We then present benchmark comparisons of several defenses against TTE, RE, and backdoor DP attacks on images. The paper concludes with a discussion of future work.
generated_abstract: Machine learning systems are increasingly deployed in security- and safety-critical applications, yet their predictions can be manipulated by carefully crafted inputs, poisoned training data, and compromised models. This paper presents a systematic study of adversarial machine learning, covering test-time evasion, data poisoning, backdoor attacks, model extraction, and privacy leakage. We organize existing attacks according to the adversary’s knowledge, objectives, and ability to modify data, and examine their effectiveness across image, text, audio, and malware-detection tasks. We compare approaches based on adversarial training, feature and input transformations, anomaly detection, robust optimization, Lipschitz constraints, certified bounds, and post-training model inspection. Our analysis shows that apparent robustness can result from gradient masking or unrealistic threat models, while many detection methods fail against adaptive attackers. Conversely, combining explicit threat modeling, strong attack evaluations, statistical monitoring, and certified or attack-aware training can substantially improve security. The results highlight an inherent trade-off among accuracy, robustness, computational cost, and usability, and provide practical recommendations for designing, evaluating, and deploying learning systems that remain dependable in adversarial environments.

original_abstract: Despite the recent progress in deep semi-supervised learning (Semi-SL), the amount of labels still plays a dominant role. The success in self-supervised learning (Self-SL) hints a promising direction to exploit the vast unlabeled data by leveraging an additional set of deterministic labels. In this paper, we propose Deep Self-Semi-Supervised learning (D$S^3$L), a flexible multi-task framework with shared parameters that integrates the rotation task in Self-SL with the consistency-based methods in deep Semi-SL. Our method is easy to implement and is complementary to all consistency-based approaches. The experiments demonstrate that our method significantly improves over the published state-of-the-art methods on several standard benchmarks, especially when fewer labels are presented.
generated_abstract: We study deep visual learning when both supervision is scarce and available labels are unreliable. This setting combines the challenges of semi-supervised learning, noisy-label learning, and representation learning, while exposing the limitations of methods that treat unlabeled examples or corrupted annotations independently. We propose a unified training framework that learns a robust representation from all images through self-supervised transformation objectives and enforces prediction consistency under stochastic and adversarial perturbations. A teacher model, updated by weight averaging, provides stable targets for unlabeled examples and guides a dynamically constructed neighborhood graph. In parallel, sample reliability is estimated from the evolution of losses and feature geometry, allowing the method to downweight or correct suspicious labels rather than discard their visual information. Task losses are balanced adaptively through gradient-based normalization, and group-aware architectures and batch-independent normalization improve stability under small batches. Experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, and real-world web datasets show consistent improvements over supervised, consistency-based, self-supervised, and robust noisy-label baselines, particularly with few labels and high corruption rates. The results demonstrate that representation quality, uncertainty-aware supervision, and weight averaging are complementary tools for reliable learning from imperfect data.

original_abstract: In many real-time applications, the deployment of deep neural networks is constrained by high computational cost and efficient lightweight neural networks are widely concerned. In this paper, we propose that depthwise convolution (DWC) is used to expand the number of channels in a bottleneck block, which is more efficient than 1 x 1 convolution. The proposed Pointwise-Standard-Depthwise network (PSDNet) based on channel expansion with DWC has fewer number of parameters, less computational cost and higher accuracy than corresponding ResNet on CIFAR datasets. To design more efficient lightweight concolutional neural netwok, Depthwise-Pointwise-Depthwise inverted bottleneck block (DPD block) is proposed and DPDNet is designed by stacking DPD block. Meanwhile, the number of parameters of DPDNet is only about 60% of that of MobileNetV2 for networks with the same number of layers, but can achieve approximated accuracy. Additionally, two hyperparameters of DPDNet can make the trade-off between accuracy and computational cost, which makes DPDNet suitable for diverse tasks. Furthermore, we find the networks with more DWC layers outperform the networks with more 1x1 convolution layers, which indicates that extracting spatial information is more important than combining channel information.
generated_abstract: The rapid growth of deep convolutional neural networks has delivered substantial improvements in visual recognition, but their computational, memory, and energy requirements hinder deployment on mobile and embedded platforms. This paper presents a systematic study of efficient convolutional network design, focusing on reducing redundancy while preserving representational capacity. We examine complementary strategies at the architectural, algorithmic, and implementation levels, including depthwise and group convolutions, channel shuffling, low-rank and vector-kernel factorization, residual and multi-branch transformations, structured pruning, weight sharing, and binary or ternary parameterization. We further discuss how normalization, activation functions, and training procedures affect the accuracy of compact models, and consider the trade-offs among parameters, multiply-add operations, latency, memory consumption, and recognition performance. Experiments on standard image-classification benchmarks, including CIFAR-10, CINIC-10, and ImageNet, together with representative detection and hyperspectral classification tasks, demonstrate that carefully designed structured models can approach the accuracy of substantially larger networks at a fraction of their cost. The results provide practical guidance for constructing efficient neural networks and highlight the importance of evaluating compressed architectures with hardware-aware baselines rather than accuracy alone.

original_abstract: Societal bias towards certain communities is a big problem that affects a lot of machine learning systems. This work aims at addressing the racial bias present in many modern gender recognition systems. We learn race invariant representations of human faces with an adversarially trained autoencoder model. We show that such representations help us achieve less biased performance in gender classification. We use variance in classification accuracy across different races as a surrogate for the racial bias of the model and achieve a drop of over 40% in variance with race invariant representations.
generated_abstract: Machine learning systems often inherit social biases from the data used to train them, yet removing sensitive information can also damage the semantic and predictive content needed for downstream tasks. We propose a general adversarial framework for learning representations that preserve task-relevant structure while suppressing demographic attributes such as gender and race. A predictor is trained to perform the primary task, while an adversary attempts to recover sensitive information from the learned representation; gradient reversal and a tunable minimax objective force the representation toward invariance. The approach supports continuous and categorical attributes, requires no parallel or manually balanced data, and can be combined with pretrained word embeddings, visual encoders, and structured prediction models. We evaluate it on word similarity and analogy benchmarks, sentiment analysis, cross-lingual transfer, image recognition, and situation recognition. Across these settings, the method substantially reduces direct and indirect bias, limits amplification of corpus-level disparities, and preserves competitive task accuracy. Experiments also show that the accuracy–fairness trade-off can be controlled explicitly, allowing practitioners to select representations appropriate for different application and policy requirements. Our results demonstrate that adversarial representation learning offers a flexible route to more robust and equitable language and vision systems.

original_abstract: Over the past 15 years, the volume, richness and quality of data collected from the combined social networking platforms has increased beyond all expectation, providing researchers from a variety of disciplines to use it in their research. Perhaps more impactfully, it has provided the foundation for a range of new products and services, transforming industries such as advertising and marketing, as well as bringing the challenges of sharing personal data into the public consciousness. But how to make sense of the ever-increasing volume of big social data so that we can better understand and improve the user experience in increasingly complex, data-driven digital systems. This link with usability and the user experience of data-driven system bridges into the wider field of HCI, attracting interdisciplinary researchers as we see the demand for consumer technologies, software and systems, as well as the integration of social networks into our everyday lives. The fact that the data largely posted on social networks tends to be textual, provides a further link to linguistics, psychology and psycholinguistics to better understand the relationship between human behaviours offline and online. #R##N#In this thesis, we present a novel conceptual framework based on a complex digital system using collected longitudinal datasets to predict system status based on the personality traits and emotions extracted from text posted by users. The system framework was built using a dataset collected from an online scholarship system in which 2000 students had their digital behaviour and social network behaviour collected for this study. We contextualise this research project with a wider review and critical analysis of the current psycholinguistics, artificial intelligence and human-computer interaction literature, which reveals a gap of mapping and understanding digital profiling against system status.
generated_abstract: This paper presents a user-centred framework for analysing personality, emotion and sentiment in social media text to support the design of more adaptive and responsible interactive systems. Drawing on established psychological models, sentiment and emotion lexicons, social-network analysis, and supervised machine-learning techniques, the framework combines linguistic, prosodic and behavioural indicators to infer individual and collective characteristics from online communication. We compare alternative representations and classifiers, including semantic orientation, word embeddings, decision trees and random forests, and examine the effects of demographic variation, rating scales and annotation quality on predictive performance. Particular attention is given to the interpretation of inferred traits, reproducibility of computational experiments, and the ethical risks associated with profiling, surveillance and the malicious use of artificial intelligence.
