Applications are considered in political forecasting, customer service, online hate monitoring, social computing and user-experience modelling. The results indicate that digital language contains useful, though imperfect and context-dependent, signals of personality and affect. Reliable deployment therefore requires transparent benchmarks, open software and data practices, uncertainty reporting, and meaningful human oversight. The paper concludes with recommendations for developing socially beneficial analytics that respect privacy, minimise bias and remain accountable to affected users.

original_abstract: In this paper, we propose an analysis mechanism based structured Analysis Discriminative Dictionary Learning (ADDL) framework. ADDL seamlessly integrates the analysis discriminative dictionary learning, analysis representation and analysis classifier training into a unified model. The applied analysis mechanism can make sure that the learnt dictionaries, representations and linear classifiers over different classes are independent and discriminating as much as possible. The dictionary is obtained by minimizing a reconstruction error and an analytical incoherence promoting term that encourages the sub-dictionaries associated with different classes to be independent. To obtain the representation coefficients, ADDL imposes a sparse l2,1-norm constraint on the coding coefficients instead of using l0 or l1-norm, since the l0 or l1-norm constraint applied in most existing DL criteria makes the training phase time consuming. The codes-extraction projection that bridges data with the sparse codes by extracting special features from the given samples is calculated via minimizing a sparse codes approximation term. Then we compute a linear classifier based on the approximated sparse codes by an analysis mechanism to simultaneously consider the classification and representation powers. Thus, the classification approach of our model is very efficient, because it can avoid the extra time-consuming sparse reconstruction process with trained dictionary for each new test data as most existing DL algorithms. Simulations on real image databases demonstrate that our ADDL model can obtain superior performance over other state-of-the-arts.
generated_abstract: We propose a tensor-based dictionary learning framework for extracting discriminative and compact representations from multiblock and multimodal data. Unlike conventional matrix-based approaches, the proposed method preserves the multilinear structure of samples and jointly models common information shared across data blocks and individual characteristics specific to each block. Sparse and nonnegative constraints are incorporated into the tensor decomposition to obtain parts-based, interpretable components and improve identifiability. To enhance recognition performance, the learned codes are further regularized by local geometric relationships and label information, allowing the dictionary to capture both reconstructive and discriminative structures. An alternating optimization algorithm is developed for efficient updating of the core tensor, dictionaries, and sparse coefficients, with low-rank approximations and online processing used to reduce computational and memory costs. The method can also operate in semi-supervised settings by exploiting structural relationships between labeled and unlabeled samples. Experiments on face, image, biomedical, and other multiview datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves competitive reconstruction quality, robust feature selection, and improved classification and recognition accuracy compared with matrix factorization, manifold learning, and existing synthesis and analysis dictionary learning methods.

original_abstract: Bursts of images exhibit significant self-similarity across both time and space. This motivates a representation of the kernels as linear combinations of a small set of basis elements. To this end, we introduce a novel basis prediction network that, given an input burst, predicts a set of global basis kernels --- shared within the image --- and the corresponding mixing coefficients --- which are specific to individual pixels. Compared to other state-of-the-art deep learning techniques that output a large tensor of per-pixel spatiotemporal kernels, our formulation substantially reduces the dimensionality of the network output. This allows us to effectively exploit larger denoising kernels and achieve significant quality improvements (over 1dB PSNR) at reduced run-times compared to state-of-the-art methods.
generated_abstract: We present a learning-based framework for restoring high-quality images from bursts of noisy, low-resolution, and misaligned photographs captured by handheld cameras. The method models burst processing as an iterative optimization problem and unrolls its solution into a recurrent convolutional network. Each iteration estimates image updates using spatially adaptive filters, while non-local attention and residual connections enable the network to exploit repeated structures and long-range dependencies. The architecture operates directly on raw sensor data, incorporates a realistic image-formation and noise model, and accepts an arbitrary number of frames without dependence on their ordering. This design supports joint alignment, demosaicing, denoising, super-resolution, and reduction of compression or sampling artifacts, while remaining computationally practical for mobile imaging. We train the model end to end using synthetic bursts generated from clean images and validate it on both simulated and real handheld captures, including challenging low-light scenes with camera and object motion. Experiments show consistent improvements over single-frame and existing multi-frame methods in quantitative fidelity and perceptual quality. The results demonstrate that combining physical modeling, adaptive filtering, and deep recurrent inference provides an effective and flexible solution for computational burst photography.

original_abstract: Models such as Sequence-to-Sequence and Image-to-Sequence are widely used in real world applications. While the ability of these neural architectures to produce variable-length outputs makes them extremely effective for problems like Machine Translation and Image Captioning, it also leaves them vulnerable to failures of the form where the model produces outputs of undesirable length. This behavior can have severe consequences such as usage of increased computation and induce faults in downstream modules that expect outputs of a certain length. Motivated by the need to have a better understanding of the failures of these models, this paper proposes and studies the novel output-size modulation problem and makes two key technical contributions. First, to evaluate model robustness, we develop an easy-to-compute differentiable proxy objective that can be used with gradient-based algorithms to find output-lengthening inputs. Second and more importantly, we develop a verification approach that can formally verify whether a network always produces outputs within a certain length. Experimental results on Machine Translation and Image Captioning show that our output-lengthening approach can produce outputs that are 50 times longer than the input, while our verification approach can, given a model and input domain, prove that the output length is below a certain size.
generated_abstract: Neural image and video captioning systems achieve impressive scores on standard benchmarks, yet their ability to ground language in visual content and withstand small input changes remains poorly understood. We present a systematic study of the robustness of encoder–decoder captioning models to adversarial perturbations. Building on gradient-based attacks for continuous images and discrete sequences, we develop methods for both targeted and untargeted attacks that manipulate an image while preserving its perceptual appearance, or modify a small number of words while largely preserving sentence meaning. Our attacks can force models to generate specified captions, insert chosen keywords, or produce semantically incorrect descriptions. Experiments across recurrent, attention-based, and object-focused captioning architectures show that high-quality captions and strong benchmark scores do not imply reliable visual grounding. Transferable perturbations often fool independently trained models, while language-only cues enable many errors even when visual evidence contradicts the generated text. We further evaluate defenses based on adversarial training, data augmentation, and robust optimization, finding that improvements against one attack do not consistently generalize to others. These results motivate evaluation protocols that combine caption quality, grounding-sensitive tests, and explicit threat models when assessing multimodal generation systems.

original_abstract: Camera network and multi-camera calibration for external parameters is a necessary step for a variety of contexts in computer vision and robotics, ranging from three-dimensional reconstruction to human activity tracking. This paper describes a method for camera network and/or multi-camera calibration suitable for specific contexts: the cameras may not all have a common field of view, or if they do, there may be some views that are 180 degrees from one another, and the network may be asynchronous. The calibration object required is one or more planar calibration patterns, rigidly attached to one another, and are distinguishable from one another, such as aruco or charuco patterns. We formulate the camera network and/or multi-camera calibration problem in this context using rigidity constraints, represented as a system of equations, and an approximate solution is found through a two-step process. Synthetic and real experiments, including scenarios of a asynchronous camera network and rotating imaging system, demonstrate the method in a variety of settings. Reconstruction accuracy error was less than 0.5 mm for all datasets. This method is suitable for new users to calibrate a camera network, and the modularity of the calibration object also allows for disassembly, shipping, and the use of this method in a variety of large and small spaces.
generated_abstract: Accurate camera localization and calibration are essential for robotic perception in unstructured agricultural environments, where reliable three-dimensional reconstruction supports tree phenotyping and autonomous manipulation. We present a vision-based system for estimating camera motion and constructing metrically consistent models of orchard trees using inexpensive RGB-D sensors mounted on a mobile robot. The system combines learned relative pose estimation with geometric refinement and robot-world, hand-eye calibration to obtain robust transformations between the cameras, robot, and scene. A semantics-aware mapping procedure integrates observations acquired from both sides of a tree row, using trunk and canopy features to correct drift and improve alignment. The resulting models are processed to estimate key morphological traits, including tree height, canopy volume, trunk diameter, branch structure, branch lengths, and branch angles. We evaluate the approach in real orchard conditions under viewpoint changes, partial occlusion, and variable illumination. Results show that learned pose corrections improve reconstruction consistency over conventional visual odometry alone, while semantic registration reduces errors caused by imperfect loop closures. The system achieves accurate trait measurements without GPS, lidar, or artificial markers, demonstrating its potential for scalable structural phenotyping and future robotic pruning applications.

original_abstract: In this paper, we propose a self-supervised learning approach that leverages multiple imaging modalities to increase data efficiency for medical image analysis. To this end, we introduce multimodal puzzle-solving proxy tasks, which facilitate neural network representation learning from multiple image modalities. These representations allow for subsequent fine-tuning on different downstream tasks. To achieve that, we employ the Sinkhorn operator to predict permutations of puzzle pieces in conjunction with a modality agnostic feature embedding. Together, they allow for a lean network architecture and increased computational efficiency. Under this framework, we propose different strategies for puzzle construction, integrating multiple medical imaging modalities, with varying levels of puzzle complexity. We benchmark these strategies in a range of experiments to assess the gains of our method in downstream performance and data-efficiency on different target tasks. Our experiments show that solving puzzles interleaved with multimodal content yields more powerful semantic representations. This allows us to solve downstream tasks more accurately and efficiently, compared to treating each modality independently. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach on two multimodal medical imaging benchmarks: the BraTS and the Prostate semantic segmentation datasets, on which we achieve competitive results to state-of-the-art solutions, at a fraction of the computational expense. We also outperform many previous solutions on the chosen benchmarks.
generated_abstract: Deep learning has transformed medical image analysis, but its success depends on large collections of expert annotations that are expensive, time-consuming, and often inconsistent. We present a self-supervised framework for learning transferable representations from unlabeled multimodal medical images. The method combines complementary proxy tasks that exploit anatomical structure, spatial correspondence, and modality relationships, including image reconstruction, geometric transformation prediction, patch ordering, and cross-modal feature prediction. A shared encoder is pretrained using these automatically generated signals and subsequently fine-tuned for segmentation, classification, and registration. The framework incorporates three-dimensional context and modality-specific branches, allowing it to learn both common anatomy and complementary information across imaging modalities. Experiments on brain tumor, abdominal, and cardiovascular datasets show that self-supervised initialization consistently improves accuracy, convergence, and robustness compared with random initialization, conventional two-dimensional transfer learning, and individual proxy tasks. Improvements are particularly pronounced when only a small fraction of labeled volumes is available and when training and test distributions differ. These results demonstrate that unlabeled medical images contain sufficient structural and cross-modal information to support effective representation learning, reducing annotation requirements while providing a practical foundation for diverse downstream clinical imaging applications.

original_abstract: Text style transfer without parallel data has achieved some practical success. However, in the scenario where less data is available, these methods may yield poor performance. In this paper, we examine domain adaptation for text style transfer to leverage massively available data from other domains. These data may demonstrate domain shift, which impedes the benefits of utilizing such data for training. To address this challenge, we propose simple yet effective domain adaptive text style transfer models, enabling domain-adaptive information exchange. The proposed models presumably learn from the source domain to: (i) distinguish stylized information and generic content information; (ii) maximally preserve content information; and (iii) adaptively transfer the styles in a domain-aware manner. We evaluate the proposed models on two style transfer tasks (sentiment and formality) over multiple target domains where only limited non-parallel data is available. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model compared to the baselines.
generated_abstract: Text style transfer aims to modify the stylistic attributes of a sentence while preserving its underlying content and meaning. Recent advances in neural language generation have produced a wide range of approaches, including disentangled representation learning, back-translation, adversarial training, reinforcement learning, retrieval-based editing, and controllable encoder–decoder architectures. However, progress remains hindered by the scarcity of parallel data, the discrete nature of language, and the difficulty of evaluating the competing objectives of stylistic accuracy, content preservation, fluency, and personalization. This paper reviews and organizes existing methods for unsupervised and supervised text style transfer, highlighting their assumptions, training signals, model architectures, and application settings. It further examines transfer across sentiment, formality, offensiveness, gender, political stance, and domain-specific styles, as well as connections to machine translation, dialogue generation, summarization, and domain adaptation. Through a systematic discussion of datasets, automatic metrics, and human evaluation protocols, the paper identifies persistent limitations, including inadequate semantic preservation and unreliable evaluation. Finally, it outlines promising directions for multi-attribute control, stronger content representations, efficient adaptation, and more comprehensive benchmarks for robust and controllable text generation.

original_abstract: In this paper, we study normalization methods for neural networks from the perspective of elimination singularity. Elimination singularities correspond to the points on the training trajectory where neurons become consistently deactivated. They cause degenerate manifolds in the loss landscape which will slow down training and harm model performances. We show that channel-based normalizations (e.g. Layer Normalization and Group Normalization) are unable to guarantee a far distance from elimination singularities, in contrast with Batch Normalization which by design avoids models from getting too close to them. To address this issue, we propose BatchChannel Normalization (BCN), which uses batch knowledge to avoid the elimination singularities in the training of channel-normalized models. Unlike Batch Normalization, BCN is able to run in both large-batch and micro-batch training settings. The effectiveness of BCN is verified on many tasks, including image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation. The code is here: this https URL.
generated_abstract: Normalization is a central component of modern deep neural networks, yet the relative advantages and limitations of existing methods remain difficult to determine across architectures, batch sizes, and visual recognition tasks. This work presents a systematic study of normalization strategies, including batch, instance, layer, group, weight, switchable, sparse switchable, and weight-standardized normalization. We examine their effects on optimization, gradient propagation, regularization, generalization, computational cost, and dependence on minibatch statistics, relating empirical behavior to recent theoretical analyses of smoothness, scale-direction decoupling, and singularities in deep networks. Experiments cover image classification, semantic and instance segmentation, object detection, video recognition, few-shot recognition, and semi-supervised learning, using both conventional and residual or densely connected architectures. Our results show that no single normalizer is uniformly optimal: batch normalization remains highly effective with sufficiently large batches, whereas group- and weight-based methods are more reliable in micro-batch and transfer-learning settings. Learned combinations of normalization scopes improve robustness, while sparse selection provides comparable benefits with lower overhead and greater interpretability. These findings yield practical guidelines for choosing normalization methods and highlight promising directions for adaptive, task-aware normalization.

original_abstract: Conventional cross-domain image-to-image translation or unsupervised domain adaptation methods assume that the source domain and target domain are closely related. This neglects a practical scenario where the domain discrepancy between the source and target is excessively large. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to learn domain adaptive features between the largely-gapped source and target domains with unlabeled domain bridges. Firstly, we introduce the framework of Cycle-consistency Flow Generative Adversarial Networks (CFGAN) that utilizes domain bridges to perform image-to-image translation between two distantly distributed domains. Secondly, we propose the Prototypical Adversarial Domain Adaptation (PADA) model which utilizes unlabeled bridge domains to align feature distribution between source and target with a large discrepancy. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed models.
generated_abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation aims to transfer predictive knowledge from labeled source data to unlabeled target data despite substantial differences in appearance, acquisition conditions, and even domain composition. Existing approaches typically align marginal feature distributions, but may discard domain-specific information, confuse class boundaries, or fail when multiple heterogeneous sources and targets are involved. We propose a unified framework for robust cross-domain representation learning that separates task-relevant content from domain-dependent variation and combines distribution alignment with semantic preservation. The framework learns shared and private representations through adversarial reconstruction and mutual-information objectives, while using class-aware prototypes and classifier discrepancy to prevent misalignment across categories. To reduce the remaining visual gap, a conditional image translation module generates realistic intermediate and target-style samples while preserving identity and labels. Moment-based and kernel-based alignment losses further match feature statistics across multiple source domains without requiring target annotations. The resulting model supports single-source, multi-source, and blended-target adaptation within one training procedure. Extensive experiments on digit, object-recognition, synthetic-to-real, semantic-segmentation, and person re-identification benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy and robustness over established adversarial, moment-matching, and image-translation methods, particularly under large domain shifts and category imbalance.

original_abstract: It is intuitive that NLP tasks for logographic languages like Chinese should benefit from the use of the glyph information in those languages. However, due to the lack of rich pictographic evidence in glyphs and the weak generalization ability of standard computer vision models on character data, an effective way to utilize the glyph information remains to be found. In this paper, we address this gap by presenting Glyce, the glyph-vectors for Chinese character representations. We make three major innovations: (1) We use historical Chinese scripts (e.g., bronzeware script, seal script, traditional Chinese, etc) to enrich the pictographic evidence in characters; (2) We design CNN structures (called tianzege-CNN) tailored to Chinese character image processing; and (3) We use image-classification as an auxiliary task in a multi-task learning setup to increase the model's ability to generalize. We show that glyph-based models are able to consistently outperform word/char ID-based models in a wide range of Chinese NLP tasks. We are able to set new state-of-the-art results for a variety of Chinese NLP tasks, including tagging (NER, CWS, POS), sentence pair classification, single sentence classification tasks, dependency parsing, and semantic role labeling. For example, the proposed model achieves an F1 score of 80.6 on the OntoNotes dataset of NER, +1.5 over BERT; it achieves an almost perfect accuracy of 99.8\% on the Fudan corpus for text classification. Code found at this https URL.
generated_abstract: Chinese characters contain rich visual and phonetic information that is largely ignored by conventional pretrained language models, which represent text primarily as discrete character or subword sequences. The resulting representations are pretrained on large-scale unlabeled Chinese text and can be fine-tuned with lightweight task-specific layers. We evaluate the model across a broad range of Chinese language understanding and generation tasks, including word segmentation, named entity recognition, part-of-speech tagging, sentence matching, sentiment classification, dependency parsing, semantic role labeling, and machine translation. Experiments show consistent improvements over strong character-, word-, and Transformer-based baselines, with especially substantial gains on tasks involving rare characters, noisy inputs, and fine-grained lexical distinctions. original_abstract: Network embedding has attracted an increasing attention over the past few years. As an effective approach to solve graph mining problems, network embedding aims to learn a low-dimensional feature vector representation for each node of a given network. The vast majority of existing network embedding algorithms, however, are only designed for unsigned networks, and the signed networks containing both positive and negative links, have pretty distinct properties from the unsigned counterpart. In this paper, we propose a deep network embedding model to learn the low-dimensional node vector representations with structural balance preservation for the signed networks. The model employs a semisupervised stacked auto-encoder to reconstruct the adjacency connections of a given signed network. As the adjacency connections are overwhelmingly positive in the real-world signed networks, we impose a larger penalty to make the auto-encoder focus more on reconstructing the scarce negative links than the abundant positive links. In addition, to preserve the structural balance property of signed networks, we design the pairwise constraints to make the positively connected nodes much closer than the negatively connected nodes in the embedding space. Based on the network representations learned by the proposed model, we conduct link sign prediction and community detection in signed networks. Extensive experimental results in real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed model over the state-of-the-art network embedding algorithms for graph representation learning in signed networks.
generated_abstract: Signed social networks contain both positive and negative relationships, but most network embedding methods use only unsigned connectivity and therefore fail to represent antagonism, distrust, and structural imbalance. The method jointly models local neighborhood structure, higher-order signed connectivity, and the relative positions of friends and enemies, using a neural embedding architecture optimized with sampled network interactions. To improve robustness in sparse networks, auxiliary signals such as user content and emotional information can be incorporated, allowing the model to infer unobserved negative as well as positive relationships. The learned representations are evaluated on node classification, signed link prediction, clustering, and visualization tasks across several real-world social media datasets. Experiments show that the proposed approach consistently outperforms traditional feature-based methods and state-of-the-art unsigned and signed network embedding baselines, particularly when labeled links are scarce. The results demonstrate that explicitly learning from both relationship polarity and network context provides effective, scalable representations for analyzing complex social networks.

original_abstract: The ability of inferring its own ego-motion, autonomous understanding the surroundings and planning trajectory are the features of autonomous robot systems. Therefore, in order to improve the perception and decision-making ability of autonomous robot systems, Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) and autonomous trajectory planning are widely researched, especially combining learning-based algorithms. #R##N#In this paper, we mainly focus on the application of learning-based approaches to perception and decision-making, and survey the current state-of-the-art SLAM and trajectory planning algorithms. Firstly, we delineate the existing classical SLAM solutions and review deep learning-based methods of environment perception and understanding, including deep learning-based monocular depth estimation, ego-motion prediction, image enhancement, object detection, semantic segmentation and their combinations with previous SLAM frameworks. Secondly, we summarize the existing path planning and trajectory planning methods and survey the navigation methods based on reinforcement learning. Finally, several challenges and promising directions are concluded to related researchers for future work in both autonomous perception and decision-making.
generated_abstract: Autonomous robots require reliable geometric and semantic perception despite the ambiguity, scale drift, illumination changes, and dynamic objects that affect monocular vision. Depth is trained from photometric reconstruction, geometric consistency, and sparse or stereo-derived supervision, while temporal and feature-level constraints improve robustness to occlusions and low-texture regions. A lightweight enhancement module preserves geometric consistency under challenging lighting, and semantic predictions are integrated with the reconstructed map to identify traversable areas and moving objects. The resulting metric or scale-consistent representation supports localization, dense or semi-dense mapping, and local trajectory replanning without requiring an explicit prior map. We evaluate the approach on driving, indoor, and aerial datasets, including sequences with dynamic objects, high dynamic range, and limited computational resources. Results show improved depth accuracy, reduced odometric drift, and more reliable obstacle avoidance than conventional monocular and learning-based baselines. The framework further demonstrates that learned representations can complement geometric optimization while remaining suitable for real-time robotic deployment.

original_abstract: Completing a corrupted image with correct structures and reasonable textures for a mixed scene remains an elusive challenge. Since the missing hole in a mixed scene of a corrupted image often contains various semantic information, conventional two-stage approaches utilizing structural information often lead to the problem of unreliable structural prediction and ambiguous image texture generation. In this paper, we propose a Semantic Guidance and Evaluation Network (SGE-Net) to iteratively update the structural priors and the inpainted image in an interplay framework of semantics extraction and image inpainting. It utilizes semantic segmentation map as guidance in each scale of inpainting, under which location-dependent inferences are re-evaluated, and, accordingly, poorly-inferred regions are refined in subsequent scales. Extensive experiments on real-world images of mixed scenes demonstrated the superiority of our proposed method over state-of-the-art approaches, in terms of clear boundaries and photo-realistic textures.
generated_abstract: We present a semantic-aware image inpainting framework for restoring large and irregular missing regions in complex urban scenes. A segmentation network first estimates the semantic layout of the damaged area using multi-scale contextual features. The predicted labels then guide a generative completion network through spatially adaptive feature modulation, allowing different object classes to receive appropriate shapes and textures. To preserve high-frequency details, the model additionally exploits contextual feature rearrangement and adversarial perceptual objectives, while an edge-aware refinement stage sharpens object boundaries. The entire system is trained end to end, but its modular design also supports user-provided semantic guidance and multiple plausible completions. We evaluate the method on Cityscapes and other public face and natural-image benchmarks with both regular and free-form masks. Compared with representative context, attention, patch-synthesis, and segmentation-guided baselines, our method produces more coherent structures, sharper textures, and improved semantic alignment, achieving consistent gains in perceptual quality and quantitative reconstruction metrics.

original_abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are well suited for spatio-temporal learning and implementations on energy-efficient event-driven neuromorphic processors. However, existing SNNs error backpropagation (BP) track methods lack proper handling of spiking discontinuities and suffer from low performance compared to BP methods for traditional artificial neural networks. In addition, a large number of time steps are typically required for SNNs to achieve decent performance, leading to high latency and rendering spike-based computation unscalable to deep architectures. We present a novel Temporal Spike Sequence Learning Backpropagation (TSSL-BP) method for training deep SNNs, which breaks down error backpropagation across two types of inter-neuron and intra-neuron dependencies. It considers the all-or-none characteristics of firing activities, capturing inter-neuron dependencies through presynaptic firing times, and internal evolution of each neuronal state through time capturing intra-neuron dependencies. For various image classification datasets, TSSL-BP efficiently trains deep SNNs within a short temporal time window of a few steps with improved accuracy and runtime efficiency including achieving more than 2% accuracy improvement over the previously reported SNN work on CIFAR10.
generated_abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer an attractive combination of biologically plausible computation, temporal information processing, and energy-efficient event-driven execution. However, their practical adoption is limited by the discontinuous spike-generation function, long temporal dependencies, and the difficulty of optimizing deep recurrent architectures. We present a direct gradient-based training framework for deep SNNs that combines spike-train temporal dynamics with surrogate-gradient backpropagation. The method propagates errors through both network depth and simulation time while retaining membrane-potential dynamics and avoiding conversion from conventionally trained artificial neural networks. An efficient implementation in PyTorch uses truncated temporal processing, adaptive optimization, and sparse event-driven operations to reduce training cost. We evaluate the framework on static and neuromorphic benchmarks, including MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, N-MNIST, and speech or event-based recognition tasks. Experiments with fully connected, convolutional, and recurrent architectures demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared with existing SNN training algorithms and, in several settings, approaches conventional deep networks. Additional analyses show that temporal coding improves performance on dynamic inputs while maintaining sparse activity, highlighting the potential of directly trained SNNs for scalable, low-power neuromorphic systems.

original_abstract: Solving grounded language tasks often requires reasoning about relationships between objects in the context of a given task. For example, to answer the question "What color is the mug on the plate?" we must check the color of the specific mug that satisfies the "on" relationship with respect to the plate. Recent work has proposed various methods capable of complex relational reasoning. However, most of their power is in the inference structure, while the scene is represented with simple local appearance features. In this paper, we take an alternate approach and build contextualized representations for objects in a visual scene to support relational reasoning. We propose a general framework of Language-Conditioned Graph Networks (LCGN), where each node represents an object, and is described by a context-aware representation from related objects through iterative message passing conditioned on the textual input. E.g., conditioning on the "on" relationship to the plate, the object "mug" gathers messages from the object "plate" to update its representation to "mug on the plate", which can be easily consumed by a simple classifier for answer prediction. We experimentally show that our LCGN approach effectively supports relational reasoning and improves performance across several tasks and datasets. Our code is available at this http URL.
generated_abstract: Visual question answering requires models to jointly understand image content, language, and the relationships among visual entities. Most existing approaches represent images and questions as independent feature streams and combine them only at a late stage, limiting their ability to capture the question-specific interactions needed for compositional reasoning. We propose a graph-based framework that learns conditioned graph structures for interpretable visual question answering. Given an image and a question, a graph learner identifies relevant objects and predicts their relationships, producing a question-dependent representation of the scene. Graph convolutional operations then propagate information over this learned structure, enabling the model to reason about attributes, spatial configurations, and interactions between entities. The resulting graph provides an explicit and visualizable account of which objects and relations support the answer, improving interpretability without requiring relation annotations. We evaluate the approach on the VQA v2 dataset and show that augmenting a simple baseline with the learned graph substantially improves performance, achieving 66.18% accuracy and competitive state-of-the-art results. Qualitative analyses further demonstrate that the inferred graphs adapt to different questions and capture meaningful relational evidence.

original_abstract: Generating formal-language represented by relational tuples, such as Lisp programs or mathematical expressions, from a natural-language input is an extremely challenging task because it requires to explicitly capture discrete symbolic structural information from the input to generate the output. Most state-of-the-art neural sequence models do not explicitly capture such structure information, and thus do not perform well on these tasks. In this paper, we propose a new encoder-decoder model based on Tensor Product Representations (TPRs) for Natural- to Formal-language generation, called TP-N2F. The encoder of TP-N2F employs TPR 'binding' to encode natural-language symbolic structure in vector space and the decoder uses TPR 'unbinding' to generate a sequence of relational tuples, each consisting of a relation (or operation) and a number of arguments, in symbolic space. TP-N2F considerably outperforms LSTM-based Seq2Seq models, creating a new state of the art results on two benchmarks: the MathQA dataset for math problem solving, and the AlgoList dataset for program synthesis. Ablation studies show that improvements are mainly attributed to the use of TPRs in both the encoder and decoder to explicitly capture relational structure information for symbolic reasoning.
generated_abstract: We present a compositional neural architecture for language understanding that combines the flexibility of deep learning with the interpretability and systematicity of symbolic representations. The model encodes words, grammatical roles, and semantic relations as distributed tensor products, allowing structured meanings to be constructed and manipulated through differentiable operations. Attention mechanisms select relevant symbols and roles, while recurrent components process variable-length input and support incremental inference. Unlike conventional sequence-to-sequence systems, the architecture exposes intermediate representations that can be inspected as lexical, syntactic, and relational structures. We evaluate the approach on natural-language question answering, semantic parsing, and reasoning tasks requiring compositional generalization, including settings with novel combinations of familiar concepts and relations. Training is performed end to end with stochastic gradient optimization and requires no explicit linguistic annotations beyond task supervision. The results show that structured representations improve performance on multi-step reasoning and systematic generalization while remaining competitive with unconstrained neural baselines. Qualitative analyses further indicate that the learned representations capture meaningful grammatical and semantic regularities. These findings suggest that tensor-product-based models provide a practical bridge between neural learning and interpretable symbolic computation for language and dialogue systems.

original_abstract: Using different sources of information to support automated extracting of relations between biomedical concepts contributes to the development of our understanding of biological systems. The primary comprehensive source of these relations is biomedical literature. Several relation extraction approaches have been proposed to identify relations between concepts in biomedical literature, namely using neural networks algorithms. The use of multichannel architectures composed of multiple data representations, as in deep neural networks, is leading to state-of-the-art results. The right combination of data representations can eventually lead us to even higher evaluation scores in relation extraction tasks. Thus, biomedical ontologies play a fundamental role by providing semantic and ancestry information about an entity. The incorporation of biomedical ontologies has already been proved to enhance previous state-of-the-art results.
generated_abstract: Biomedical relation extraction can benefit from domain knowledge encoded in ontologies, particularly when annotated training data are scarce. We present BO-LSTM, a recurrent neural network for detecting and classifying relations between biomedical entities that represents each entity not only through its textual embedding, but also through the sequence of concepts along its ontology ancestry. The model integrates lexical, positional, and ontology-based information using long short-term memory units, enabling it to exploit semantic similarities and distinctions that may be absent from the training corpus. We evaluate BO-LSTM on drug–drug interaction extraction using the SemEval 2013 Task 9.2 corpus, incorporating concepts from ChEBI, the Human Phenotype Ontology, and Gene Ontology. The ontology-enhanced model improves both interaction detection and relation classification, with the largest gains observed in the setting with limited annotations. We further adapt the approach to phenotype–gene relation extraction and introduce a corpus of 228 abstracts annotated for these relations. Experiments demonstrate that the same architecture transfers effectively across biomedical relation types. These results show that combining neural representations with structured biomedical knowledge can improve robustness and reduce dependence on large manually labeled datasets.

original_abstract: Recent advances in language representation using neural networks have made it viable to transfer the learned internal states of a trained model to downstream natural language processing tasks, such as named entity recognition (NER) and question answering. It has been shown that the leverage of pre-trained language models improves the overall performance on many tasks and is highly beneficial when labeled data is scarce. In this work, we employ a pre-trained BERT with Conditional Random Fields (CRF) architecture to the NER task on the Portuguese language, combining the transfer capabilities of BERT with the structured predictions of CRF. We explore feature-based and fine-tuning training strategies for the BERT model. Our fine-tuning approach obtains new state-of-the-art results on the HAREM I dataset, improving the F1-score by 3.2 points on the selective scenario (5 NE classes) and by 3.8 points on the total scenario (10 NE classes).
generated_abstract: Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing, supporting information extraction, question answering, and search applications. Although contextual language models have substantially improved NER in English, their impact on Portuguese remains insufficiently explored. This paper presents a systematic evaluation of contextual representations for Portuguese NER, examining how they interact with conventional word embeddings, corpus size, and textual diversity. We compare 16 combinations of shallow and contextual embeddings, including representations derived from pretrained neural language models, using neural sequence-tagging architectures and the HAREM evaluation corpus. Our experiments investigate whether larger and more diverse unlabeled corpora consistently produce better representations and identify the most effective adaptation strategies for the target task. The results show that contextual embeddings provide substantial gains over static word representations, particularly when combined with complementary lexical information. They also demonstrate that corpus composition and diversity are important factors, not merely the amount of pretraining data. The best-performing system surpasses previously reported Portuguese NER results by 5.99 absolute percentage points, establishing a new state of the art and providing practical guidance for selecting and integrating pretrained representations in Portuguese language-processing systems.

original_abstract: RDMA is an exciting technology that enables a host to access the memory of a remote host without involving the remote CPU. Prior work shows how to use RDMA to improve the performance of distributed in-memory storage systems. However, RDMA is widely believed to have scalability issues, due to the amount of active protocol state that needs to be cached in the limited NIC cache. These concerns led to several software-based proposals to enhance scalability by trading off performance. In this work, we revisit these trade-offs in light of newer RDMA hardware and propose new guidelines for scaling RDMA. We show that using one-sided remote memory primitives leads to higher performance compared to send/receive and kernel-based systems in rack-scale environments. Based on these insights, we design and implement Storm, a transactional dataplane using one-sided read and write-based RPC primitives. We show that Storm outperforms eRPC, FaRM, and LITE by 3.3x, 3.6x, and 17.1x, respectively, on an Infinband EDR cluster with Mellanox ConnectX-4 NICs.
generated_abstract: Modern datacenter networks provide bandwidth and latency comparable to local memory, yet distributed systems continue to treat communication as an expensive resource. This paper explores the design of a distributed in-memory database that makes network access a first-class operation rather than minimizing it through rigid data partitioning. We present an RDMA-based architecture for executing transactions across machines, combining one-sided reads and atomic operations with optimistic concurrency control, efficient remote procedure calls, and decentralized coordination. The design carefully accounts for practical bottlenecks beyond the network, including congestion, PCIe transfers, address translation, memory layout, and persistent-memory durability. It supports replicated state and synchronous mirroring while preserving strong consistency and availability, and avoids centralized lock managers and application-specific co-partitioning. We implement the system on commodity servers and high-speed RDMA fabrics and evaluate it using microbenchmarks, key-value workloads, and TPC-C-style transactions. Results show that distributed transactions can achieve low microsecond-scale latency and near-linear throughput as machines are added, while maintaining predictable tail behavior under contention. The findings demonstrate that, with suitable hardware-aware mechanisms, communication and distributed coordination need not be inherent scalability bottlenecks.

original_abstract: Modern text-to-speech (TTS) systems are able to generate audio that sounds almost as natural as human speech. However, the bar of developing high-quality TTS systems remains high since a sizable set of studio-quality   pairs is usually required. Compared to commercial data used to develop state-of-the-art systems, publicly available data are usually worse in terms of both quality and size. Audio generated by TTS systems trained on publicly available data tends to not only sound less natural, but also exhibits more background noise. In this work, we aim to lower TTS systems' reliance on high-quality data by providing them the textual knowledge extracted by deep pre-trained language models during training. In particular, we investigate the use of BERT to assist the training of Tacotron-2, a state of the art TTS consisting of an encoder and an attention-based decoder. BERT representations learned from large amounts of unlabeled text data are shown to contain very rich semantic and syntactic information about the input text, and have potential to be leveraged by a TTS system to compensate the lack of high-quality data. We incorporate BERT as a parallel branch to the Tacotron-2 encoder with its own attention head. For an input text, it is simultaneously passed into BERT and the Tacotron-2 encoder. The representations extracted by the two branches are concatenated and then fed to the decoder. As a preliminary study, although we have not found incorporating BERT into Tacotron-2 generates more natural or cleaner speech at a human-perceivable level, we observe improvements in other aspects such as the model is being significantly better at knowing when to stop decoding such that there is much less babbling at the end of the synthesized audio and faster convergence during training.
generated_abstract: We present a data-efficient end-to-end text-to-speech system that combines contextual language representations with Transformer-based acoustic modeling. The proposed model uses phoneme sequences together with embeddings extracted from a pretrained bidirectional language model, allowing the encoder to represent lexical, syntactic, and contextual information that is unavailable to conventional phoneme-only systems. A multi-head self-attention architecture replaces recurrent components, improving parallel training and modeling long-range dependencies in text. The resulting mel-spectrograms are converted to waveforms with a non-autoregressive flow-based neural vocoder, enabling fast inference while preserving naturalness. To reduce the dependence on expensive paired text–speech recordings, we further exploit unpaired text and speech through language-model pretraining and acoustic-domain initialization, followed by fine-tuning on a small parallel corpus. Experiments on in-domain and out-of-domain utterances show that contextual representations improve pronunciation, prosody, and robustness, particularly for rare words and complex sentence structures. The proposed system achieves substantially faster training and synthesis than recurrent sequence-to-sequence baselines, while producing speech quality comparable to strong autoregressive TTS systems and remaining effective when only limited paired data are available.

original_abstract: Decentralized solutions to finite-sum minimization are of significant importance in many signal processing, control, and machine learning applications. In such settings, the data is distributed over a network of arbitrarily-connected nodes and raw data sharing is prohibitive often due to communication or privacy constraints. In this article, we review decentralized stochastic first-order optimization methods and illustrate some recent improvements based on gradient tracking and variance reduction, focusing particularly on smooth and strongly-convex objective functions. We provide intuitive illustrations of the main technical ideas as well as applications of the algorithms in the context of decentralized training of machine learning models.
generated_abstract: We study decentralized finite-sum optimization over networks in which each agent stores a local collection of training examples and can communicate only with its neighbors. The objective is to minimize the sum of smooth, strongly convex local losses, while reducing both stochastic-gradient noise and the communication required to reach an accurate solution. We propose a decentralized variance-reduced method that combines local stochastic gradient estimators with consensus and gradient tracking. The method requires only a constant amount of memory per agent, supports heterogeneous data sizes and unbalanced computation, and can be implemented over directed as well as undirected connected graphs. Under standard smoothness, strong-convexity, and network-connectivity assumptions, we establish linear convergence in expectation to the exact global minimizer. The resulting complexity improves over decentralized stochastic gradient methods by removing the persistent variance floor and achieves favorable dependence on the condition number, local data size, and network mixing time. We also develop a mini-batch and communication-efficient variant that trades local computation for fewer exchanges. Numerical experiments on distributed classification and regression problems demonstrate faster convergence and lower communication cost than consensus, diffusion, gradient-tracking, and existing decentralized variance-reduction baselines.

original_abstract: We present Location Field Descriptors, a novel approach for single image 3D model retrieval in the wild. In contrast to previous methods that directly map 3D models and RGB images to an embedding space, we establish a common low-level representation in the form of location fields from which we compute pose invariant 3D shape descriptors. Location fields encode correspondences between 2D pixels and 3D surface coordinates and, thus, explicitly capture 3D shape and 3D pose information without appearance variations which are irrelevant for the task. This early fusion of 3D models and RGB images results in three main advantages: First, the bottleneck location field prediction acts as a regularizer during training. Second, major parts of the system benefit from training on a virtually infinite amount of synthetic data. Finally, the predicted location fields are visually interpretable and unblackbox the system. We evaluate our proposed approach on three challenging real-world datasets (Pix3D, Comp, and Stanford) with different object categories and significantly outperform the state-of-the-art by up to 20% absolute in multiple 3D retrieval metrics.
generated_abstract: We present a learning-based framework for reconstructing the complete 3D geometry of an object from a single RGB image. Unlike methods that predict a single deterministic shape or rely on dense voxel grids, our approach combines a compact latent representation of 3D point clouds with image-based inference, allowing efficient generation of detailed and diverse shapes. We first train an autoencoder on large-scale CAD models to learn a structured embedding space that captures object geometry. An image encoder then predicts a distribution over this space, conditioned on the visible evidence and category-level shape priors. Sampling from the predicted distribution produces multiple plausible reconstructions, explicitly modeling the ambiguity caused by occlusion and unknown viewpoints. A view-consistency objective ensures that generated point clouds agree with the input image, while metric-learning constraints improve geometric discrimination between related shapes. We evaluate the method on synthetic and real-world benchmarks, including single-view reconstruction and shape completion tasks. The proposed model achieves more accurate reconstructions than existing voxel-, image-, and point-based baselines, while producing sharper details and greater diversity, demonstrating the value of latent shape matching for robust 3D perception.

original_abstract: Rotation detection is a challenging task due to the difficulties of locating the multi-angle objects and separating them accurately and quickly from the background. Though considerable progress has been made, there still exist challenges for rotating objects with large aspect ratio, dense distribution and category extremely imbalance. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end refined single-stage rotation detector for fast and accurate positioning objects. Considering the shortcoming of feature misalignment in the current refined single-stage detector, we design a feature refinement module to improve detection performance, which is especially effective in the long tail data set. The key idea of feature refinement module is to re-encode the position information of the current refined bounding box to the corresponding feature points through feature interpolation to realize feature reconstruction and alignment. Extensive experiments on two remote sensing public datasets DOTA, HRSC2016 as well as scene text data ICDAR2015 show the state-of-the-art accuracy and speed of our detector. Source code and the models will be made public available upon the publish of the paper.
generated_abstract: Detecting oriented and densely packed objects in aerial and natural images remains challenging because objects vary substantially in scale, aspect ratio, and direction, while nearby instances and cluttered backgrounds cause inaccurate localization and missed detections. We propose a unified single-stage framework for robust oriented object detection that combines multi-scale feature representation, orientation-aware refinement, and an IoU-guided regression objective. The detector first extracts semantically strong features through a lightweight feature pyramid and adaptively selects spatial context according to the estimated object geometry. A refinement head then progressively adjusts coarse horizontal or rotated proposals, aligning classification features with the refined object regions and improving consistency between confidence and localization quality. To avoid ambiguity in angle and vertex regression, oriented boxes are represented with a periodic orientation encoding and optimized using a geometry-aware loss that considers overlap and center distance. The entire network is trained end to end without additional proposal generation or costly rotated post-processing. Extensive experiments on DOTA, HRSC2016, UCAS-AOD, and scene-text benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over representative one-stage and two-stage detectors, particularly for small, elongated, arbitrarily oriented, and densely arranged objects, while preserving efficient inference.

original_abstract: Existing conversational systems tend to generate generic responses. Recently, Background Based Conversations (BBCs) have been introduced to address this issue. Here, the generated responses are grounded in some background information. The proposed methods for BBCs are able to generate more informative responses, they either cannot generate natural responses or have difficulty in locating the right background information. In this paper, we propose a Reference-aware Network (RefNet) to address the two issues. Unlike existing methods that generate responses token by token, RefNet incorporates a novel reference decoder that provides an alternative way to learn to directly cite a semantic unit (e.g., a span containing complete semantic information) from the background. Experimental results show that RefNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both automatic and human evaluations, indicating that RefNet can generate more appropriate and human-like responses.
generated_abstract: Neural dialogue systems can generate fluent responses, yet they often produce generic, repetitive, or factually unsupported utterances because they rely primarily on conversational history. We present an end-to-end framework for knowledge-grounded response generation that integrates document retrieval, machine reading, and neural decoding. Given a multi-turn conversation and a collection of external documents, the model first selects relevant knowledge using context-aware attention, then extracts and represents supporting information through a bidirectional reading-comprehension module. A response decoder combines dialogue context and the selected evidence, while a pointer-generation mechanism copies entities and factual phrases that are rare or absent from the vocabulary. To improve conversational quality, we further introduce a diversity-aware training objective that reduces the preference for frequent generic words. The framework can generate responses that are both natural and explicitly grounded in source documents, while retaining the flexibility to produce content not copied directly from them. Experiments on document-grounded and open-domain conversation benchmarks show consistent improvements over retrieval, standard sequence-to-sequence, and previously proposed knowledge-aware baselines in informativeness, knowledge relevance, response diversity, and human-rated coherence. Analysis also demonstrates that learned knowledge selection provides interpretable evidence for generated responses.

original_abstract: Cryptocurrencies have garnered much attention in recent years, both from the academic community and industry. One interesting aspect of cryptocurrencies is their explicit consideration of incentives at the protocol level. Understanding how to incorporate this into the models used to design cryptocurrencies has motivated a large body of work, yet many open problems still exist and current systems rarely deal with incentive related problems well. This issue arises due to the gap between Cryptography and Distributed Systems security, which deals with traditional security problems that ignore the explicit consideration of incentives, and Game Theory, which deals best with situations involving incentives. With this work, we aim to offer a systematization of the work that relates to this problem, considering papers that blend Game Theory with Cryptography or Distributed systems and discussing how they can be related. This gives an overview of the available tools, and we look at their (potential) use in practice, in the context of existing blockchain based systems that have been proposed or implemented.
generated_abstract: Blockchain systems replace trusted intermediaries with distributed protocols whose security and performance depend not only on cryptography, but also on the incentives of economically motivated participants. This paper surveys game-theoretic approaches to the design and analysis of blockchain systems. We organize existing work around consensus and mining, information propagation, reward and fee allocation, pool formation, proof-of-stake, decentralization, and off-chain mechanisms. We examine how strategic behavior produces selfish mining, transaction withholding, pool infiltration, free riding, wealth concentration, and other deviations from prescribed protocols. Particular attention is given to the limitations of Nash equilibrium and to models incorporating costly computation, bounded rationality, coalitional behavior, imperfect information, and non-myopic responses. We compare proposed countermeasures and incentive mechanisms using criteria including incentive compatibility, Sybil resistance, collusion resistance, efficiency, fairness, and security under Byzantine faults. The survey also highlights tensions between profitability and decentralization, and between scalability and robust consensus. Finally, we identify methodological and practical gaps, including the need for realistic dynamic models, empirical validation, automated attack discovery, and mechanisms whose formal guarantees remain meaningful in open, evolving blockchain ecosystems.

original_abstract: The use of background knowledge remains largely unexploited in many text classification tasks. In this work, we explore word taxonomies as means for constructing new semantic features, which may improve the performance and robustness of the learned classifiers. We propose tax2vec, a parallel algorithm for constructing taxonomy based features, and demonstrate its use on six short-text classification problems, including gender, age and personality type prediction, drug effectiveness and side effect prediction, and news topic prediction. The experimental results indicate that the interpretable features constructed using tax2vec can notably improve the performance of classifiers; the constructed features, in combination with fast, linear classifiers tested against strong baselines, such as hierarchical attention neural networks, achieved comparable or better classification results on short documents. Further, tax2vec can also serve for extraction of corpus-specific keywords. Finally, we investigated the semantic space of potential features where we observe a similarity with the well known Zipf's law.
generated_abstract: We present a hybrid framework for text classification that combines semantic knowledge, graph structure, and neural representation learning. Documents, words, and concepts are modeled as a heterogeneous graph, with lexical and ontological relations obtained from resources such as WordNet and multilingual semantic repositories. To represent textual content, we integrate contextual language embeddings with subword and phrase information, while graph convolution and neighborhood aggregation capture relational dependencies and structural similarity among documents and concepts. We further introduce a prototype-based classification layer that supports both conventional and low-resource classification by comparing document representations with class prototypes. Feature selection and interpretable symbolic graph patterns are used to reduce sparsity, improve efficiency, and expose the evidence underlying predictions. The framework is evaluated on news, review, short-message, sentiment, and specialized biological text datasets, including settings with limited labeled data and previously unseen classes. Across these tasks, the proposed approach consistently improves over traditional bag-of-words models, standalone deep classifiers, and shallow node-embedding baselines. Results indicate that combining distributional semantics with explicit knowledge and graph topology yields more robust, transferable, and interpretable representations for document classification.

original_abstract: Language models have become a key step to achieve state-of-the art results in many different Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. Leveraging the huge amount of unlabeled texts nowadays available, they provide an efficient way to pre-train continuous word representations that can be fine-tuned for a downstream task, along with their contextualization at the sentence level. This has been widely demonstrated for English using contextualized representations (Dai and Le, 2015; Peters et al., 2018; Howard and Ruder, 2018; Radford et al., 2018; Devlin et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019b). In this paper, we introduce and share FlauBERT, a model learned on a very large and heterogeneous French corpus. Models of different sizes are trained using the new CNRS (French National Centre for Scientific Research) Jean Zay supercomputer. We apply our French language models to diverse NLP tasks (text classification, paraphrasing, natural language inference, parsing, word sense disambiguation) and show that most of the time they outperform other pre-training approaches. Different versions of FlauBERT as well as a unified evaluation protocol for the downstream tasks, called FLUE (French Language Understanding Evaluation), are shared to the research community for further reproducible experiments in French NLP.
generated_abstract: Word sense disambiguation remains a challenging task because lexical ambiguity depends on subtle syntactic, semantic, and contextual cues, while manually sense-annotated data are scarce, particularly for languages other than English. We present a resource-efficient neural approach to multilingual word sense disambiguation that combines contextual Transformer representations with lexical knowledge derived from WordNet and Wiktionary. The system uses automatically extracted sense definitions and examples to construct training data, aligns heterogeneous sense inventories, and compresses closely related senses to reduce the output space. A shared encoder is first trained on multilingual text and then fine-tuned with available annotated corpora, enabling transfer from English and other resource-rich languages to low-resource settings. We evaluate the method on standard English resources and on French verb disambiguation, including data drawn from Wiktionary and manually annotated test sets. Experiments show that contextual representations substantially outperform static embeddings and traditional knowledge-based baselines, while sense compression improves coverage without reducing precision. The results demonstrate that collaboratively edited lexical resources, multilingual pretraining, and semi-supervised learning can provide a practical foundation for accurate WSD when task-specific annotations are limited.

original_abstract: High storage and computational costs obstruct deep neural networks to be deployed on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation aims to train a compact student network by transferring knowledge from a larger pre-trained teacher model. However, most existing methods on knowledge distillation ignore the valuable information among training process associated with training results. In this paper, we provide a new Collaborative Teaching Knowledge Distillation (CTKD) strategy which employs two special teachers. Specifically, one teacher trained from scratch (i.e., scratch teacher) assists the student step by step using its temporary outputs. It forces the student to approach the optimal path towards the final logits with high accuracy. The other pre-trained teacher (i.e., expert teacher) guides the student to focus on a critical region which is more useful for the task. The combination of the knowledge from two special teachers can significantly improve the performance of the student network in knowledge distillation. The results of experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet datasets verify that the proposed knowledge distillation method is efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
generated_abstract: We present a framework for constructing compact and accurate neural networks for visual question answering on resource-constrained devices. Although modern convolutional architectures achieve strong performance on image and language tasks, their depth, width, and parameter redundancy make them costly to store and execute, while directly designing a small model often leads to substantial accuracy degradation. Our method combines automated architecture exploration with knowledge transfer from a high-capacity teacher. Candidate student networks are generated progressively under explicit computation and memory budgets, using efficient convolutional building blocks and structured connectivity. During training, the student is guided not only by ground-truth answers but also by the teacher’s soft predictions, intermediate representations, and visual attention patterns, allowing it to learn informative multimodal representations despite its reduced capacity. We further apply channel pruning and low-precision quantization to obtain deployable models without irregular sparse operations. Experiments on established visual question answering benchmarks show that the proposed students retain most of the teacher’s accuracy while substantially reducing parameters, memory use, and inference time. The results demonstrate that jointly optimizing architecture, distillation, and compression is more effective than applying these techniques independently, enabling practical on-device visual question answering.

original_abstract: This work investigates if the current neural architectures are adequate for learning symbolic rewriting. Two kinds of data sets are proposed for this research -- one based on automated proofs and the other being a synthetic set of polynomial terms. The experiments with use of the current neural machine translation models are performed and its results are discussed. Ideas for extending this line of research are proposed and its relevance is motivated.
generated_abstract: We present a learning-based framework for assisting the formalization and verification of mathematics. The system translates informal, LaTeX-based mathematical statements and proofs into the formal language of the Mizar proof assistant, while exploiting the syntactic and semantic structure of mathematical expressions. Building on attention-based sequence transduction, we investigate Transformer models adapted to the structured nature of formal mathematics and compare them with recurrent and tree-based architectures. To improve reliability beyond surface-level translation, generated statements are checked by the formal verifier, and neural premise selection is used to retrieve relevant definitions, lemmas, and previously established facts from large libraries. We further explore data augmentation, structured representations, and learning-assisted reasoning inspired by symbolic mathematics, logical entailment, and inductive logic programming. Experiments on aligned informal–formal corpora show that neural models can generate valid formal statements and proof fragments at useful rates, although performance remains sensitive to terminology, long-range dependencies, and library context. Combining translation with verification and automated deduction substantially improves practical utility, suggesting a path toward scalable semi-automated formalization and theorem proving. The resulting system provides both readable informal output and machine-checkable mathematical knowledge.

original_abstract: Zero-shot learning (ZSL) has received extensive attention recently especially in areas of fine-grained object recognition, retrieval, and image captioning. Due to the complete lack of training samples and high requirement of defense transferability, the ZSL model learned is particularly vulnerable against adversarial attacks. Recent work also showed adversarially robust generalization requires more data. This may significantly affect the robustness of ZSL. However, very few efforts have been devoted towards this direction. In this paper, we take an initial attempt, and propose a generic formulation to provide a systematical solution (named ATZSL) for learning a robust ZSL model. It is capable of achieving better generalization on various adversarial objects recognition while only losing a negligible performance on clean images for unseen classes, by casting ZSL into a min-max optimization problem. To address it, we design a defensive relation prediction network, which can bridge the seen and unseen class domains via attributes to generalize prediction and defense strategy. Additionally, our framework can be extended to deal with the poisoned scenario of unseen class attributes. An extensive group of experiments are then presented, demonstrating that ATZSL obtains remarkably more favorable trade-off between model transferability and robustness, over currently available alternatives under various settings.
generated_abstract: Zero-shot learning enables visual recognition of classes for which no labeled images are available, but existing models are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations and often fail under the domain shift between seen and unseen categories. We propose a robust zero-shot learning framework that jointly learns semantic visual representations and adversarially resistant classifiers. A semantic encoder maps class attributes, textual descriptions, and relational information to discriminative visual prototypes, while a conditional feature generator synthesizes representative features for unseen classes. To improve transferability, training alternates between worst-case perturbation generation and model optimization, enforcing consistency between clean and perturbed representations and preserving semantic relations among class prototypes. The resulting classifier is trained on both real seen-class features and synthesized unseen-class features, enabling generalized zero-shot recognition without access to unseen images. We evaluate the method on standard benchmark datasets under clean, white-box, and black-box attacks using multiple perturbation norms. Experiments show that the proposed approach improves the harmonic mean of seen- and unseen-class accuracy while substantially reducing attack success rates. These results demonstrate that semantic feature synthesis and principled adversarial training can jointly address the recognition and robustness challenges of zero-shot learning.

original_abstract: Polygonal meshes provide an efficient representation for 3D shapes. They explicitly captureboth shape surface and topology, and leverage non-uniformity to represent large flat regions as well as sharp, intricate features. This non-uniformity and irregularity, however, inhibits mesh analysis efforts using neural networks that combine convolution and pooling operations. In this paper, we utilize the unique properties of the mesh for a direct analysis of 3D shapes using MeshCNN, a convolutional neural network designed specifically for triangular meshes. Analogous to classic CNNs, MeshCNN combines specialized convolution and pooling layers that operate on the mesh edges, by leveraging their intrinsic geodesic connections. Convolutions are applied on edges and the four edges of their incident triangles, and pooling is applied via an edge collapse operation that retains surface topology, thereby, generating new mesh connectivity for the subsequent convolutions. MeshCNN learns which edges to collapse, thus forming a task-driven process where the network exposes and expands the important features while discarding the redundant ones. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MeshCNN on various learning tasks applied to 3D meshes.
generated_abstract: We present a deep neural network architecture for learning directly on three-dimensional triangle meshes. Unlike voxel-, multi-view-, or point-based methods, our approach preserves the original surface representation and exploits its connectivity while avoiding the memory and resolution limitations of volumetric convolutions. The network defines convolutional features on mesh edges using the local neighborhoods of their incident triangles, allowing information to be propagated across the surface without requiring a shared parameterization or point correspondence.
