We introduce a learned pooling operation based on iterative edge collapses, which progressively simplifies the mesh while retaining geometrically and semantically important structure. A corresponding unpooling operation records the collapse history and enables accurate dense predictions for segmentation. The entire pipeline, including feature extraction, pooling, and task-specific prediction, is trained end-to-end. We evaluate the method on shape classification and semantic segmentation benchmarks, using meshes with widely varying resolutions and tessellations. The results show that the proposed representation achieves competitive or superior accuracy while using substantially fewer samples than competing approaches. Its ability to adapt the mesh hierarchy to the task also produces interpretable, compact shape representations and robust predictions across diverse object categories.

original_abstract: We present a target-driven navigation approach for improving the cross-target and cross-scene generalization for visual navigation. Our approach incorporates an information-theoretic regularization into a deep reinforcement learning (RL) framework. First, we present a supervised generative model to constrain the intermediate process of the RL policy, which is used to generate a future observation from a current observation and a target. Next, we predict a navigation action by analyzing the difference between the generated future and the current. Our approach takes into account the connection between current observations and targets, and the interrelation between actions and visual transformations. This results in a compact and generalizable navigation model. We perform experiments on the AI2-THOR framework and the Active Vision Dataset (AVD) and show at least 7.8% improvement in navigation success rate and 5.7% in SPL, compared to the supervised baseline, in unexplored environments.
generated_abstract: We present a learning-based framework for mapless visual navigation in previously unseen environments. The system combines a deep perception module, which predicts short-horizon waypoints from onboard camera observations, with a model-based planner and feedback controller that converts these predictions into smooth, dynamically feasible actions. This hybrid design separates visual understanding from low-level control, reducing the need for explicit localization, dense geometric maps, or hand-tuned navigation rules while retaining the robustness of classical planning. To improve generalization and data efficiency, the perception network is trained with self-supervised auxiliary objectives, synthetic visual variation, and demonstrations collected from a range of environments and controllers. During deployment, the planner continuously filters uncertain or inconsistent predictions and replans around previously unseen obstacles and moving agents. We evaluate the approach in photorealistic simulation and on physical ground and aerial robots across indoor, outdoor, and cluttered settings. Compared with end-to-end policies, geometric mapping pipelines, and purely model-free reinforcement learning, our method achieves higher goal-reaching success, better path efficiency, and improved robustness to appearance changes and sparse visual observations. The results demonstrate that combining learned representations with explicit trajectory optimization offers a practical route toward transferable autonomous navigation.

original_abstract: Quizbowl is a scholastic trivia competition that tests human knowledge and intelligence; additionally, it supports diverse research in question answering (QA). A Quizbowl question consists of multiple sentences whose clues are arranged by difficulty (from obscure to obvious) and uniquely identify a well-known entity such as those found on Wikipedia. Since players can answer the question at any time, an elite player (human or machine) demonstrates its superiority by answering correctly given as few clues as possible. We make two key contributions to machine learning research through Quizbowl: (1) collecting and curating a large factoid QA dataset and an accompanying gameplay dataset, and (2) developing a computational approach to playing Quizbowl that involves determining both what to answer and when to answer. Our Quizbowl system has defeated some of the best trivia players in the world over a multi-year series of exhibition matches. Throughout this paper, we show that collaborations with the vibrant Quizbowl community have contributed to the high quality of our dataset, led to new research directions, and doubled as an exciting way to engage the public with research in machine learning and natural language processing.
generated_abstract: We present a neural question answering system for quiz bowl that combines document retrieval, contextual language understanding, and decision-making under uncertainty. The system encodes questions with deep bidirectional representations, identifies salient clues and long-range references, and searches a large text collection for supporting evidence. Retrieved passages are scored by a neural reader and complementary lexical models, while calibrated confidence estimates determine whether the system should answer or abstain. To improve robustness, we train with diverse question sources and adversarially written examples designed to expose reliance on superficial lexical and positional cues. We evaluate on standard and newly collected trivia questions, including questions requiring multi-sentence reasoning, entity resolution, and recognition of when evidence is insufficient. The results show substantial improvements over retrieval-only, recurrent, and memory-based baselines, although performance remains below that of expert human players on adversarial and compositionally difficult questions. In a cooperative setting, exposing the system’s evidence and uncertainty helps human players distinguish reliable predictions from guesses and improves overall team performance. Our analysis identifies calibration, evidence selection, and syntactic variation as central remaining challenges for reliable open-domain question answering.

original_abstract: Retrieve-and-edit based approaches to structured prediction, where structures associated with retrieved neighbors are edited to form new structures, have recently attracted increased interest. However, much recent work merely conditions on retrieved structures (e.g., in a sequence-to-sequence framework), rather than explicitly manipulating them. We show we can perform accurate sequence labeling by explicitly (and only) copying labels from retrieved neighbors. Moreover, because this copying is label-agnostic, we can achieve impressive performance in zero-shot sequence-labeling tasks. We additionally consider a dynamic programming approach to sequence labeling in the presence of retrieved neighbors, which allows for controlling the number of distinct (copied) segments used to form a prediction, and leads to both more interpretable and accurate predictions.
generated_abstract: We present a unified neural framework for sequence labeling that combines contextual representation learning, retrieval, and structured prediction to improve performance across domains and languages. The model encodes an input sentence with a bidirectional Transformer and retrieves similar labeled examples from a source corpus. Rather than generating labels independently, it uses the retrieved sequences as prototypes, adapting their decisions to the target sentence through an attention-based editing mechanism. Character-level representations and auxiliary segmentation and part-of-speech objectives provide robustness to unknown words, noisy text, and languages with ambiguous word boundaries. The framework can be trained with standard supervised data, transferred across domains and languages, and extended to settings with limited or no token-level target annotations. We evaluate it on named entity recognition, part-of-speech tagging, chunking, and cross-lingual transfer benchmarks, including newswire, social media, and e-commerce data. Results show consistent improvements over feature-based systems, recurrent and convolutional sequence taggers, and strong pretrained-language-model baselines. Ablation studies demonstrate that retrieval contributes complementary information to contextual embeddings, while auxiliary tasks improve generalization in low-resource settings. The approach also offers interpretable predictions by exposing the examples and edits that support each labeling decision.

original_abstract: Contextual word representations, typically trained on unstructured, unlabeled text, do not contain any explicit grounding to real world entities and are often unable to remember facts about those entities. We propose a general method to embed multiple knowledge bases (KBs) into large scale models, and thereby enhance their representations with structured, human-curated knowledge. For each KB, we first use an integrated entity linker to retrieve relevant entity embeddings, then update contextual word representations via a form of word-to-entity attention. In contrast to previous approaches, the entity linkers and self-supervised language modeling objective are jointly trained end-to-end in a multitask setting that combines a small amount of entity linking supervision with a large amount of raw text. After integrating WordNet and a subset of Wikipedia into BERT, the knowledge enhanced BERT (KnowBert) demonstrates improved perplexity, ability to recall facts as measured in a probing task and downstream performance on relationship extraction, entity typing, and word sense disambiguation. KnowBert's runtime is comparable to BERT's and it scales to large KBs.
generated_abstract: We present a knowledge-enhanced framework for language understanding that combines contextual language representations with information from structured knowledge graphs and unstructured text. The approach first encodes documents using a pretrained Transformer, then identifies entity mentions and links them to candidate knowledge-graph entities. A graph-based module retrieves relevant neighbors, relations, entity descriptions, and commonsense facts, while an attention mechanism selectively integrates this information with token and span representations. This design supports joint reasoning over linguistic context and external facts without relying on task-specific syntactic features or extensive manual engineering. We evaluate the framework on relation extraction, entity typing, entity linking, natural language inference, and reading comprehension, using both standard supervised settings and low-resource and cross-domain conditions. Across experiments, knowledge integration consistently improves performance over strong pretrained-language-model baselines, with the largest gains on examples requiring entity disambiguation, long-range reasoning, and implicit commonsense knowledge. Ablation studies show that contextual representations, entity linking quality, and adaptive knowledge selection are complementary; indiscriminate graph expansion, in contrast, introduces noise. The results demonstrate that combining pretrained language models with explicit, dynamically retrieved knowledge provides a practical route toward more factual, interpretable, and data-efficient language understanding.

original_abstract: Selecting in-domain data from a large pool of diverse and out-of-domain data is a non-trivial problem. In most cases simply using all of the available data will lead to sub-optimal and in some cases even worse performance compared to carefully selecting a matching set. This is true even for data-inefficient neural models. Acoustic Latent Dirichlet Allocation (aLDA) is shown to be useful in a variety of speech technology related tasks, including domain adaptation of acoustic models for automatic speech recognition and entity labeling for information retrieval. In this paper we propose to use aLDA as a data similarity criterion in a data selection framework. Given a large pool of out-of-domain and potentially mismatched data, the task is to select the best-matching training data to a set of representative utterances sampled from a target domain. Our target data consists of around 32 hours of meeting data (both far-field and close-talk) and the pool contains 2k hours of meeting, talks, voice search, dictation, command-and-control, audio books, lectures, generic media and telephony speech data. The proposed technique for training data selection, significantly outperforms random selection, posterior-based selection as well as using all of the available data.
generated_abstract: Automatic speech recognition of broadcast media is challenging because acoustic conditions, speakers, recording channels and speaking styles vary substantially within and across programmes. Conventional genre labels provide only a coarse description of this variability, while training on heterogeneous data can cause negative transfer. This paper investigates unsupervised discovery and exploitation of latent acoustic domains for robust multi-genre speech recognition. Latent Dirichlet Allocation is applied to speech-derived representations to assign each recording a mixture of hidden domain properties. These representations are used both to organise large broadcast archives and to guide acoustic model adaptation, including neural-network adaptation through domain codes. We further examine domain-aware selection of training data, choosing utterances that are acoustically relevant to a target set while avoiding detrimental examples. Experiments on extensive BBC broadcast data, together with diverse speech from telephone, meeting, lecture and read-speech domains, show that latent domains capture distinctions not represented by programme genre or metadata. Domain-informed adaptation and selective training consistently outperform pooled baselines, yielding relative word error rate reductions of up to 13% for deep neural network systems and complementary gains from targeted data selection. The results demonstrate the value of unsupervised domain modelling for scalable speech recognition in heterogeneous media archives.

original_abstract: With advancements in deep model architectures, tasks in computer vision can reach optimal convergence provided proper data preprocessing and model parameter initialization. However, training on datasets with low feature-richness for complex applications limit and detriment optimal convergence below human performance. In past works, researchers have provided external sources of complementary data at the cost of supplementary hardware, which are fed in streams to counteract this limitation and boost performance. We propose a generative multi-stream architecture, eliminating the need for additional hardware with the intent to improve feature richness without risking impracticability. We also introduce the compact spatio-temporal residual block to the standard 3-dimensional convolutional model, C3D. Our rC3D model performs comparatively to the top C3D residual variant architecture, the pseudo-3D model, on the FASL-RGB dataset. Our methods have achieved 95.62% validation accuracy with a variance of 1.42% from training, outperforming past models by 0.45% in validation accuracy and 5.53% in variance.
generated_abstract: We present a deep learning framework for recognizing American Sign Language gestures in continuous video. Unlike recognition from isolated images or pre-segmented clips, our method must identify meaningful signing intervals while modeling both local motion and long-range temporal dependencies. The proposed architecture combines complementary visual modalities, including RGB appearance, optical flow, and depth, with a spatiotemporal feature extractor based on pseudo-3D residual convolutions. This design captures motion efficiently while retaining the representational strength and transferability of pretrained two-dimensional networks. The resulting clip-level features are processed by a recurrent convolutional sequence model to classify signs and determine their temporal boundaries. A fully convolutional segmentation component is used to emphasize the signer and reduce background variation, while multimodal feature fusion improves robustness to illumination, viewpoint, and signing speed. We evaluate the system on continuous videos containing both isolated word sequences and sentence-level signing, using annotations for each semantic gesture interval. Experiments show that integrating appearance, motion, depth, and recurrent temporal modeling substantially improves recognition and localization compared with image-based, single-stream, and fixed-window baselines. The results demonstrate the potential of efficient spatiotemporal residual networks for practical continuous sign language understanding.

original_abstract: While deep learning is successful in a number of applications, it is not yet well understood theoretically. A satisfactory theoretical characterization of deep learning however, is beginning to emerge. It covers the following questions: 1) representation power of deep networks 2) optimization of the empirical risk 3) generalization properties of gradient descent techniques --- why the expected error does not suffer, despite the absence of explicit regularization, when the networks are overparametrized? In this review we discuss recent advances in the three areas. In approximation theory both shallow and deep networks have been shown to approximate any continuous functions on a bounded domain at the expense of an exponential number of parameters (exponential in the dimensionality of the function). However, for a subset of compositional functions, deep networks of the convolutional type can have a linear dependence on dimensionality, unlike shallow networks. In optimization we discuss the loss landscape for the exponential loss function and show that stochastic gradient descent will find with high probability the global minima. To address the question of generalization for classification tasks, we use classical uniform convergence results to justify minimizing a surrogate exponential-type loss function under a unit norm constraint on the weight matrix at each layer -- since the interesting variables for classification are the weight directions rather than the weights. Our approach, which is supported by several independent new results, offers a solution to the puzzle about generalization performance of deep overparametrized ReLU networks, uncovering the origin of the underlying hidden complexity control.
generated_abstract: This paper develops a theoretical perspective on why highly overparameterized deep neural networks can be efficiently optimized and still generalize. We synthesize results on the approximation and representation advantages of depth, showing how compositional structure, hierarchical features, and piecewise-linear activations can overcome limitations of shallow models and the curse of dimensionality. We then examine the optimization landscape of wide ReLU and convolutional networks, where suitable initialization, residual or identity structures, and random or stochastic gradient methods can yield polynomial-time convergence despite nonconvexity, spurious minima, and saddle points. In overparameterized regimes, interpolation is not necessarily synonymous with overfitting: the geometry of the data, kernel spectra, and the implicit bias of optimization can control prediction risk and produce double-descent behavior. Gradient descent is shown to induce effective regularization through minimum-norm, margin-maximizing, balanced, or otherwise complexity-controlled solutions, while noise can favor broad and robust minima. Connections with conjugate kernels and random-feature models clarify which aspects of deep learning arise from optimization and which arise from representation. Together, these results identify a coherent set of mechanisms linking expressivity, optimization, and generalization, while highlighting important gaps for realistic architectures and data distributions.

original_abstract: We present a novel framework for machine translation evaluation using neural networks in a pairwise setting, where the goal is to select the better translation from a pair of hypotheses, given the reference translation. In this framework, lexical, syntactic and semantic information from the reference and the two hypotheses is compacted into relatively small distributed vector representations, and fed into a multi-layer neural network that models the interaction between each of the hypotheses and the reference, as well as between the two hypotheses. These compact representations are in turn based on word and sentence embeddings, which are learned using neural networks. The framework is flexible, allows for efficient learning and classification, and yields correlation with humans that rivals the state of the art.
generated_abstract: We present a learning-based metric for automatic machine translation evaluation that combines lexical, syntactic, semantic, and discourse information. Unlike conventional measures based primarily on n-gram overlap, our approach represents words and multiword expressions in a continuous vector space and composes these representations to model the meaning of complete sentences. Candidate translations are compared with human references using features derived from aligned words, phrases, part-of-speech categories, syntactic structures, and rhetorical relations. A pairwise learning-to-rank framework is trained on human preferences, allowing the metric to learn which forms of evidence are most useful for distinguishing better from worse translations rather than relying on manually selected weights. We evaluate the method on the WMT metrics shared-task data at both segment and system levels, and compare it with BLEU, error-rate measures, linguistic-feature metrics, and existing learned evaluators. The results show that incorporating distributed representations and structured linguistic information improves agreement with human judgments, particularly for heterogeneous translation systems whose outputs differ substantially in vocabulary or surface form. The findings demonstrate that semantic and discourse-aware representations provide complementary information to lexical matching and offer a practical direction for more reliable automatic MT evaluation.

original_abstract: Recent studies have shown that deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to various attacks, including evasion attacks and poisoning attacks. On the defense side, there have been intensive interests in provable robustness against evasion attacks. In this paper, we focus on improving model robustness against more diverse threat models. Specifically, we provide the first unified framework using smoothing functional to certify the model robustness against general adversarial attacks. In particular, we propose the first robust training process RAB to certify against backdoor attacks. We theoretically prove the robustness bound for machine learning models based on the RAB training process, analyze the tightness of the robustness bound, as well as proposing different smoothing noise distributions such as Gaussian and Uniform distributions. Moreover, we evaluate the certified robustness of a family of "smoothed" DNNs which are trained in a differentially private fashion. In addition, we theoretically show that for simpler models such as K-nearest neighbor models, it is possible to train the robust smoothed models efficiently. For K=1, we propose an exact algorithm to smooth the training process, eliminating the need to sample from a noise distribution.Empirically, we conduct comprehensive experiments for different machine learning models such as DNNs, differentially private DNNs, and KNN models on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets to provide the first benchmark for certified robustness against backdoor attacks. In particular, we also evaluate KNN models on a spambase tabular dataset to demonstrate its advantages. Both the theoretic analysis for certified model robustness against arbitrary backdoors, and the comprehensive benchmark on diverse ML models and datasets would shed light on further robust learning strategies against training time or even general adversarial attacks on ML models.
generated_abstract: Data poisoning attacks threaten machine learning systems by manipulating training data to induce targeted or broad failures at inference time. Although a large body of work has introduced poisoning strategies, backdoor attacks, detection methods, and certified defenses, comparisons are difficult because studies use inconsistent threat models, datasets, evaluation protocols, and assumptions about attacker knowledge. We present a systematic empirical study of poisoning robustness across diverse learning algorithms and benchmark datasets. We evaluate clean-label, label-flipping, availability, and backdoor attacks under realistic constraints, comparing optimization-based and generative attack methods with statistical, differential privacy, augmentation, ensemble, and certification-based defenses. Our analysis measures attack success, clean accuracy, poison budget, computational cost, transferability, and robustness to adaptive adversaries. Results show that attack effectiveness is highly sensitive to experimental design and often decreases substantially outside the narrow settings in which it was developed. Conversely, several defenses that appear effective against individual attacks fail under modest changes to the threat model, while strong data augmentation and partition-based aggregation provide comparatively consistent protection. We release a reproducible evaluation framework and recommendations for reporting poisoning experiments, enabling fairer comparisons and clearer progress toward secure, dependable machine learning.

original_abstract: Human beings are creatures of habit. In their daily life, people tend to repeatedly consume similar types of food items over several days and occasionally switch to consuming different types of items when the consumptions become overly monotonous. However, the novel and repeat consumption behaviors have not been studied in food recommendation research. More importantly, the ability to predict daily eating habits of individuals is crucial to improve the effectiveness of food recommender systems in facilitating healthy lifestyle change. In this study, we analyze the patterns of repeat food consumptions using large-scale consumption data from a popular online fitness community called MyFitnessPal (MFP), conduct an offline evaluation of various state-of-the-art algorithms in predicting the next-day food consumption, and analyze their performance across different demographic groups and contexts. The experiment results show that algorithms incorporating the exploration-and-exploitation and temporal dynamics are more effective in the next-day recommendation task than most state-of-the-art algorithms.
generated_abstract: Food choices are increasingly recorded, shared, and recommended through digital platforms, creating opportunities to support healthier eating at scale. Yet existing food recommender systems often optimize popularity, similarity, or engagement, while overlooking nutritional quality, perception biases, and the distinction between repeating familiar foods and discovering suitable alternatives. We present a data-driven framework for health-aware food recommendation that integrates food diaries, social media, recipe content, and consumption history. We first characterize dietary behavior using large-scale user-generated data, examining the relationship between food exposure, self-monitoring, social context, and diet success. We then estimate food healthiness from ingredients, nutritional information, images, and user perceptions, and identify plausible substitutes through distributional similarity in consumption contexts. To model realistic recommendations, our approach combines user preferences with recency, item quality, and exploration of novel foods. Experiments on public food diaries and online recipe collections show that these signals improve prediction of subsequent consumption and enable recommendations that are both personalized and nutritionally superior. We further find that popularity-driven methods frequently favor unhealthy recipes, whereas simple health-aware filtering and meal-plan construction substantially expand healthy choices without eliminating personalization. The results highlight the need for recommender systems that treat health, variety, and repeat consumption as interconnected objectives.

original_abstract: Face detection has witnessed significant progress due to the advances of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Its central issue in recent years is how to improve the detection performance of tiny faces. To this end, many recent works propose some specific strategies, redesign the architecture and introduce new loss functions for tiny object detection. In this report, we start from the popular one-stage RetinaNet approach and apply some recent tricks to obtain a high performance face detector. Specifically, we apply the Intersection over Union (IoU) loss function for regression, employ the two-step classification and regression for detection, revisit the data augmentation based on data-anchor-sampling for training, utilize the max-out operation for classification and use the multi-scale testing strategy for inference. As a consequence, the proposed face detection method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the most popular and challenging face detection benchmark WIDER FACE dataset.
generated_abstract: Face detection in unconstrained images remains challenging because faces may be tiny, blurred, partially occluded, rotated, and surrounded by clutter. We present a single-stage face detector designed to improve robustness across a wide range of scales while maintaining practical inference speed. The proposed network uses a residual backbone and a hierarchical feature pyramid to combine low-level facial details with high-level semantic and contextual information. Scale-specific detection layers, densely distributed anchors, and adaptive anchor matching improve the representation and recall of small faces. An attention-guided context module emphasizes informative facial and surrounding regions, while selective refinement reduces the influence of easy negative anchors and provides better initialization for bounding-box regression. To address severe foreground-background imbalance, we employ focal classification loss together with an overlap-based localization objective. Training is strengthened by scale-aware data augmentation, hard-example mining, and synthetic enhancement of low-resolution faces. Extensive experiments on WIDER FACE, FDDB, AFW, and PASCAL Face demonstrate consistent improvements over representative one- and two-stage detectors, particularly on the hard subset containing tiny and occluded faces. The resulting model offers a favorable accuracy-speed trade-off for real-world face analysis applications.

original_abstract: Federated learning (FL) rests on the notion of training a global model in a decentralized manner. Under this setting, mobile devices perform computations on their local data before uploading the required updates to improve the global model. However, when the participating clients implement an uncoordinated computation strategy, the difficulty is to handle the communication efficiency (i.e., the number of communications per iteration) while exchanging the model parameters during aggregation. Therefore, a key challenge in FL is how users participate to build a high-quality global model with communication efficiency. We tackle this issue by formulating a utility maximization problem, and propose a novel crowdsourcing framework to leverage FL that considers the communication efficiency during parameters exchange. First, we show an incentive-based interaction between the crowdsourcing platform and the participating client's independent strategies for training a global learning model, where each side maximizes its own benefit. We formulate a two-stage Stackelberg game to analyze such scenario and find the game's equilibria. Second, we formalize an admission control scheme for participating clients to ensure a level of local accuracy. Simulated results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed solution with up to 22% gain in the offered reward.
generated_abstract: Federated learning enables mobile and edge devices to collaboratively train machine-learning models without transferring their private data, but its practical deployment is constrained by heterogeneous computation, wireless communication, data quality, energy budgets, and user incentives. This paper develops an integrated framework for efficient and sustainable federated learning in resource-constrained edge networks. We formulate the interaction among the service provider and participating devices as a hierarchical optimization or Stackelberg game, in which the provider determines rewards and training requirements while devices select their participation, local computation, communication resources, and update frequency. The proposed design jointly captures model accuracy, convergence time, energy consumption, communication cost, and privacy risk. To reduce bandwidth usage and mitigate statistical and systems heterogeneity, devices perform adaptive local updates and communicate compressed model information, while robust aggregation limits the effect of unreliable or malicious participants. We derive tractable solutions and distributed algorithms using convex approximation and dual decomposition, and establish convergence and incentive-compatibility properties under standard smoothness assumptions. Experiments and simulations on representative learning tasks show that the framework substantially reduces communication and energy consumption, improves convergence under heterogeneous conditions, and provides effective rewards that encourage reliable participation without exposing raw user data.

original_abstract: Specifying a complete domain model is time-consuming, which has been a bottleneck of AI planning technique application in many real-world scenarios. Most classical domain-model learning approaches output a domain model in the form of the declarative planning language, such as STRIPS or PDDL, and solve new planning instances by invoking an existing planner. However, planning in such a representation is sensitive to the accuracy of the learned domain model which probably cannot be used to solve real planning problems. In this paper, to represent domain models in a vectorization representation way, we propose a novel framework based on graph neural network (GNN) integrating model-free learning and model-based planning, called LP-GNN. By embedding propositions and actions in a graph, the latent relationship between them is explored to form a domain-specific heuristics. We evaluate our approach on five classical planning domains, comparing with the classical domain-model learner ARMS. The experimental results show that the domain models learned by our approach are much more effective on solving real planning problems.
generated_abstract: Automated acquisition of action models is a fundamental bottleneck for applying classical planning in real-world environments, where complete symbolic descriptions are rarely available. We present a data-driven framework that learns relational action models from heterogeneous demonstrations, textual descriptions, and visual transition data. The approach combines distributed representations of action and object concepts with a graph-based neural architecture that captures interactions among entities and generalizes across domains. A constrained symbolic decoding stage converts the learned representations into interpretable preconditions, effects, and, where available, action costs. The resulting models are validated through safe planning and refined using execution feedback, while a classical planner supplies structured supervision and exposes inconsistencies in the learned dynamics. We employ adaptive stochastic optimization to train the neural components efficiently under sparse and noisy observations. Experiments on benchmark planning domains, image-based puzzles, and simulated manipulation tasks show that the method learns useful models from substantially fewer traces than prior approaches, transfers knowledge between related domains, and produces plans that are both effective and more robust than purely subsymbolic policies. These results demonstrate a practical bridge between deep representation learning and symbolic, relational planning.

original_abstract: Statistical language modeling techniques have successfully been applied to source code, yielding a variety of new software development tools, such as tools for code suggestion and improving readability. A major issue with these techniques is that code introduces new vocabulary at a far higher rate than natural language, as new identifier names proliferate. But traditional language models limit the vocabulary to a fixed set of common words. For code, this strong assumption has been shown to have a significant negative effect on predictive performance. But the open vocabulary version of the neural network language models for code have not been introduced in the literature. We present a new open-vocabulary neural language model for code that is not limited to a fixed vocabulary of identifier names. We employ a segmentation into subword units, subsequences of tokens chosen based on a compression criterion, following previous work in machine translation. Our network achieves best in class performance, outperforming even the state-of-the-art methods of Hellendoorn and Devanbu that are designed specifically to model code. Furthermore, we present a simple method for dynamically adapting the model to a new test project, resulting in increased performance. We showcase our methodology on code corpora in three different languages of over a billion tokens each, hundreds of times larger than in previous work. To our knowledge, this is the largest neural language model for code that has been reported.
generated_abstract: We present a neural framework for learning useful representations of source code from large-scale repositories. Treating code as a structured language, our approach combines token, subword, and contextual representations with recurrent and attention-based architectures to capture both local syntax and long-range dependencies. The model is trained primarily from unlabeled code and can be adapted to downstream software engineering tasks with limited task-specific supervision. To address the open vocabulary and highly repetitive nature of programs, we incorporate subword modeling and a pointer mechanism that can copy identifiers and other locally defined symbols. We evaluate the framework on code completion, identifier naming, code summarization, syntax-error repair, and bug detection across several programming languages and real-world datasets. The results show consistent improvements over n-gram, conventional recurrent, and non-neural baselines, particularly for rare identifiers and constructs requiring extended context. Qualitative analyses indicate that the learned representations encode syntactic regularities, API usage patterns, naming conventions, and semantic relationships between program elements. These findings demonstrate that naturalness-based neural modeling can support practical tools for program understanding and generation while reducing reliance on manually engineered rules.

original_abstract: This paper contributes to the challenge of learning a function on streamed multimodal data through evaluation. The core of the result of our paper is the combination of two quite different approaches to this problem. One comes from the mathematically principled technology of signatures and log-signatures as representations for streamed data, while the other draws on the techniques of recurrent neural networks (RNN). The ability of the former to manage high sample rate streams and the latter to manage large scale nonlinear interactions allows hybrid algorithms that are easy to code, quicker to train, and of lower complexity for a given accuracy. #R##N#We illustrate the approach by approximating the unknown functional as a controlled differential equation. Linear functionals on solutions of controlled differential equations are the natural universal class of functions on data streams. Following this approach, we propose a hybrid Logsig-RNN algorithm that learns functionals on streamed data. By testing on various datasets, i.e. synthetic data, NTU RGB+D 120 skeletal action data, and Chalearn2013 gesture data, our algorithm achieves the outstanding accuracy with superior efficiency and robustness.
generated_abstract: Skeleton-based human action recognition requires representations that capture both the spatial structure of articulated bodies and the temporal evolution of motion. We propose a continuous-time framework that models skeleton sequences as paths and processes them with a neural controlled differential equation. The path signature provides a principled representation of ordered spatial and temporal interactions, while the differential-equation formulation offers adaptive, continuous-depth feature extraction and avoids restricting observations to a fixed number of discrete layers. To preserve body structure, joint trajectories are organized according to the human-skeleton topology, and multiple streams encode positions, motions, and selected pairwise relations. Efficient truncated signatures are computed using optimized algebraic operations and are subsequently mapped to discriminative action embeddings by a lightweight neural network. The approach is robust to variable frame rates, temporal resampling, and irregularly sampled sequences, and can incorporate attention to informative joints and motion intervals. Experiments on large-scale NTU RGB+D and NTU RGB+D 120 benchmarks, together with several gesture and interaction datasets, demonstrate competitive or superior recognition performance with fewer recurrent computations. Ablation studies show that combining spatial signatures with continuous temporal dynamics substantially improves robustness and generalization.

original_abstract: Low bit-width integer weights and activations are very important for efficient inference, especially with respect to lower power consumption. We propose Monte Carlo methods to quantize the weights and activations of pre-trained neural networks without any re-training. By performing importance sampling we obtain quantized low bit-width integer values from full-precision weights and activations. The precision, sparsity, and complexity are easily configurable by the amount of sampling performed. Our approach, called Monte Carlo Quantization (MCQ), is linear in both time and space, with the resulting quantized, sparse networks showing minimal accuracy loss when compared to the original full-precision networks. Our method either outperforms or achieves competitive results on multiple benchmarks compared to previous quantization methods that do require additional training.
generated_abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable performance across vision, speech, and language tasks, but their computational, memory, and energy demands hinder deployment on mobile, embedded, and other resource-constrained platforms. This paper reviews methods for developing efficient neural networks through parameter pruning, sparse connectivity, weight sharing, low-bit and ternary quantization, integer-only computation, and binary convolutions. We examine approaches that compress pretrained models without retraining as well as techniques that incorporate discrete representations during optimization, including learned quantizers, stochastic rounding, reparameterization, and hardware-aware mixed-precision search. We further discuss how conditional computation, residual architectures, adaptive representations, and specialized accelerators improve the trade-off among accuracy, latency, memory, and energy consumption. Experimental findings reported across image classification, speech recognition, and language modeling demonstrate that substantial reductions in model size and arithmetic complexity can often be obtained with little or no loss in predictive quality. Finally, we identify unresolved challenges involving training stability, outlier handling, hardware diversity, reproducibility, and the environmental cost of large-scale learning, and outline directions toward accurate, efficient, and sustainable deep learning systems.

original_abstract: Many recent works demonstrated that Deep Learning models are vulnerable to adversarial examples.Fortunately, generating adversarial examples usually requires white-box access to the victim model, and the attacker can only access the APIs opened by cloud platforms. Thus, keeping models in the cloud can usually give a (false) sense of security.Unfortunately, cloud-based image classification service is not robust to simple transformations such as Gaussian Noise, Salt-and-Pepper Noise, Rotation and Monochromatization. In this paper,(1) we propose one novel attack method called Image Fusion(IF) attack, which achieve a high bypass rate,can be implemented only with OpenCV and is difficult to defend; and (2) we make the first attempt to conduct an extensive empirical study of Simple Transformation (ST) attacks against real-world cloud-based classification services. Through evaluations on four popular cloud platforms including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Clarifai, we demonstrate that ST attack has a success rate of approximately 100% except Amazon approximately 50%, IF attack have a success rate over 98% among different classification services. (3) We discuss the possible defenses to address these security challenges.Experiments show that our defense technology can effectively defend known ST attacks.
generated_abstract: Deep learning has enabled cloud-based image detection services to recognize objects at scale, yet their robustness to natural geometric changes remains poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the vulnerability of black-box object detectors to affine transformations, including translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing. Unlike conventional adversarial attacks that modify individual pixels and require access to model gradients, our attacks operate directly on the input image and require only queries to the deployed service. We evaluate their effectiveness against representative local detectors based on SSD and Faster R-CNN as well as commercial cloud APIs. Across diverse images and detection tasks, small, visually plausible transformations can substantially reduce detection confidence, suppress target objects, or cause incorrect bounding boxes and labels. The results demonstrate that concealing model architectures in the cloud does not provide meaningful protection against spatial attacks. We further examine the transferability of transformations across models and services and study practical defenses based on geometric augmentation, transformation-aware training, and input preprocessing. Experiments show that combining these defenses improves detection stability while preserving normal accuracy. Our findings establish affine robustness as an important security requirement for real-world image detection systems.

original_abstract: Gaze correction aims to redirect the person's gaze into the camera by manipulating the eye region, and it can be considered as a specific image resynthesis problem. Gaze correction has a wide range of applications in real life, such as taking a picture with staring at the camera. In this paper, we propose a novel method that is based on the inpainting model to learn from the face image to fill in the missing eye regions with new contents representing corrected eye gaze. Moreover, our model does not require the training dataset labeled with the specific head pose and eye angle information, thus, the training data is easy to collect. To retain the identity information of the eye region in the original input, we propose a self-guided pretrained model to learn the angle-invariance feature. Experiments show our model achieves very compelling gaze-corrected results in the wild dataset which is collected from the website and will be introduced in details. Code is available at this https URL.
generated_abstract: Generative adversarial networks have become a powerful framework for learning complex data distributions and producing realistic synthetic content. This paper reviews the foundations, training strategies, and broad applications of GANs, with emphasis on recent methods that improve stability, controllability, diversity, and perceptual quality. We first describe the adversarial generator–discriminator formulation and examine important developments including Wasserstein objectives with gradient penalties, spectral normalization, self-supervised discrimination, and adversarial hard-example generation. We then discuss conditional and multi-domain translation, disentangled representations, semantic manipulation, image inpainting, facial attribute and expression editing, gaze redirection, motion transfer, and high-resolution image synthesis. Super-resolution methods are considered in detail, highlighting perceptual and adversarial losses that recover convincing high-frequency textures while limiting artifacts. Across these applications, attention mechanisms, semantic guidance, exemplar conditioning, anatomical constraints, and multi-scale architectures enable more precise and realistic results. We also summarize common evaluation measures and identify persistent challenges, including mode collapse, unstable optimization, limited data, hallucinated details, temporal inconsistency, and the ethical risks of synthetic media. The review concludes with promising directions for scalable, interpretable, controllable, and responsibly deployed generative models.

original_abstract: Classical approaches for one-class problems such as one-class SVM (Scholkopf et al., 1999) and isolation forest (Liu et al., 2008) require careful feature engineering when applied to structured domains like images. To alleviate this concern, state-of-the-art methods like DeepSVDD (Ruff et al., 2018) consider the natural alternative of minimizing a classical one-class loss applied to the learned final layer representations. However, such an approach suffers from the fundamental drawback that a representation that simply collapses all the inputs minimizes the one class loss; heuristics to mitigate collapsed representations provide limited benefits. In this work, we propose Deep Robust One Class Classification (DROCC) method that is robust to such a collapse by training the network to distinguish the training points from their perturbations, generated adversarially. DROCC is motivated by the assumption that the interesting class lies on a locally linear low dimensional manifold. Empirical evaluation demonstrates DROCC's effectiveness on two different one-class problem settings and on a range of real-world datasets across different domains - images(CIFAR and ImageNet), audio and timeseries, offering up to 20% increase in accuracy over the state-of-the-art in anomaly detection.
generated_abstract: Detecting anomalous acoustic events is essential for reliable speech interfaces and embedded sensing, yet collecting representative examples of every possible anomaly is impractical. We present a lightweight, largely unsupervised framework for detecting out-of-distribution speech and environmental sounds using self-supervised representation learning. The model is trained only on examples from a designated normal class and learns to discriminate among automatically generated transformations of those examples. At inference time, inconsistency across transformation predictions provides an anomaly score, while a compact convolutional or recurrent backbone enables deployment on resource-constrained devices. We investigate the effects of pretrained visual and temporal representations, model capacity, transformation design, and limited labeled data, and compare the approach with reconstruction-, density-, nearest-neighbor-, softmax-confidence-, and adversarial-learning baselines. Experiments on the Speech Commands benchmark and additional audio anomaly settings show that transformation-based supervision produces informative features and substantially improves detection of unseen and near-distribution anomalies. The method remains effective with few normal examples, benefits from auxiliary outlier data and semi-supervised calibration, and achieves a favorable accuracy–memory–latency trade-off. These results demonstrate that self-supervised classification is a practical alternative to explicit generative modeling for robust, label-efficient audio anomaly detection.

original_abstract: The lack of large-scale real datasets with annotationsmakes transfer learning a necessity for video activity under-standing. Within this scope, we aim at developing an effec-tive method for low-shot transfer learning for first-personaction classification. We leverage independently trained lo-cal visual cues to learn representations that can be trans-ferred from a source domain providing primitive action la-bels to a target domain with only a handful of examples.Such visual cues include object-object interactions, handgrasps and motion within regions that are a function of handlocations. We suggest a framework based on meta-learningto appropriately extract the distinctive and domain invari-ant components of the deployed visual cues, so to be able totransfer action classification models across public datasetscaptured with different scene configurations. We thoroughlyevaluate our methodology and report promising results overstate-of-the-art action classification approaches for bothinter-class and inter-dataset transfer.
generated_abstract: Recognizing human actions from only a few labeled examples is particularly challenging because actions vary in duration, appearance, viewpoint, and temporal structure. We present a meta-learning framework for few-shot action recognition that learns to compare videos through temporally aligned, object-aware representations. Instead of relying on global video pooling, our model extracts segment-level appearance and motion features, attends to discriminative moments, and aggregates relations between corresponding temporal regions of a query video and support examples. Class prototypes are formed from the support set, allowing the model to recognize previously unseen actions without fine-tuning. We train the system episodically across diverse action datasets and investigate the effects of temporal modeling, spatial attention, video length, and feature transfer from large-scale image and video recognition models. Experiments on standard benchmarks, including UCF101, HMDB51, and Olympic Sports, show consistent improvements over metric-learning, recurrent, and conventional fine-tuning baselines in one-shot and few-shot settings. The results demonstrate that explicitly modeling temporal relations and human-object interactions is important for rapid action recognition, and that the learned representation transfers effectively across domains and action categories.

original_abstract: Grounding language to visual relations is critical to various language-and-vision applications. In this work, we tackle two fundamental language-and-vision tasks: image-text matching and image captioning, and demonstrate that neural scene graph generators can learn effective visual relation features to facilitate grounding language to visual relations and subsequently improve the two end applications. By combining relation features with the state-of-the-art models, our experiments show significant improvement on the standard Flickr30K and MSCOCO benchmarks. Our experimental results and analysis show that relation features improve downstream models' capability of capturing visual relations in end vision-and-language applications. We also demonstrate the importance of learning scene graph generators with visually relevant relations to the effectiveness of relation features.
generated_abstract: We propose a relation-aware framework for learning fine-grained correspondences between images and sentences. Existing cross-modal retrieval methods commonly represent each modality as a global vector, which can overlook the interactions among objects and the compositional structure expressed in language. Our approach first constructs a visual scene representation containing objects, attributes, and pairwise relationships, and encodes it with a graph-based message-passing network. In parallel, a recurrent language encoder represents sentences while attending to informative words and phrases. A cross-modal alignment module then matches visual entities and relational propositions, combining local correspondence scores with global semantic compatibility. To improve discriminative learning, we employ hard-negative mining and an instance-level objective before optimizing the final ranking loss. The model is trained end to end using deep visual features and requires no manually written descriptions of scene graphs at inference time. Experiments on the MS COCO and Flickr30K benchmarks show consistent improvements over global embedding, attention-based, and generative matching methods for both image-to-text and text-to-image retrieval. Qualitative analyses further demonstrate that explicit relational reasoning improves alignment for complex scenes containing multiple interacting objects, while providing interpretable evidence for the predicted matches.

original_abstract: We present an overview of the EmotionX 2019 Challenge, held at the 7th International Workshop on Natural Language Processing for Social Media (SocialNLP), in conjunction with IJCAI 2019. The challenge entailed predicting emotions in spoken and chat-based dialogues using augmented EmotionLines datasets. EmotionLines contains two distinct datasets: the first includes excerpts from a US-based TV sitcom episode scripts (Friends) and the second contains online chats (EmotionPush). A total of thirty-six teams registered to participate in the challenge. Eleven of the teams successfully submitted their predictions performance evaluation. The top-scoring team achieved a micro-F1 score of 81.5% for the spoken-based dialogues (Friends) and 79.5% for the chat-based dialogues (EmotionPush).
generated_abstract: Recognizing emotions in conversational text requires more than identifying isolated affective words, because an utterance is strongly influenced by preceding turns, speaker responses, and the implicit meanings of dialogue. This paper presents a contextual neural approach for classifying emotions in multi-party conversations. We use a pretrained language model to encode each utterance together with relevant conversational context, and fine-tune the resulting representations for utterance-level emotion prediction. To address the limited size and imbalance of available training data, we apply post-training on in-domain conversations, weighted loss functions, and pooling strategies that emphasize the most informative contextual features. Experiments are conducted on the Friends and EmotionPush portions of the EmotionLines corpus, which contain automatically transcribed and manually annotated dialogues. The proposed system is compared with conventional recurrent and pretrained-language-model baselines using micro-F1 and class-sensitive evaluation. Results show that incorporating neighboring utterances consistently improves recognition, particularly for emotions expressed indirectly or through conversational responses. The findings demonstrate the value of transfer learning and context modeling for dialogue emotion recognition, while also highlighting persistent challenges involving neutral utterances, subtle affect, and domain variation between scripted and spontaneous conversations.

original_abstract: Evaluating the readability of a text can significantly facilitate the precise expression of information in a written form. The formulation of text readability assessment demands the identification of meaningful properties of the text and correct conversion of features to the right readability level. Sophisticated features and models are being used to evaluate the comprehensibility of texts accurately. Still, these models are challenging to implement, heavily language-dependent, and do not perform well on short texts. Deep reinforcement learning models are demonstrated to be helpful in further improvement of state-of-the-art text readability assessment models. The main contributions of the proposed approach are the automation of feature extraction, loosening the tight language dependency of text readability assessment task, and efficient use of text by finding the minimum portion of a text required to assess its readability. The experiments on Weebit, Cambridge Exams, and Persian readability datasets display the model's state-of-the-art precision, efficiency, and the capability to be applied to other languages.
generated_abstract: We present a reinforcement learning framework for readability-aware text simplification that generates fluent, comprehensible, and meaning-preserving text without relying exclusively on reference simplifications. The model combines a pretrained bidirectional Transformer encoder with an attention-based sequence-to-sequence generator equipped with copying and coverage mechanisms, enabling it to retain important content and handle rare terminology. A readability estimator, trained using lexical, syntactic, semantic, and neural representations, provides a continuous difficulty signal, while auxiliary rewards measure semantic similarity, grammaticality, and content preservation. The generator is first initialized through supervised learning and subsequently optimized with self-critical policy gradients, allowing the training objective to better reflect human judgments than token-level likelihood alone. We evaluate the approach on general-domain, learner-oriented, and medical simplification datasets using automatic metrics and human assessments of simplicity, fluency, adequacy, and readability. The proposed system produces significantly easier text while maintaining competitive meaning preservation and grammaticality, and achieves stronger overall quality than neural machine translation and conventional reinforcement-learning baselines. Further experiments show that readability-aware rewards improve generalization across domains and remain effective when parallel training data are limited.

original_abstract: Domain adaptation performance of a learning algorithm on a target domain is a function of its source domain error and a divergence measure between the data distribution of these two domains. We present a study of various distance-based measures in the context of NLP tasks, that characterize the dissimilarity between domains based on sample estimates. We first conduct analysis experiments to show which of these distance measures can best differentiate samples from same versus different domains, and are correlated with empirical results. Next, we develop a DistanceNet model which uses these distance measures, or a mixture of these distance measures, as an additional loss function to be minimized jointly with the task's loss function, so as to achieve better unsupervised domain adaptation. Finally, we extend this model to a novel DistanceNet-Bandit model, which employs a multi-armed bandit controller to dynamically switch between multiple source domains and allow the model to learn an optimal trajectory and mixture of domains for transfer to the low-resource target domain. We conduct experiments on popular sentiment analysis datasets with several diverse domains and show that our DistanceNet model, as well as its dynamic bandit variant, can outperform competitive baselines in the context of unsupervised domain adaptation.
generated_abstract: Transferring knowledge across domains, languages, and tasks can substantially reduce the annotation required for training neural models, but inappropriate sources or training schedules may cause negative transfer. We present an adaptive framework for selecting and weighting auxiliary data during transfer learning. The method represents source and target examples with contextualized neural encoders and learns a task-aware compatibility function that balances similarity, diversity, and expected learning progress. A bandit-based controller uses validation improvements as feedback to choose among candidate domains, languages, or auxiliary tasks, while Bayesian optimization determines their mixing proportions and curriculum. The representation learner is trained jointly with supervised source objectives and domain-alignment losses, allowing shared information to be exploited while preserving source- or task-specific structure. The approach is applicable to classification and sequence-labeling problems and requires no labeled target data beyond a small development set, when available. Across sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, part-of-speech tagging, parsing, and cross-domain image benchmarks, the proposed strategy consistently outperforms uniform mixing, fixed similarity heuristics, and standard domain-adversarial or moment-matching baselines. Analysis shows that learned selection is interpretable, transfers across model architectures, and substantially reduces negative transfer in heterogeneous multilingual settings.

original_abstract: Mobile edge caching can effectively reduce service delay but may introduce information staleness, calling for timely content refreshing. However, content refreshing consumes additional transmission resources and may degrade the delay performance of mobile systems. In this work, we propose a freshness-aware refreshing scheme to balance the service delay and content freshness measured by Age of Information (AoI). Specifically, the cached content items will be refreshed to the up-to-date version upon user requests if the AoI exceeds a certain threshold (named as refreshing window). The average AoI and service delay are derived in closed forms approximately, which reveals an AoI-delay tradeoff relationship with respect to the refreshing window. In addition, the refreshing window is optimized to minimize the average delay while meeting the AoI requirements, and the results indicate to set a smaller refreshing window for the popular content items. Extensive simulations are conducted on the OMNeT++ platform to validate the analytical results. The results indicate that the proposed scheme can restrain frequent refreshing as the request arrival rate increases, whereby the average delay can be reduced by around 80% while maintaining the AoI below one second in heavily-loaded scenarios.
generated_abstract: This paper investigates fresh content delivery in cache-enabled heterogeneous wireless networks, where reducing latency alone is insufficient because cached information may become stale. We develop a unified framework that jointly considers content placement, cache updating, and wireless delivery under limited storage, backhaul, and energy resources. Content requests and source updates are modeled as stochastic processes, and freshness is quantified by the age of information together with service delay. Using stochastic network analysis, we derive tractable expressions for cache-hit probability, average age, delivery latency, and energy consumption under heterogeneous base-station densities and cooperative edge caching. The resulting formulation exposes the tradeoffs among caching popular content, refreshing rapidly changing content, and reserving resources for uncached requests. We establish structural properties of the optimal update and placement decisions and propose a low-complexity alternating optimization algorithm that combines popularity-aware placement with threshold-based freshness control. Numerical results demonstrate that jointly optimizing caching and updating substantially improves freshness and delay compared with static caching, popularity-only replacement, and request-driven update schemes. The proposed framework also shows how cooperation and adaptive refresh rates can provide robust performance under time-varying demand and content dynamics.

original_abstract: Big data production in industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) is evident due to the massive deployment of sensors and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. However, big data processing is challenging due to limited computational, networking and storage resources at IoT device-end. Big data analytics (BDA) is expected to provide operational- and customer-level intelligence in IIoT systems. Although numerous studies on IIoT and BDA exist, only a few studies have explored the convergence of the two paradigms. In this study, we investigate the recent BDA technologies, algorithms and techniques that can lead to the development of intelligent IIoT systems. We devise a taxonomy by classifying and categorising the literature on the basis of important parameters (e.g. data sources, analytics tools, analytics techniques, requirements, industrial analytics applications and analytics types). We present the frameworks and case studies of the various enterprises that have benefited from BDA. We also enumerate the considerable opportunities introduced by BDA in IIoT.We identify and discuss the indispensable challenges that remain to be addressed as future research directions as well.
generated_abstract: The rapid growth of the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) has enabled manufacturing systems to collect heterogeneous, high-volume, and high-velocity data from machines, sensors, enterprise applications, and human operators. However, converting these data into reliable operational knowledge remains difficult because of noise, dimensionality, latency, interoperability, and security constraints. This paper presents a scalable architecture for industrial big data analytics that integrates device data ingestion, edge and fog processing, cloud-based storage, distributed analytics, and decision support. The architecture employs standardized device representations and synchronization, slicing, splitting, and indexing strategies to support efficient data management. Edge components reduce communication latency and network congestion, while Hadoop and Spark provide distributed storage and machine-learning capabilities. An ensemble-based preprocessing stage identifies and removes noisy observations before predictive models are trained. The framework supports applications including condition monitoring, anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, energy management, and adaptive production planning. Its design also considers context-aware access control, data provenance, and secure communication for sensitive industrial environments. The proposed approach offers a flexible foundation for transforming raw IIoT data into actionable insights and highlights research challenges concerning scalability, privacy, model transferability, and real-time deployment.

original_abstract: Incentive mechanisms are central to the functionality of permissionless blockchains: they incentivize participants to run and secure the underlying consensus protocol. Designing incentive-compatible incentive mechanisms is notoriously challenging, however. Even systems with strong theoretical security guarantees in traditional settings, where users are either Byzantine or honest, often exclude analysis of rational users, who may exploit incentives to deviate from honest behavior. As a result, most public blockchains today use incentive mechanisms whose security properties are poorly understood and largely untested. In this work, we propose SquirRL, a framework for using deep reinforcement learning to identify attack strategies on blockchain incentive mechanisms. With minimal setup, SquirRL replicates known theoretical results on the Bitcoin protocol. In more complex and realistic settings, as when mining power varies over time, it identifies attack strategies superior to those known in the literature. Finally, SquirRL yields results suggesting that classical selfish mining attacks against Bitcoin lose effectiveness in the presence of multiple attackers. These results shed light on why selfish mining, which is unobserved to date in the wild, may be a poor attack strategy.
generated_abstract: Mining pools mitigate the variance of Bitcoin rewards but concentrate substantial computational power in the hands of a few operators, creating incentives for strategic behavior. In particular, pool operators can infiltrate competing pools and withhold valid blocks, reducing rivals’ revenue while preserving the infiltrators’ expected rewards. Existing analyses of block withholding attacks largely focus on one-shot interactions between two pools and therefore overlook the dynamic and adaptive nature of competition among several pools. We formulate block withholding as a finite stochastic game in which pool operators repeatedly choose how much computational power to devote to honest mining or infiltration, and rewards and computational shares evolve according to observed outcomes. We then apply deep reinforcement learning to compute effective strategies and characterize the resulting long-run behavior. Simulations calibrated to Bitcoin mining-pool distributions over the past four years show that withholding can be profitable even when attackers initially control less than one quarter of the network’s computational power. Under favorable conditions, strategic infiltration enables participating pools to expand their effective share toward majority control. These results demonstrate that pool-level incentives can undermine Bitcoin’s decentralization and highlight the need for reward mechanisms and monitoring procedures that discourage persistent block withholding.

original_abstract: We introduce a comprehensive benchmark for local features and robust estimation algorithms, focusing on the downstream task -- the accuracy of the reconstructed camera pose -- as our primary metric. Our pipeline's modular structure allows us to easily integrate, configure, and combine methods and heuristics. We demonstrate this by embedding dozens of popular algorithms and evaluating them, from seminal works to the cutting edge of machine learning research. We show that with proper settings, classical solutions may still outperform the perceived state of the art. #R##N#Besides establishing the actual state of the art, the experiments conducted in this paper reveal unexpected properties of SfM pipelines that can be exploited to help improve their performance, for both algorithmic and learned methods. Data and code are online this https URL, providing an easy-to-use and flexible framework for the benchmarking of local feature and robust estimation methods, both alongside and against top-performing methods. This work provides the basis for an open challenge on wide-baseline image matching this https URL .
generated_abstract: We introduce LightGlue, a fast and flexible local feature matcher for geometric computer vision. Existing learned matchers use heavy attention networks with fixed computational budgets, making them unnecessarily expensive when images are easy to match and unreliable when the number of keypoints varies substantially. LightGlue addresses these limitations with an adaptive architecture that dynamically adjusts both its depth and the number of processed keypoints. A confidence-based mechanism enables early stopping when the matching problem is sufficiently solved, while point pruning removes features that are unlikely to participate in reliable correspondences. The matcher operates directly on local features produced by a range of detectors and descriptors, and is trained end to end on diverse image pairs with geometric supervision. Experiments on image matching, homography estimation, relative pose estimation, visual localization, and 3D reconstruction show that LightGlue matches or surpasses the accuracy of state-of-the-art learned and handcrafted approaches while requiring substantially less computation. On modern GPUs, it operates in real time and provides especially large speedups on easy image pairs, making learned matching practical for interactive and large-scale vision systems.

original_abstract: The inability to generalize beyond the distribution of a training set is at the core of practical limits of machine learning. We show that the common practice of mixing and shuffling training examples when training deep neural networks is not optimal. On the opposite, partitioning the training data into non-i.i.d. subsets can serve to guide the model to rely on reliable statistical patterns while ignoring spurious correlations in the training data. We demonstrate multiple use cases where these subsets are built using unsupervised clustering, prior knowledge, or other meta-data from existing datasets. The approach is supported by recent results on a causal view of generalization, it is simple to apply, and it demonstrably improves generalization. Applied to the task of visual question answering, we obtain state-of-the-art performance on VQA-CP. We also show improvements over data augmentation using equivalent questions on GQA. Finally, we show a small improvement when training a model simultaneously on VQA v2 and Visual Genome, treating them as two distinct environments rather than one aggregated training set.
generated_abstract: Visual question answering systems often achieve high accuracy by exploiting language priors and dataset-specific correlations rather than grounding their predictions in image evidence. This behavior causes substantial failures under changes in answer distributions, linguistic formulation, object categories, and visual domains. We present a causal framework for robust visual question answering that separates task-relevant visual information from spurious language and appearance factors. The model combines multimodal representation learning with counterfactual training: for each question–image pair, it constructs interventions that vary nuisance cues while preserving the underlying answer, and contrasts them with minimally changed examples that should produce different answers. An invariant prediction objective further encourages the same decision rule across environments, while structured visual reasoning and external semantic knowledge support novel objects and compositional queries. We evaluate the approach on standard and bias-sensitive VQA benchmarks, as well as diagnostic datasets for compositional reasoning, rephrasing robustness, and out-of-distribution generalization. Results show improved visual grounding, consistency, and robustness compared with strong attention, adversarial, and pretrained multimodal baselines, with only minor changes in in-domain accuracy. Analyses demonstrate that gains arise from reduced reliance on question-only shortcuts rather than from exploiting benchmark-specific artifacts.

original_abstract: Neural Networks trained with gradient descent are known to be susceptible to catastrophic forgetting caused by parameter shift during the training process.
