In the context of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) this results in poor performance on heterogeneous datasets and on sub-tasks like rare phrase translation. On the other hand, non-parametric approaches are immune to forgetting, perfectly complementing the generalization ability of NMT. However, attempts to combine non-parametric or retrieval based approaches with NMT have only been successful on narrow domains, possibly due to over-reliance on sentence level retrieval. We propose a novel n-gram level retrieval approach that relies on local phrase level similarities, allowing us to retrieve neighbors that are useful for translation even when overall sentence similarity is low. We complement this with an expressive neural network, allowing our model to extract information from the noisy retrieved context. We evaluate our semi-parametric NMT approach on a heterogeneous dataset composed of WMT, IWSLT, JRC-Acquis and OpenSubtitles, and demonstrate gains on all 4 evaluation sets. The semi-parametric nature of our approach opens the door for non-parametric domain adaptation, demonstrating strong inference-time adaptation performance on new domains without the need for any parameter updates.
generated_abstract: Neural machine translation has achieved impressive fluency, but it may omit source content, mishandle rare terminology, and fail to exploit previously translated material. We present a retrieval-augmented translation framework that combines a general neural model with translation memories and phrase-based resources available at inference time. For each input sentence, the system retrieves relevant bilingual examples from large parallel collections, identifies aligned translation pieces and fuzzy matches, and encodes the retrieved target-side information through a gated auxiliary pathway. The decoder can therefore reuse reliable phrases while retaining the flexibility of end-to-end neural generation. We further investigate alternative integration strategies, including retrieval-guided scoring, phrase-level constrained search, and neural combination of phrase-based and neural system outputs. The approach is implemented with subword modeling and Transformer-based sequence transduction, and trained efficiently using standard stochastic optimization. Experiments across multiple language pairs, domains, and data conditions show consistent improvements over strong neural and phrase-based baselines, with particularly large gains for repeated domain terminology, rare words, and high-quality translation-memory matches. Analysis using challenge sets demonstrates that retrieval improves adequacy without substantially reducing fluency, while dynamic access to external examples enables effective adaptation without retraining the core model.

original_abstract: The problem of characterizing testable graph properties (properties that can be tested with a number of queries independent of the input size) is a fundamental problem in the area of property testing. While there has been some extensive prior research characterizing testable graph properties in the dense graphs model and we have good understanding of the bounded degree graphs model, no similar characterization has been known for general graphs, with no degree bounds. In this paper we take on this major challenge and consider the problem of characterizing all testable graph properties in general planar graphs. #R##N#We consider the model in which a general planar graph can be accessed by the random neighbor oracle that allows access to any given vertex and access to a random neighbor of a given vertex. We show that, informally, a graph property $P$ is testable with one-sided error for general planar graphs if and only if testing $P$ can be reduced to testing for a finite family of finite forbidden subgraphs. While our presentation focuses on planar graphs, our approach extends easily to general minor-free graphs. #R##N#Our analysis of the necessary condition relies on a recent construction of canonical testers in the random neighbor oracle model that is applied here to the one-sided error model for testing in planar graphs. The sufficient condition in the characterization reduces the problem to the task of testing $H$-freeness in planar graphs, and is the main and most challenging technical contribution of the paper: we show that for planar graphs (with arbitrary degrees), the property of being $H$-free is testable with one-sided error for every finite graph $H$, in the random neighbor oracle model.
generated_abstract: We study the design and limitations of sublinear-time algorithms for testing and estimating properties of large graphs. Our results address several graph models, including bounded-degree, general, minor-free, planar, and scale-free graphs, as well as random-order streaming. We develop techniques based on local exploration, random walks, hyperfinite decompositions, canonical testers, and carefully balanced sampling schemes. These methods yield constant-query testers for broad families of sparse graph properties, including minor-closed properties, properties of hyperfinite graphs, and all properties on a natural class of hierarchical scale-free multigraphs. We also obtain efficient one-sided algorithms for detecting cycles and tree minors and constant-time procedures for testing bipartiteness in arbitrary planar and minor-free graphs. For general graphs, we establish connections between constant-query testing and constant-space random-order streaming, thereby extending the scope of streaming emulation beyond bounded-degree inputs. In a complementary direction, we give sublinear algorithms for estimating the number of triangles and, more generally, \(k\)-cliques, together with nearly matching query lower bounds. Collectively, these results demonstrate that substantial structural information and accurate global statistics can often be obtained without reading the entire graph.

original_abstract: Machine learning research has advanced in multiple aspects, including model structures and learning methods. The effort to automate such research, known as AutoML, has also made significant progress. However, this progress has largely focused on the architecture of neural networks, where it has relied on sophisticated expert-designed layers as building blocks---or similarly restrictive search spaces. Our goal is to show that AutoML can go further: it is possible today to automatically discover complete machine learning algorithms just using basic mathematical operations as building blocks. We demonstrate this by introducing a novel framework that significantly reduces human bias through a generic search space. Despite the vastness of this space, evolutionary search can still discover two-layer neural networks trained by backpropagation. These simple neural networks can then be surpassed by evolving directly on tasks of interest, e.g. CIFAR-10 variants, where modern techniques emerge in the top algorithms, such as bilinear interactions, normalized gradients, and weight averaging. Moreover, evolution adapts algorithms to different task types: e.g., dropout-like techniques appear when little data is available. We believe these preliminary successes in discovering machine learning algorithms from scratch indicate a promising new direction for the field.
generated_abstract: Automated machine learning seeks to reduce the human effort required to construct effective learning systems by treating model design, optimization, and training procedures as objects of search. This paper reviews the rapidly developing landscape of AutoML, covering neural architecture search, hyperparameter optimization, learned optimizers, automated data augmentation, evolutionary methods, reinforcement learning, and program-synthesis approaches. We organize existing methods according to their search spaces, optimization strategies, resource-allocation mechanisms, and sources of supervision. We discuss how differentiable relaxation, weight sharing, early stopping, population-based training, and surrogate modeling improve search efficiency, while transfer learning and hardware-aware objectives enable deployment under practical constraints. Particular attention is given to the relationship between neural and symbolic methods, including systems that learn programs, reusable modules, or optimization rules rather than fixed predictors. Through a critical analysis of commonly used benchmarks and evaluation protocols, we highlight substantial concerns involving proxy-task bias, instability across random seeds, computational cost, and reproducibility. We conclude by outlining open challenges, including joint optimization of architectures and training algorithms, reliable multi-objective evaluation, generalization across tasks and hardware, and the development of open-ended systems capable of discovering increasingly capable learning procedures.

original_abstract: Visual navigation tasks in real-world environments often require both self-motion and place recognition feedback. While deep reinforcement learning has shown success in solving these perception and decision-making problems in an end-to-end manner, these algorithms require large amounts of experience to learn navigation policies from high-dimensional data, which is generally impractical for real robots due to sample complexity. In this paper, we address these problems with two main contributions. We first leverage place recognition and deep learning techniques combined with goal destination feedback to generate compact, bimodal image representations that can then be used to effectively learn control policies from a small amount of experience. Second, we present an interactive framework, CityLearn, that enables for the first time training and deployment of navigation algorithms across city-sized, realistic environments with extreme visual appearance changes. CityLearn features more than 10 benchmark datasets, often used in visual place recognition and autonomous driving research, including over 100 recorded traversals across 60 cities around the world. We evaluate our approach on two CityLearn environments, training our navigation policy on a single traversal. Results show our method can be over 2 orders of magnitude faster than when using raw images, and can also generalize across extreme visual changes including day to night and summer to winter transitions.
generated_abstract: Autonomous navigation in large, previously unseen environments requires agents to recognize places despite substantial changes in viewpoint and appearance, maintain a useful estimate of their location, and select actions that lead reliably to a goal. We present a learning-based framework for visual navigation that combines robust place representations with goal-conditioned policy learning. The system uses deep convolutional features enhanced by semantic and temporal information to identify revisited locations from a single forward-facing camera, while a recurrent belief module integrates observations and supports decision making under partial observability. A distributed reinforcement-learning procedure enables efficient training across diverse simulated indoor and outdoor environments, and auxiliary objectives for depth, loop closure, and localization encourage the emergence of spatially meaningful representations. We evaluate the framework on challenging street-view, indoor, and robotic navigation benchmarks, including unseen maps, reversed traversals, severe illumination changes, and long-range routes. Results show that combining recognition and control substantially improves localization accuracy, navigation success, and transfer to new environments compared with image retrieval, model-free policies, and conventional mapping baselines. The findings highlight the importance of multimodal supervision, realistic interactive environments, and explicit evaluation of computation, robustness, and generalization for deployable visual navigation systems.

original_abstract: In person re-identification (Re-ID), supervised methods usually need a large amount of expensive label information, while unsupervised ones are still unable to deliver satisfactory identification performance. In this paper, we introduce a novel person Re-ID task called unsupervised cross-camera person Re-ID, which only needs the within-camera (intra-camera) label information but not cross-camera (inter-camera) labels which are more expensive to obtain. In real-world applications, the intra-camera label information can be easily captured by tracking algorithms or few manual annotations. In this situation, the main challenge becomes the distribution discrepancy across different camera views, caused by the various body pose, occlusion, image resolution, illumination conditions, and background noises in different cameras. To address this situation, we propose a novel Adversarial Camera Alignment Network (ACAN) for unsupervised cross-camera person Re-ID. It consists of the camera-alignment task and the supervised within-camera learning task. To achieve the camera alignment, we develop a Multi-Camera Adversarial Learning (MCAL) to map images of different cameras into a shared subspace. Particularly, we investigate two different schemes, including the existing GRL (i.e., gradient reversal layer) scheme and the proposed scheme called "other camera equiprobability" (OCE), to conduct the multi-camera adversarial task. Based on this shared subspace, we then leverage the within-camera labels to train the network. Extensive experiments on five large-scale datasets demonstrate the superiority of ACAN over multiple state-of-the-art unsupervised methods that take advantage of labeled source domains and generated images by GAN-based models. In particular, we verify that the proposed multi-camera adversarial task does contribute to the significant improvement.
generated_abstract: Unsupervised person re-identification is essential for large-scale surveillance, yet its performance is severely degraded by camera-specific appearance, domain shifts, and the absence of identity annotations in the target network. We propose a unified framework for learning camera-invariant and identity-discriminative representations from labeled source data and unlabeled target videos. The method first separates shared identity information from camera-private appearance factors, while adversarial image translation reduces the visual discrepancy between domains without requiring paired samples. A camera-aware feature alignment objective further suppresses view-specific bias. To exploit target data, we construct reliable tracklet and neighborhood relations, generate soft identity labels through iterative graph propagation, and optimize the network with a combination of classification, triplet, and consistency losses. An exemplar memory maintains globally stable target representations and prevents error accumulation during self-training. The framework is implemented on a deep residual backbone and trained end to end with alternating representation learning and label refinement. Extensive experiments on image and video person re-identification benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements over supervised-source transfer, adversarial adaptation, clustering, and tracklet-association baselines, confirming that jointly modeling domain, camera, and neighborhood invariance enables effective unsupervised cross-domain re-identification.

original_abstract: This paper proposes a framework which is able to generate a sequence of three-dimensional human dance poses for a given music. The proposed framework consists of three components: a music feature encoder, a pose generator, and a music genre classifier. We focus on integrating these components for generating a realistic 3D human dancing move from music, which can be applied to artificial agents and humanoid robots. The trained dance pose generator, which is a generative autoregressive model, is able to synthesize a dance sequence longer than 5,000 pose frames. Experimental results of generated dance sequences from various songs show how the proposed method generates human-like dancing move to a given music. In addition, a generated 3D dance sequence is applied to a humanoid robot, showing that the proposed framework can make a robot to dance just by listening to music.
generated_abstract: We present a deep learning framework for generating realistic and musically synchronized human dance motion from audio. The proposed system learns an end-to-end mapping from music to sequences of full-body skeletal poses, combining a deep convolutional music encoder with an autoregressive motion decoder. The encoder extracts hierarchical temporal representations directly from audio, while residual connections, batch normalization, and adaptive optimization facilitate stable training. To model long-range choreographic structure, we investigate recurrent and temporal convolutional sequence models and use scheduled sampling to reduce the discrepancy between training and inference. Human motion is represented with quaternion joint rotations and constrained through forward kinematics, avoiding discontinuities and physically invalid bone configurations. The decoder is trained with objectives that jointly encourage accurate pose reconstruction, temporal smoothness, and alignment between motion accents and musical rhythm. We evaluate the approach on paired music-dance recordings using quantitative motion and beat-synchronization measures, as well as subjective assessments of realism and musicality. Experiments demonstrate that the model generates diverse, coherent dance sequences for previously unseen songs and produces more natural motion and stronger musical alignment than conventional recurrent and feature-based baselines.

original_abstract: What is the current state-of-the-art for image restoration and enhancement applied to degraded images acquired under less than ideal circumstances? Can the application of such algorithms as a pre-processing step to improve image interpretability for manual analysis or automatic visual recognition to classify scene content? While there have been important advances in the area of computational photography to restore or enhance the visual quality of an image, the capabilities of such techniques have not always translated in a useful way to visual recognition tasks. Consequently, there is a pressing need for the development of algorithms that are designed for the joint problem of improving visual appearance and recognition, which will be an enabling factor for the deployment of visual recognition tools in many real-world scenarios. To address this, we introduce the UG^2 dataset as a large-scale benchmark composed of video imagery captured under challenging conditions, and two enhancement tasks designed to test algorithmic impact on visual quality and automatic object recognition. Furthermore, we propose a set of metrics to evaluate the joint improvement of such tasks as well as individual algorithmic advances, including a novel psychophysics-based evaluation regime for human assessment and a realistic set of quantitative measures for object recognition performance. We introduce six new algorithms for image restoration or enhancement, which were created as part of the IARPA sponsored UG^2 Challenge workshop held at CVPR 2018. Under the proposed evaluation regime, we present an in-depth analysis of these algorithms and a host of deep learning-based and classic baseline approaches. From the observed results, it is evident that we are in the early days of building a bridge between computational photography and visual recognition, leaving many opportunities for innovation in this area.
generated_abstract: Modern visual recognition systems achieve excellent performance on curated datasets but can fail under the blur, noise, compression, rain, and low resolution encountered in real-world imagery, particularly from unmanned aerial vehicles. Image restoration is often applied as a preprocessing step, although optimizing perceptual quality or pixel fidelity does not necessarily improve recognition and may remove task-relevant information. We investigate the relationship between image restoration and downstream recognition through a unified experimental framework. A range of restoration and enhancement methods, including denoising, deblurring, super-resolution, deraining, artifact removal, and learned image-to-image translation, are evaluated with contemporary convolutional architectures across natural and aerial benchmarks. We compare conventional distortion and perceptual measures with classification accuracy and analyze the effects of image quality, scale, and computational cost. Our results show that restoration benefits are strongly task- and degradation-dependent: visually pleasing outputs can leave recognition unchanged or even reduce performance, whereas task-driven processing that preserves discriminative structures provides more consistent gains. The study highlights the limitations of standard image-quality metrics, establishes practical baselines for robust recognition, and motivates jointly optimized restoration and recognition models for deployment in unconstrained sensing environments.

original_abstract: A classifier trained on a dataset seldom works on other datasets obtained under different conditions due to domain shift. This problem is commonly addressed by domain adaptation methods. In this work we introduce a novel deep learning framework which unifies different paradigms in unsupervised domain adaptation. Specifically, we propose domain alignment layers which implement feature whitening for the purpose of matching source and target feature distributions. Additionally, we leverage the unlabeled target data by proposing the Min-Entropy Consensus loss, which regularizes training while avoiding the adoption of many user-defined hyper-parameters. We report results on publicly available datasets, considering both digit classification and object recognition tasks. We show that, in most of our experiments, our approach improves upon previous methods, setting new state-of-the-art performances.
generated_abstract: Deep neural networks often suffer substantial performance degradation when applied to data collected under different visual conditions. Although unsupervised domain adaptation methods can reduce this domain shift, many require additional adversarial modules, target-domain training, or careful optimization, limiting their practical use. We present a simple and effective adaptation framework that exploits the statistics of intermediate feature representations to improve transfer between domains. Building on batch normalization, the method separates domain-invariant parameters from domain-specific activation statistics and updates the latter using unlabeled target data. We further incorporate decorrelation and consistency constraints to obtain more stable, discriminative representations while preserving the source classification objective. The resulting model can be optimized end to end with standard stochastic gradient methods and introduces little computational or memory overhead. Unlike approaches based on image generation, pseudo-labeling, or explicit distribution discriminators, it requires no target annotations and can be applied to existing convolutional architectures, including deep residual networks. Experiments on digit, object-recognition, synthetic-to-real, and robotic-vision benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over source-only models and competitive domain-adaptation baselines. The approach also supports online adaptation, enabling a trained system to adjust continuously as operating conditions change.

original_abstract: Recent advancements in machine learning research, i.e., deep learning, introduced methods that excel conventional algorithms as well as humans in several complex tasks, ranging from detection of objects in images and speech recognition to playing difficult strategic games. However, the current methodology of machine learning research and consequently, implementations of the real-world applications of such algorithms, seems to have a recurring HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known) issue. In this work, we elaborate on the algorithmic, economic and social reasons and consequences of this phenomenon. We present examples from current common practices of conducting machine learning research (e.g. avoidance of reporting negative results) and failure of generalization ability of the proposed algorithms and datasets in actual real-life usage. Furthermore, a potential future trajectory of machine learning research and development from the perspective of accountable, unbiased, ethical and privacy-aware algorithmic decision making is discussed. We would like to emphasize that with this discussion we neither claim to provide an exhaustive argumentation nor blame any specific institution or individual on the raised issues. This is simply a discussion put forth by us, insiders of the machine learning field, reflecting on us.
generated_abstract: Machine learning research increasingly relies on large-scale experimentation, automated design, and benchmark-driven evaluation, yet the reliability of its conclusions is often difficult to assess. This paper examines methodological and scientific challenges that arise across modern deep learning, including nondeterministic optimization, extensive hyperparameter and architecture search, benchmark reuse, publication and reporting biases, and the fragile interpretation of model behavior. We argue that impressive improvements in isolated scores do not necessarily indicate meaningful progress: random search can rival sophisticated neural architecture search methods, results may vary substantially across seeds, and performance can decline on newly collected test data. Automated systems also introduce concerns involving privacy, fairness, accountability, and distributional shift that are not captured by standard accuracy metrics. Drawing on theoretical results, empirical comparisons, and practices from reproducible science, we propose a broader framework for evaluating machine learning contributions. This framework emphasizes preregistered or results-blind evaluation, complete reporting of score distributions and computational costs, independent test sets, strong random and human-designed baselines, transparent release of code and data, and explicit analysis of failures and societal risks. These practices can improve the credibility, usefulness, and cumulative progress of empirical machine learning.

original_abstract: In this paper, we address the open question: "What do adversarially robust models look at?" Recently, it has been reported in many works that there exists the trade-off between standard accuracy and adversarial robustness. According to prior works, this trade-off is rooted in the fact that adversarially robust and standard accurate models might depend on very different sets of features. However, it has not been well studied what kind of difference actually exists. In this paper, we analyze this difference through various experiments visually and quantitatively. Experimental results show that adversarially robust models look at things at a larger scale than standard models and pay less attention to fine textures. Furthermore, although it has been claimed that adversarially robust features are not compatible with standard accuracy, there is even a positive effect by using them as pre-trained models particularly in low resolution datasets.
generated_abstract: Deep neural networks achieve remarkable performance on visual recognition tasks, yet their predictions remain vulnerable to adversarial perturbations and difficult to interpret reliably. In this work, we study the robustness of model explanations alongside the robustness of model decisions. We show that an input can be modified by a small, often imperceptible perturbation so that the classifier preserves its predicted label and confidence while attribution methods produce substantially different explanations. This phenomenon affects gradient-based saliency maps, integrated gradients, DeepLIFT, class activation methods, and exemplar-based explanations. We develop optimization-based procedures for constructing such interpretation attacks and evaluate them across image-classification models, architectures, and datasets. Our experiments demonstrate that explanation instability is widespread, including for models trained with adversarial training, smoothing, or other robustness-oriented procedures. Analysis of local loss geometry and the Hessian indicates that attribution methods are sensitive to directions that need not alter the decision itself. These results show that predictive robustness does not imply interpretive robustness and that visually plausible explanations cannot be trusted without systematic evaluation. We conclude with recommendations for assessing explanation stability and designing attribution methods that remain faithful under realistic perturbations.

original_abstract: Deep learning natural language processing models often use vector word embeddings, such as word2vec or GloVe, to represent words. A discrete sequence of words can be much more easily integrated with downstream neural layers if it is represented as a sequence of continuous vectors. Also, semantic relationships between words, learned from a text corpus, can be encoded in the relative configurations of the embedding vectors. However, storing and accessing embedding vectors for all words in a dictionary requires large amount of space, and may stain systems with limited GPU memory. Here, we used approaches inspired by quantum computing to propose two related methods, {\em word2ket} and {\em word2ketXS}, for storing word embedding matrix during training and inference in a highly efficient way. Our approach achieves a hundred-fold or more reduction in the space required to store the embeddings with almost no relative drop in accuracy in practical natural language processing tasks.
generated_abstract: Modern neural language models achieve strong performance but impose substantial memory and computation costs, limiting their deployment on mobile, embedded, and resource-constrained systems. This paper presents a unified study of memory-efficient methods for neural text generation, covering compressed word representations, parameter sparsity, low-rank and tensor-based factorization, quantization, and memory-aware training. We analyze how these techniques affect both optimization and downstream generation quality, with particular attention to attention-based sequence-to-sequence models. Building on pretrained contextual representations, we investigate whether compression can preserve the semantic and syntactic information needed for translation, summarization, question answering, and dialogue. We further examine mixed- and low-precision arithmetic, gradient checkpointing, microbatching, and dynamic sparse reparameterization as complementary approaches for reducing training and inference costs. Experiments on standard language-generation benchmarks show that substantial reductions in model size and peak memory are possible with minimal degradation in BLEU, ROUGE, and task accuracy. The results highlight important trade-offs between compression rate, computational overhead, and generalization, and provide practical guidelines for selecting and combining techniques when deploying modern neural language systems under strict resource budgets.

original_abstract: Recently, the problem of allocating one resource per agent with initial endowments (\emph{house markets}) has seen a renewed interest: indeed, while in the general domain Top Trading Cycle is known to be the only procedure guaranteeing Pareto-optimality, individual rationality, and strategy proofness, the situation differs in single-peaked domains. Bade (2019) presented the Crawler, an alternative procedure enjoying the same properties (with the additional advantage of being implementable in obviously dominant strategies); while Damamme et al. (2015) showed that allowing mutually beneficial swap-deals among the agents was already enough to guarantee Pareto-optimality. In this paper we significantly deepen our understanding of this decentralized procedures: we show in particular that the single-peaked domains happen to be ``maximal'' if one wishes to guarantee this convergence property. Interestingly, we also observe that the set of allocations reachable by swap-deals always contains the outcome of the Crawler. To further investigate how these different mechanisms compare, we pay special attention to the average and minimum rank of the resource obtained by the agents in the outcome allocation. We provide theoretical bounds on the loss potentially induced by these procedures with respect to these criteria, and complement these results with an extensive experimental study which shows how different variants of swap dynamics behave. In fact, even the simplest dynamics exhibit very good results, and it is possible to further guide the process towards our objectives, if one is ready to sacrifice a bit in terms of decentralization. On our way, we also show that a simple variant of the Crawler allows to check efficiently that an allocation is Pareto-optimal in single-peaked domains.
generated_abstract: We study object allocation by means of mutually beneficial swaps between agents connected in a social network. Each agent initially owns one object, and a swap is possible only between neighboring agents who both prefer the other’s object to their own. Our focus is on single-peaked preferences, a natural restriction in which objects are arranged on a common axis and each agent has an ideal object. We investigate three fundamental questions: whether a given allocation can be reached, whether a specified agent can obtain a specified object, and whether a sequence of swaps can lead to a Pareto-efficient allocation. We identify structural properties of swap sequences under single-peakedness and provide polynomial-time algorithms for several important network classes, including paths and trees. We also establish computational hardness for broader classes of social networks, showing that the preference restriction alone does not eliminate the combinatorial difficulty of decentralized reallocation. Our results clarify the interaction between the geometry of preferences and the topology of communication, and complement centralized mechanisms for housing markets and resource exchange by characterizing when simple local trades can implement globally desirable outcomes.

original_abstract: Time series forecasting is one of the challenging problems for humankind. The traditional forecasting methods using mean regression models have severe shortcomings in reflecting real-world fluctuations. While new probabilistic methods rush to rescue, they fight with technical difficulties like quantile crossing or selecting a prior distribution. To meld the different strengths of these fields while avoiding their weaknesses, as well as, to push the boundary of the state-of-the-art, we introduce ForGAN - one step ahead probabilistic forecasting with generative adversarial networks. ForGAN utilizes the power of the conditional generative adversarial network to learn the data generating distribution and compute probabilistic forecasts from it. We argue how to evaluate ForGAN in opposition to regression methods. To investigate probabilistic forecasting of ForGAN, we create a new dataset and demonstrate our method abilities on it. This dataset will be made publicly available for comparison. Furthermore, we test ForGAN on two publicly available datasets, namely Mackey-Glass dataset and Internet traffic dataset (A5M), where the impressive performance of ForGAN demonstrate its high capability in forecasting future values.
generated_abstract: Reliable short-term earthquake forecasting requires models that represent both the complex temporal structure of seismicity and the substantial uncertainty in future events. We present a conditional generative adversarial framework for probabilistic earthquake forecasting from seismic catalogs and auxiliary observations. A recurrent generator produces ensembles of future event sequences conditioned on recent seismic activity, while a discriminator distinguishes generated sequences from observed catalog segments. To stabilize training and capture multimodal behavior, we combine recurrent architectures with feature normalization, curriculum learning, and an information-based latent representation. The resulting model generates realistic sequences containing clustered events, quiet intervals, and varying magnitudes without imposing a fixed parametric form or spatial grid. We evaluate the approach using synthetic catalogs and regional earthquake data, comparing distributional, temporal, and event-level forecasts with statistical baselines and deterministic neural models. Generated ensembles reproduce key catalog properties, including magnitude distributions, interevent-time variability, and short-term clustering, while providing calibrated predictive uncertainty. The framework is computationally efficient at inference time and can incorporate imperfect phase detections and auxiliary seismic features. These results demonstrate the potential of adversarial sequence models as flexible tools for operational earthquake forecasting and probabilistic seismicity analysis.

original_abstract: The authors present a visual instrument developed as part of the creation of the artwork Learning to See. The artwork explores bias in artificial neural networks and provides mechanisms for the manipulation of specifically trained-for real-world representations. The exploration of these representations acts as a metaphor for the process of developing a visual understanding and/or visual vocabulary of the world. These representations can be explored and manipulated in real time, and have been produced in such a way so as to reflect specific creative perspectives that call into question the relationship between how both artificial neural networks and humans may construct meaning.
generated_abstract: Recent advances in deep learning have made it possible to generate images by separating visual content from artistic style, translating between image domains, and representing diverse painting styles in a continuous embedding space. These techniques offer powerful tools for creative practice, but they also raise questions about the role of human intention and agency when artistic decisions are mediated by autonomous systems. This paper examines human control in AI-assisted artistic image generation and proposes a framework for meaningful creative control. We describe a system that combines neural style representations with conditional image translation, allowing users to select, interpolate, and apply styles while retaining influence over composition, content, and refinement. Rather than treating the model as an autonomous artist, we analyze it as a responsive instrument whose outputs should track the user’s aesthetic goals and remain traceable to identifiable human choices. We discuss how interface design, adjustable constraints, visual feedback, and transparent provenance can support this relationship. The resulting framework connects technical methods for neural artistic generation with ethical principles of responsible innovation, offering guidelines for designing generative art systems that expand creative possibilities without displacing meaningful human authorship.

original_abstract: In this paper, we propose a communication-efficient decentralized machine learning (ML) algorithm, coined quantized group ADMM (Q-GADMM). Every worker in Q-GADMM communicates only with two neighbors, and updates its model via the alternating direct method of multiplier (ADMM), thereby ensuring fast convergence while reducing the number of communication rounds. Furthermore, each worker quantizes its model updates before transmissions, thereby decreasing the communication payload sizes. We prove that Q-GADMM converges for convex loss functions, and numerically show that Q-GADMM yields 7x less communication cost while achieving almost the same accuracy and convergence speed compared to a baseline without quantization, group ADMM (GADMM).
generated_abstract: Machine learning at the wireless edge can exploit distributed data and computation while preserving data locality, but its scalability is fundamentally limited by communication overhead, unreliable links, heterogeneous devices, and non-IID data. We first review decentralized optimization and federated learning algorithms, emphasizing the roles of local computation, consensus, momentum, adaptive aggregation, and primal-dual methods. We then examine communication-reduction techniques, including quantization, sparsification, sign and ternary gradients, error compensation, lazy and event-triggered updates, knowledge distillation, and periodic model averaging. The impact of wireless impairments is analyzed through client selection, resource allocation, interference management, over-the-air aggregation, and device-to-device cooperation. We highlight fundamental tradeoffs among convergence accuracy, communication rounds, payload size, computation, energy consumption, latency, and robustness to stragglers and topology changes. original_abstract: When one wants to train a neural network to perform semantic segmentation, creating pixel-level annotations for each of the images in the database is a tedious task. If he works with aerial or satellite images, which are usually very large, it is even worse. With that in mind, we investigate how to use image-level annotations in order to perform semantic segmentation. Image-level annotations are much less expensive to acquire than pixel-level annotations, but we lose a lot of information for the training of the model. From the annotations of the images, the model must find by itself how to classify the different regions of the image. In this work, we use the method proposed by Anh and Kwak [1] to produce pixel-level annotation from image level annotation. We compare the overall quality of our generated dataset with the original dataset. In addition, we propose an adaptation of the AffinityNet that allows us to directly perform a semantic segmentation. Our results show that the generated labels lead to the same performances for the training of several segmentation networks. Also, the quality of semantic segmentation performed directly by the AffinityNet and the Random Walk is close to the one of the best fully-supervised approaches.
generated_abstract: Semantic segmentation of high-resolution remote-sensing imagery is essential for large-scale land-cover mapping, yet the acquisition of pixel-level annotations is costly and difficult to scale. A classification network first generates class-discriminative activation maps, which are expanded using learned pixel affinities and random-walk propagation to recover object extent while preserving semantic boundaries. Saliency and boundary cues provide additional constraints, and an encoder–decoder segmentation network refines the resulting pseudo-labels at full resolution. The framework supports modern residual and pyramid-context backbones while remaining compatible with compact architectures for efficient inference. We evaluate the approach on challenging aerial and satellite benchmarks, including urban and land-cover scenes with substantial variation in scale, orientation, and appearance. Results show that jointly learning propagation and segmentation substantially improves over direct use of activation maps and other weakly supervised baselines, approaching fully supervised performance while reducing annotation effort by an order of magnitude. The experiments demonstrate that weak labels can enable accurate, scalable mapping of buildings, roads, vegetation, and other semantic classes in very high-resolution imagery.

original_abstract: The advice model of online computation captures the setting in which the online algorithm is given some partial information concerning the request sequence. This paradigm allows to establish tradeoffs between the amount of this additional information and the performance of the online algorithm. However, unlike real life in which advice is a recommendation that we can chose to follow or to ignore based on trustworthiness, in the current advice model, the online algorithm treats it as infallible. This means that if the advice is corrupt or, worse, if it comes from a malicious source, the algorithm may perform poorly. In this work, we study online computation in a setting in which the advice is provided by an untrusted source. Our objective is to quantify the impact of untrusted advice so as to design and analyze online algorithms that are resilient and perform well even when the advice is generated in a malicious, adversarial manner. To this end, we focus on well-studied online problems such as ski rental, online bidding, bin packing, and list update. For ski-rental and online bidding, we show how to obtain algorithms that are Pareto-optimal with respect to the competitive ratios achieved; this improves upon the framework of Purohit et al. [NeurIPS 2018] in which Pareto-optimality is not necessarily guaranteed. For bin packing and list update, we give online algorithms with worst-case tradeoffs in their competitiveness, depending on whether the advice is trusted or not; this is motivated by work of Lykouris and Vassilvitskii [ICML 2018] on the paging problem, but in which the competitiveness depends on the reliability of the advice.
generated_abstract: Online computation must make decisions without knowing future requests, but its performance can improve substantially when limited information about the future is available. This paper surveys and develops techniques for designing and analyzing online algorithms with advice, randomness, and machine-learned predictions. We focus particularly on bin packing and caching, two settings that illustrate the range of possible tradeoffs between information and competitive performance. For bin packing, we review sharp advances in purely online upper and lower bounds, as well as advice-based algorithms that approach optimality with a small amount of information per item. We also discuss lower bounds showing that exact or near-optimal performance requires substantially more advice. For caching and related metric problems, we explain connections between randomized algorithms and sublinear advice, and present prediction-augmented strategies that remain robust when predictions are inaccurate while improving performance when they are reliable. A central theme is that advice and predictions can be treated as resources whose value can be quantified independently of their source. The resulting perspective unifies classical competitive analysis with modern learning-augmented online computation and identifies directions for algorithms that are both theoretically robust and practically effective.

original_abstract: In the last decade, numerous supervised deep learning approaches requiring large amounts of labeled data have been proposed for visual-inertial odometry (VIO) and depth map estimation. To overcome the data limitation, self-supervised learning has emerged as a promising alternative, exploiting constraints such as geometric and photometric consistency in the scene. In this study, we introduce a novel self-supervised deep learning-based VIO and depth map recovery approach (SelfVIO) using adversarial training and self-adaptive visual-inertial sensor fusion. SelfVIO learns to jointly estimate 6 degrees-of-freedom (6-DoF) ego-motion and a depth map of the scene from unlabeled monocular RGB image sequences and inertial measurement unit (IMU) readings. The proposed approach is able to perform VIO without the need for IMU intrinsic parameters and/or the extrinsic calibration between the IMU and the camera. estimation and single-view depth recovery network. We provide comprehensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations of the proposed framework comparing its performance with state-of-the-art VIO, VO, and visual simultaneous localization and mapping (VSLAM) approaches on the KITTI, EuRoC and Cityscapes datasets. Detailed comparisons prove that SelfVIO outperforms state-of-the-art VIO approaches in terms of pose estimation and depth recovery, making it a promising approach among existing methods in the literature.
generated_abstract: We present an unsupervised deep learning framework for persistent monocular visual odometry and depth estimation in challenging environments. The proposed system learns six-degree-of-freedom camera motion and dense scene depth directly from unlabeled image sequences, avoiding the need for ground-truth poses or depth measurements. To improve robustness under perceptual degradation, occlusion, rapid motion, and illumination changes, the framework combines geometry-based view synthesis with feature-level reconstruction, adaptive masking, and consistency constraints that preserve the relative scale of predictions across consecutive frames. These mechanisms enable the network to maintain a coherent trajectory over long sequences, addressing a major limitation of existing unsupervised methods whose independently estimated scales often lead to drift and broken trajectories. We evaluate the approach on sequences collected during the DARPA Subterranean Challenge, as well as on the KITTI and Cityscapes benchmarks. Experiments show substantial improvements over state-of-the-art unsupervised depth and visual odometry methods in smoke, darkness, blur, and other perceptually degraded conditions. On standard benchmarks, the method achieves competitive or leading performance for both pose estimation and depth recovery, demonstrating its suitability for autonomous navigation in previously unseen and extreme environments.

original_abstract: Counting people or objects with significantly varying scales and densities has attracted much interest from the research community and yet it remains an open problem. In this paper, we propose a simple but an efficient and effective network, named DENet, which is composed of two components, i.e., a detection network (DNet) and an encoder-decoder estimation network (ENet). We first run DNet on an input image to detect and count individuals who can be segmented clearly. Then, ENet is utilized to estimate the density maps of the remaining areas, where the numbers of individuals cannot be detected. We propose a modified Xception as an encoder for feature extraction and a combination of dilated convolution and transposed convolution as a decoder. In the ShanghaiTech Part A, UCF and WorldExpo'10 datasets, our DENet achieves lower Mean Absolute Error (MAE) than those of the state-of-the-art methods.
generated_abstract: Accurate crowd analysis requires both reliable global counts and precise localization, yet detection-based methods degrade in heavily congested scenes while density regression cannot identify individuals. We propose a unified point-supervised framework that combines detection and density estimation through spatially adaptive feature learning. A lightweight convolutional backbone with dilated convolutions extracts high-resolution contextual representations, while parallel detection and regression branches predict head locations, bounding boxes, and density maps. An attention-based decision module estimates the reliability of each branch at every image region and fuses their outputs, favoring detection in sparse areas and density regression in highly congested regions. To avoid the need for costly bounding-box annotations, point annotations are converted into probabilistic supervision and used to generate size-aware pseudo boxes that are refined online during training. We further introduce a spatially aware composition loss that jointly constrains total count, local density, and object localization. The resulting network produces accurate counts, high-quality density maps, and interpretable individual detections in scenes with substantial scale, perspective, and illumination variation. Experiments on several challenging crowd and vehicle-counting benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art detection, regression, and hybrid methods while retaining efficient end-to-end inference.

original_abstract: Pre-trained language models have been dominating the field of natural language processing in recent years, and have led to significant performance gains for various complex natural language tasks. One of the most prominent pre-trained language models is BERT (Bi-directional Encoders for Transformers), which was released as an English as well as a multilingual version. Although multilingual BERT performs well on many tasks, recent studies showed that BERT models trained on a single language significantly outperform the multilingual results. Training a Dutch BERT model thus has a lot of potential for a wide range of Dutch NLP tasks. While previous approaches have used earlier implementations of BERT to train their Dutch BERT, we used RoBERTa, a robustly optimized BERT approach, to train a Dutch language model called RobBERT. We show that RobBERT improves state of the art results in Dutch-specific language tasks, and also outperforms other existing Dutch BERT-based models in sentiment analysis. These results indicate that RobBERT is a powerful pre-trained model for fine-tuning for a large variety of Dutch language tasks. We publicly release this pre-trained model in hope of supporting further downstream Dutch NLP applications.
generated_abstract: This paper investigates gender and social bias in Dutch natural language processing models used for automated recruitment and job-title understanding. We compare multilingual and monolingual transformer representations, including multilingual BERT and BERTje, with static word embeddings and contextual baselines. Models are evaluated on Dutch named-entity recognition, job-title classification, and ontology expansion using large contemporary Dutch corpora and manually annotated benchmark data. To measure representational bias, we adapt association- and template-based tests to Dutch, examine model behavior across gendered occupations and pronoun contexts, and assess whether observed associations affect downstream predictions. We further investigate mitigation through gender-neutralization, adversarial training, and fairness-constrained fine-tuning, reporting changes in both bias indicators and predictive performance. Results show that monolingual pretraining substantially improves Dutch task performance, but does not eliminate stereotypical associations inherited from the training data. Bias is sensitive to context, model architecture, and evaluation definition; mitigation methods reduce selected disparities while sometimes lowering accuracy or removing meaningful occupational information. The findings emphasize that fairness cannot be established through a single metric and that responsible deployment requires transparent data documentation, task-specific evaluation, and continued attention to the social consequences of automated employment systems.

original_abstract: Building robust and real-time classifiers with diverse datasets are one of the most significant challenges to deep learning researchers. It is because there is a considerable gap between a model built with training (seen) data and real (unseen) data in applications. Recent works including Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL), have attempted to deal with this problem of overcoming the apparent gap through transfer learning. In this paper, we propose a novel model, called Class Representative Learning Model (CRL), that can be especially effective in image classification influenced by ZSL. In the CRL model, first, the learning step is to build class representatives to represent classes in datasets by aggregating prominent features extracted from a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). Second, the inferencing step in CRL is to match between the class representatives and new data. The proposed CRL model demonstrated superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art research in ZSL and mobile deep learning. The proposed CRL model has been implemented and evaluated in a parallel environment, using Apache Spark, for both distributed learning and recognition. An extensive experimental study on the benchmark datasets, ImageNet-1K, CalTech-101, CalTech-256, CIFAR-100, shows that CRL can build a class distribution model with drastic improvement in learning and recognition performance without sacrificing accuracy compared to the state-of-the-art performances in image classification.
generated_abstract: Modern visual recognition systems are typically trained for a single dataset, task, or label vocabulary, limiting their ability to generalize to new domains and unseen categories. We present a unified framework for learning universal visual representations that supports supervised recognition, transfer learning, zero-shot classification, and open-world recognition. Our approach combines a shared convolutional backbone with lightweight domain- and task-specific residual adapters, preserving common visual features while allowing efficient specialization. Semantic information from attributes, textual descriptions, and distributed word representations is integrated through a visual-space embedding, reducing the domain-shift and hubness problems common in zero-shot prediction. Episodic training simulates disjoint training and test classes, encouraging the representation to generalize beyond the categories observed during optimization. We further introduce an open-set decision mechanism that detects out-of-distribution examples and permits incremental incorporation of new classes without retraining the entire model. Across diverse datasets spanning object, fine-grained, action, and digit recognition, the proposed representation consistently improves transfer and generalized zero-shot performance while requiring substantially fewer task-specific parameters than independently trained networks. These results demonstrate that universality and specialization can be achieved jointly, providing an accurate and computationally efficient foundation for scalable visual recognition.

original_abstract: Lexical relations describe how concepts are semantically related, in the form of relation triples. The accurate prediction of lexical relations between concepts is challenging, due to the sparsity of patterns indicating the existence of such relations. We propose the Knowledge-Enriched Meta-Learning (KEML) framework to address the task of lexical relation classification. In KEML, the LKB-BERT (Lexical Knowledge Base-BERT) model is presented to learn concept representations from massive text corpora, with rich lexical knowledge injected by distant supervision. A probabilistic distribution of auxiliary tasks is defined to increase the model's ability to recognize different types of lexical relations. We further combine a meta-learning process over the auxiliary task distribution and supervised learning to train the neural lexical relation classifier. Experiments over multiple datasets show that KEML outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
generated_abstract: Recognizing lexical semantic relations between word pairs is essential for taxonomy construction, knowledge graph completion, and natural language understanding, yet existing systems require substantial labeled data and often fail for rare or unseen relations. We present a meta-learning framework for few-shot lexical relation classification that combines contextual language representations with explicit relational information. A pretrained bidirectional encoder represents the words and their sentential contexts, while a relation module constructs pair representations using vector differences, composition, dependency paths, and external commonsense knowledge. We train the model episodically across relation-disjoint tasks, learning an initialization that can rapidly adapt to a new relation from only a few examples. To improve robustness in low-resource and cross-domain settings, we incorporate subword representations and a probabilistic adaptation mechanism that captures ambiguity in the support set. Experiments on benchmarks covering synonymy, antonymy, hypernymy, meronymy, and other lexical relations show consistent improvements over supervised distributional, pattern-based, and pretrained-language-model baselines. The proposed approach generalizes to unseen lexical items, alleviates data sparsity, and demonstrates that meta-learned relational representations provide an effective bridge between distributional semantics and structured linguistic knowledge.

original_abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has seen an explosion of research in the past few years. A variety of methods have been proposed to perform NAS, including reinforcement learning, Bayesian optimization with a Gaussian process model, evolutionary search, and gradient descent. In this work, we design a NAS algorithm that performs Bayesian optimization using a neural network model. #R##N#We develop a path-based encoding scheme to featurize the neural architectures that are used to train the neural network model. This strategy is particularly effective for encoding architectures in cell-based search spaces. After training on just 200 random neural architectures, we are able to predict the validation accuracy of a new architecture to within one percent of its true accuracy on average, for popular search spaces. This may be of independent interest beyond Bayesian neural architecture search. #R##N#We test our algorithm on the NASBench (Ying et al. 2019) and DARTS (Liu et al. 2018) search spaces, and we show that our algorithm outperforms other NAS methods including evolutionary search, reinforcement learning, AlphaX, ASHA, and DARTS. Our algorithm is over 100x more efficient than random search, and 3.8x more efficient than the next-best algorithm on the NASBench dataset. As there have been problems with fair and reproducible experimental evauations in the field of NAS, we adhere to the recent NAS research checklist (Lindauer and Hutter 2019) to facilitate NAS research. In particular, our implementation has been made publicly available, including all details needed to fully reproduce our results.
generated_abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) can discover effective networks, but its computational cost and the discrete, graph-structured nature of architecture spaces make efficient search difficult. Bayesian optimization offers a principled framework for selecting promising architectures while accounting for uncertainty, yet conventional surrogates rely on representations and similarity measures that inadequately capture neural connectivity. We present a graph-based Bayesian optimization approach for NAS that learns architecture representations from directed acyclic graph structure and uses calibrated predictive uncertainty to balance exploration and exploitation. The method supports both sequential and parallel evaluation, incorporates multiple objectives such as accuracy, parameter count, and inference latency, and can exploit partially trained networks and performance predictors to reduce evaluation cost. We evaluate it on reproducible NAS benchmarks and image-classification search spaces, comparing against random search, evolutionary methods, reinforcement learning, differentiable search, and existing Bayesian optimization techniques. Across experiments, the proposed method identifies high-performing and efficient architectures with substantially fewer evaluations, while maintaining robust rankings under noisy and incomplete observations. Ablation studies show that graph-aware representations, uncertainty calibration, and explicit search-phase evaluation are all essential for reliable gains over strong random and bandit-based baselines.

original_abstract: Inductive representation learning on temporal graphs is an important step toward salable machine learning on real-world dynamic networks. The evolving nature of temporal dynamic graphs requires handling new nodes as well as capturing temporal patterns. The node embeddings, which are now functions of time, should represent both the static node features and the evolving topological structures. Moreover, node and topological features can be temporal as well, whose patterns the node embeddings should also capture. We propose the temporal graph attention (TGAT) layer to efficiently aggregate temporal-topological neighborhood features as well as to learn the time-feature interactions. For TGAT, we use the self-attention mechanism as building block and develop a novel functional time encoding technique based on the classical Bochner's theorem from harmonic analysis. By stacking TGAT layers, the network recognizes the node embeddings as functions of time and is able to inductively infer embeddings for both new and observed nodes as the graph evolves. The proposed approach handles both node classification and link prediction task, and can be naturally extended to include the temporal edge features. We evaluate our method with transductive and inductive tasks under temporal settings with two benchmark and one industrial dataset. Our TGAT model compares favorably to state-of-the-art baselines as well as the previous temporal graph embedding approaches.
generated_abstract: We propose a dynamic graph representation learning framework for analyzing evolving political discourse. The framework models politicians, political concepts, media sources, and lexical entities as nodes in a continuously changing heterogeneous graph, while time-stamped interactions and textual co-occurrences define its edges. To integrate structural, semantic, and temporal information, the model combines inductive neighborhood aggregation with graph attention and self-attention over event histories. Textual content is encoded as dense document representations and enriched with psychologically motivated linguistic features, including categories derived from LIWC. A variational generative objective learns uncertainty-aware node embeddings, while invertible transformations provide flexible latent distributions and stable reconstruction of observed graph evolution. The resulting representations can be used for node classification, link prediction, event forecasting, discourse clustering, and detection of emerging political alignments. Experiments on longitudinal political speech and media datasets show that the proposed approach consistently outperforms static network embeddings, random-walk methods, conventional graph convolutional models, and sequence-based baselines. It also supports inductive inference for newly appearing actors and improves prediction when observations are sparse. Qualitative analyses indicate that the learned embeddings capture meaningful semantic, relational, and temporal patterns in political communication.

original_abstract: This paper proposes a new method for live free-viewpoint human performance capture with dynamic details (e.g., cloth wrinkles) using a single RGBD camera. Our main contributions are: (i) a multi-layer representation of garments and body, and (ii) a physics-based performance capture procedure. We first digitize the performer using multi-layer surface representation, which includes the undressed body surface and separate clothing meshes. For performance capture, we perform skeleton tracking, cloth simulation, and iterative depth fitting sequentially for the incoming frame. By incorporating cloth simulation into the performance capture pipeline, we can simulate plausible cloth dynamics and cloth-body interactions even in the occluded regions, which was not possible in previous capture methods. Moreover, by formulating depth fitting as a physical process, our system produces cloth tracking results consistent with the depth observation while still maintaining physical constraints. Results and evaluations show the effectiveness of our method. Our method also enables new types of applications such as cloth retargeting, free-viewpoint video rendering and animations.
generated_abstract: We present a learning-based framework for reconstructing detailed, animatable humans from monocular RGB video. Given a short sequence of a clothed person moving freely, our method estimates temporally consistent body pose, personalized shape, clothing geometry, and appearance without requiring markers, calibration, or multi-view imagery. A parametric body model provides a compact representation of articulated pose and underlying body shape, while a learned deformation field captures clothing and hair that cannot be explained by the model alone. To handle the severe depth ambiguity and occlusions inherent in monocular input, we combine image evidence from multiple frames in a canonical body coordinate system and use differentiable rendering to enforce consistency with silhouettes, semantic parts, keypoints, and appearance. The network is initialized with synthetic supervision and refined through self-supervised objectives on the input sequence, enabling adaptation to individual subjects and garments. A temporal deformation model further suppresses jitter while preserving medium- and high-frequency cloth details. Experiments on several benchmarks and unconstrained videos show that the proposed approach produces more accurate geometry, stable motion, and improved visual fidelity than existing model-fitting and feed-forward methods, while operating sufficiently fast for practical avatar creation, virtual try-on, and free-viewpoint video applications.

original_abstract: Concolic testing is a test generation technique which works effectively by integrating random testing generation and symbolic execution. Existing concolic testing engines focus on numeric programs. Heap-manipulating programs make extensive use of complex heap objects like trees and lists. Testing such programs is challenging due to multiple reasons. Firstly, test inputs for such program are required to satisfy non-trivial constraints which must be specified precisely. Secondly, precisely encoding and solving path conditions in such programs are challenging and often expensive. In this work, we propose the first concolic testing engine called CSF for heap-manipulating programs based on separation logic. CSF effectively combines specification-based testing and concolic execution for test input generation. It is evaluated on a set of challenging heap-manipulating programs. The results show that CSF generates valid test inputs with high coverage efficiently. Furthermore, we show that CSF can be potentially used in combination with precondition inference tools to reduce the user effort.
generated_abstract: We present a compositional framework for automated reasoning about heap-manipulating programs that combines symbolic execution, separation logic, and search-based input generation. The framework represents program states using symbolic heaps with inductive predicates, enabling precise descriptions of unbounded data structures while preserving information about shape, size, and stored values. A context-sensitive lazy-initialisation procedure constructs only feasible, fully specified inputs and uses separation-logic preconditions to avoid exploring invalid heap configurations. To address path conditions involving complex structural constraints, we translate the resulting symbolic obligations into optimisation problems and solve them through guided search. The approach also supports selective exploration: inexpensive dynamic testing is used to identify promising execution regions, while symbolic reasoning generates inputs for difficult branch conditions and deeper paths. We provide soundness results for the compositional execution rules and show how inferred resource descriptions can be used to diagnose failures and construct reusable test components. An implementation targeting heap-based Java programs and JavaScript data-structure libraries demonstrates substantial reductions in infeasible executions and invalid test cases, while improving structural coverage and exposing faults that are missed by conventional fuzzing and symbolic execution alone.

original_abstract: In this paper, we propose an efficient online multi-object tracking framework based on the GMPHD filter and occlusion group management scheme where the GMPHD filter utilizes hierarchical data association to reduce the false negatives caused by miss detection. The hierarchical data association consists of two steps: detection-to-track and track-to-track associations, which can recover the lost tracks and their switched IDs. In addition, the proposed framework is equipped with an object grouping management scheme which handles occlusion problems with two main parts. The first part is "track merging" which can merge the false positive tracks caused by false positive detections from occlusions, where the false positive tracks are usually occluded with a measure. The measure is the occlusion ratio between visual objects, sum-of-intersection-over-area (SIOA) we defined instead of the IOU metric. The second part is "occlusion group energy minimization (OGEM)" which prevents the occluded true positive tracks from false "track merging". We define each group of the occluded objects as an energy function and find an optimal hypothesis which makes the energy minimal. We evaluate the proposed tracker in benchmark datasets such as MOT15 and MOT17 which are built for multi-person tracking. An ablation study in training dataset shows that not only "track merging" and "OGEM" complement each other but also the proposed tracking method has more robust performance and less sensitive to parameters than baseline methods. Also, SIOA works better than IOU for various sizes of false positives. Experimental results show that the proposed tracker efficiently handles occlusion situations and achieves competitive performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods. Especially, our method shows the best multi-object tracking accuracy among the online and real-time executable methods.
generated_abstract: We present an online multi-object tracking framework designed for real-time operation in crowded and dynamically changing scenes. The method follows a tracking-by-detection strategy, combining deep object detections with motion prediction and appearance-based association. To reduce failures caused by missed or noisy detections, candidate locations are generated from both detector responses and track predictions, while a confidence-aware management scheme handles track initiation, occlusion, recovery, and termination. A learned appearance representation is used to distinguish targets with similar motion or overlapping bounding boxes, and adaptive weighting balances spatial proximity, temporal consistency, and visual similarity during association. The framework is designed to operate without future observations and can incorporate heterogeneous detectors and image evidence when detections are unreliable. We evaluate the approach on standard multiple-object tracking benchmarks and vehicle-tracking sequences using CLEAR MOT and identity-preservation metrics. Results show that the proposed system achieves a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost, reducing identity switches and fragmented trajectories while maintaining real-time throughput. The experiments further demonstrate that robust motion prediction and complementary visual cues are particularly beneficial during occlusion, abrupt motion, and substantial changes in detection quality.

original_abstract: Recent research advances in Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing have introduced novel tasks that are paving the way for solving AI-complete problems. One of those tasks is called Visual Question Answering (VQA). A VQA system must take an image and a free-form, open-ended natural language question about the image, and produce a natural language answer as the output. Such a task has drawn great attention from the scientific community, which generated a plethora of approaches that aim to improve the VQA predictive accuracy. Most of them comprise three major components: (i) independent representation learning of images and questions; (ii) feature fusion so the model can use information from both sources to answer visual questions; and (iii) the generation of the correct answer in natural language. With so many approaches being recently introduced, it became unclear the real contribution of each component for the ultimate performance of the model. The main goal of this paper is to provide a comprehensive analysis regarding the impact of each component in VQA models. Our extensive set of experiments cover both visual and textual elements, as well as the combination of these representations in form of fusion and attention mechanisms. Our major contribution is to identify core components for training VQA models so as to maximize their predictive performance.
generated_abstract: We propose an adaptive cross-modal embedding framework for aligning images and text in a shared semantic space. Existing image-text retrieval methods often rely on fixed visual regions and uniform language representations, which can obscure fine-grained correspondences between objects, attributes, actions, and phrases. Our approach learns modality-specific representations jointly with an adaptive alignment mechanism that selects and weights image regions according to the linguistic content, while allowing words and phrases to attend to relevant visual evidence. A stacked cross-modal interaction module captures both local correspondences and global contextual compatibility, and a bidirectional ranking objective trains the model to retrieve matching images and descriptions while separating hard negative pairs. The framework is compatible with convolutional or residual visual features, pretrained word representations, and fully attentive sequence encoders. We evaluate it on standard MS-COCO and Flickr30K benchmarks for image-to-text and text-to-image retrieval. Experiments show consistent improvements over global embedding, concatenation, and compact bilinear baselines, with particularly strong gains in challenging fine-grained matching cases. Qualitative analyses demonstrate interpretable alignments between words and image regions, confirming that adaptive cross-modal reasoning improves both retrieval accuracy and semantic grounding.

original_abstract: Relational reasoning - the ability to model interactions and relations between objects - is valuable for robust multi-object tracking and pivotal for trajectory prediction. In this paper, we propose MOHART, a class-agnostic, end-to-end multi-object tracking and trajectory prediction algorithm, which explicitly accounts for permutation invariance in its relational reasoning. We explore a number of permutation invariant architectures and show that multi-headed self-attention outperforms the provided baselines and better accounts for complex physical interactions in a challenging toy experiment. We show on three real-world tracking datasets that adding relational reasoning capabilities in this way increases the tracking and trajectory prediction performance, particularly in the presence of ego-motion, occlusions, crowded scenes, and faulty sensor inputs.
