To the best of our knowledge, MOHART is the first fully end-to-end multi-object tracking from vision approach applied to real-world data reported in the literature.
generated_abstract: We present a unified transformer-based framework for multi-object tracking that learns to detect, associate, and update object identities directly from video. Unlike conventional tracking-by-detection pipelines, which rely on separate detectors, handcrafted association rules, and fragile appearance models, our method represents targets as a permutation-invariant set of track queries. Each query attends jointly to image features and the history of its corresponding trajectory, allowing the model to reason about appearance, motion, occlusion, and interactions among objects. Track queries are propagated across frames and updated through a recurrent attention mechanism, while new queries are introduced to discover previously unseen objects. A set-based objective supervises detection and identity preservation without requiring heuristic non-maximum suppression or explicit pairwise matching at inference time. The architecture is compatible with multi-scale visual features and can incorporate complementary sensor information when available. We evaluate the approach on established pedestrian and vehicle tracking benchmarks, including MOT and traffic-scene datasets. Results demonstrate competitive or superior accuracy, improved robustness to missed detections and long occlusions, and substantially simpler inference than traditional tracking systems, while maintaining efficient operation suitable for real-time applications.

original_abstract: While deep learning in 3D domain has achieved revolutionary performance in many tasks, the robustness of these models has not been sufficiently studied or explored. Regarding the 3D adversarial samples, most existing works focus on manipulation of local points, which may fail to invoke the global geometry properties, like robustness under linear projection that preserves the Euclidean distance, i.e., isometry. In this work, we show that existing state-of-the-art deep 3D models are extremely vulnerable to isometry transformations. Armed with the Thompson Sampling, we develop a black-box attack with success rate over 95\% on ModelNet40 data set. Incorporating with the Restricted Isometry Property, we propose a novel framework of white-box attack on top of spectral norm based perturbation. In contrast to previous works, our adversarial samples are experimentally shown to be strongly transferable. Evaluated on a sequence of prevailing 3D models, our white-box attack achieves success rates from 98.88\% to 100\%. It maintains a successful attack rate over 95\% even within an imperceptible rotation range $[\pm 2.81^{\circ}]$.
generated_abstract: Deep neural networks for 3D point-cloud analysis achieve strong performance in classification, segmentation, and detection, yet their reliability under adversarial manipulation remains poorly understood. We present a systematic study of adversarial vulnerability in point-cloud models and introduce a query-efficient framework for generating imperceptible, physically plausible attacks. The method first estimates point importance using model responses and geometric saliency, then adaptively selects points for perturbation, removal, or insertion through gradient-free optimization. A sequential sampling strategy balances exploration of candidate modifications with exploitation of high-impact regions, enabling attacks against both differentiable and black-box models without constructing a substitute network. We evaluate the approach on PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN, and other architectures, including models designed to preserve local geometry and rotation invariance. Experiments on standard 3D shape and indoor-scene benchmarks show that small changes to a limited fraction of points can cause substantial accuracy degradation and transfer across architectures and orientations. We further investigate defenses based on augmentation, distillation, geometric constraints, and adversarial training, demonstrating that apparent robustness can result from masked gradients or restricted threat models. These findings emphasize the need for comprehensive, geometry-aware robustness evaluation before deploying 3D learning systems in safety-critical applications.

original_abstract: A single-point feature has shown its effectiveness in object detection. However, for instance segmentation, it does not lead to satisfactory results. The reasons are two folds. Firstly, it has limited representation capacity. Secondly, it could be misaligned with potential instances. To address the above issues, we propose a new point-based framework, namely PointINS, to segment instances from single points. The core module of our framework is instance-aware convolution, including the instance-agnostic feature and instance-aware weights. Instance-agnostic feature for each Point-of-Interest (PoI) serves as a template for potential instance masks. In this way, instance-aware features are computed by convolving this template with instance-aware weights for following mask prediction. Given the independence of instance-aware convolution, PointINS is general and practical as a one-stage detector for anchor-based and anchor-free frameworks. In our extensive experiments, we show the effectiveness of our framework on RetinaNet and FCOS. With ResNet101 backbone, PointINS achieves 38.3 mask mAP on challenging COCO dataset, outperforming its competitors by a large margin. The code will be made publicly available.
generated_abstract: Instance-level visual understanding is essential for autonomous manipulation, yet existing segmentation systems often trade accuracy for speed, require extensive category-specific annotation, and are sensitive to scale, occlusion, and clutter. We present a unified, efficient framework for detecting and segmenting objects in challenging robotic scenes. The model combines a fully convolutional, anchor-free detection backbone with multi-scale feature aggregation, adaptive convolution, and a lightweight instance-mask head. A meta-learned optimization strategy enables rapid adaptation to new object categories from limited examples, while uncertainty-aware localization and learned proposal ranking improve the reliability of overlapping predictions. To preserve fine boundaries without expensive region repooling, the framework predicts compact instance representations that are decoded at arbitrary image resolutions. We evaluate the approach on COCO, Cityscapes, KINS, and a warehouse manipulation benchmark, including categories and viewpoints not observed during training. The proposed system achieves competitive detection and mask accuracy relative to two-stage methods, while substantially reducing computation and memory use. It operates in real time on an embedded platform and improves downstream grasp selection and pick-and-place success, demonstrating that adaptable single-stage instance segmentation can provide a practical perception foundation for autonomous robotic manipulation.

original_abstract: To increase productivity, today's compilers offer a two-fold abstraction: they hide hardware complexity from the software developer, and they support many architectures and programming languages. At the same time, due to fierce market competition, most processor vendors do not disclose many of their implementation details. These factors force software developers to treat both compilers and architectures as black boxes. In practice, this leads to a suboptimal compiler behavior where the maximum potential of improving an application's resource usage, such as execution time, is often not realized. This paper exposes missed optimization opportunities and is of interest to all three communities, compiler engineers, software developers and hardware architects. By exploiting the behavior of the standard optimization levels, such as the -O3, of the LLVM v6.0 compiler, we show how to reveal hidden cross-architecture and architecture-dependent potential optimizations on two popular processors: the Intel i5-6300U, widely used in portable PCs, and the ARM Cortex-A53-based Broadcom BCM2837 used in the Raspberry Pi 3B+. The classic nightly regression testing can then be extended to use the resource usage and compilation information collected while exploiting subsequences of the standard optimization levels. This provides a systematic means of detecting and tracking missed optimization opportunities. The enhanced nightly regression system is capable of driving the improvement and tuning of the compiler's common optimizer
generated_abstract: Energy efficiency is a critical requirement for embedded and Internet of Things systems, yet compiler optimization is typically guided by generic heuristics that cannot account for the characteristics of individual applications, processors, or energy constraints. This paper investigates compiler autotuning as a means of making energy consumption visible and actionable at the software level. It examines the relationship between execution time, code size, and energy use, and evaluates how optimization selection and phase ordering can be learned from program features and empirical measurements. The study compares conventional compiler optimization levels with reduced optimization sets, machine-learning-based prediction, logic-programming approaches, and iterative search across embedded benchmarks and platforms. Results show that no single optimization or fixed compiler setting is consistently optimal: effective choices depend strongly on program structure and target architecture. Nevertheless, relatively small, guided searches can achieve substantial improvements while exploring only a minute fraction of the available configuration space. The paper argues that combining energy models, static and dynamic program information, and reproducible autotuning workflows can provide practical energy transparency. Such an approach enables multi-objective optimization of energy, performance, and code size, supporting the development of more efficient and sustainable embedded software.

original_abstract: We are witnessing a confluence of vision, speech and dialog system technologies that are enabling the IVAs to learn audio-visual groundings of utterances and have conversations with users about the objects, activities and events surrounding them. Recent progress in visual grounding techniques and Audio Understanding are enabling machines to understand shared semantic concepts and listen to the various sensory events in the environment. With audio and visual grounding methods, end-to-end multimodal SDS are trained to meaningfully communicate with us in natural language about the real dynamic audio-visual sensory world around us. In this work, we explore the role of `topics' as the context of the conversation along with multimodal attention into such an end-to-end audio-visual scene-aware dialog system architecture. We also incorporate an end-to-end audio classification ConvNet, AclNet, into our models. We develop and test our approaches on the Audio Visual Scene-Aware Dialog (AVSD) dataset released as a part of the DSTC7. We present the analysis of our experiments and show that some of our model variations outperform the baseline system released for AVSD.
generated_abstract: We present an end-to-end multimodal neural model for audio-visual scene-aware dialogue, enabling systems to answer questions about objects, actions, and events in video. Our approach combines hierarchical recurrent dialogue modeling with multimodal video representations derived from appearance, motion, and audio. A temporal attention mechanism selects relevant moments, while modality attention dynamically weighs visual and acoustic features for each generated response. To represent conversational context, the model encodes the dialogue history and conditions a recurrent decoder that produces answers word by word. We additionally investigate pretrained word embeddings and compact audio representations obtained from convolutional audio classifiers, as well as features from video description and visual question answering systems. We evaluate the approach on the Audio Visual Scene-Aware Dialog dataset, consisting of approximately 9,000 everyday videos and ten-round question-and-answer conversations collected through crowdsourcing. Experiments show that incorporating multimodal attention substantially improves response generation over text-only and single-modality baselines. Audio is particularly useful when relevant events are not fully observable visually, while temporal attention improves grounding in dynamic scenes. The results demonstrate the value of integrating video understanding, audio classification, and generative dialogue for conversational agents operating in realistic environments.

original_abstract: We address the challenging problem of generating facial attributes using a single image in an unconstrained pose. In contrast to prior works that largely consider generation on 2D near-frontal images, we propose a GAN-based framework to generate attributes directly on a dense 3D representation given by UV texture and position maps, resulting in photorealistic, geometrically-consistent and identity-preserving outputs. Starting from a self-occluded UV texture map obtained by applying an off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction method, we propose two novel components. First, a texture completion generative adversarial network (TC-GAN) completes the partial UV texture map. Second, a 3D attribute generation GAN (3DA-GAN) synthesizes the target attribute while obtaining an appearance consistent with 3D face geometry and preserving identity. Extensive experiments on CelebA, LFW and IJB-A show that our method achieves consistently better attribute generation accuracy than prior methods, a higher degree of qualitative photorealism and preserves face identity information.
generated_abstract: We present a two-stage framework for high-fidelity face swapping in unconstrained images. The goal is to transfer the identity of a source face to a target image while preserving the target’s pose, expression, illumination, background, and other nonidentity attributes. Our method first generates an identity-preserving face through an adaptive embedding integration module, which combines identity features extracted from the source with multiscale attributes of the target. A second refinement network, equipped with a dedicated occlusion-aware strategy, restores details that should remain in front of the synthesized face, such as hair, glasses, and hands. This design avoids the excessive information loss and visual artifacts common in conventional encoder-decoder and image-translation approaches. We train the framework with adversarial, reconstruction, perceptual, and identity-preserving objectives, enabling it to generalize to identities unseen during training. Extensive experiments on faces collected in the wild demonstrate that the proposed approach produces realistic, high-resolution results while maintaining strong identity similarity and accurate attribute preservation. It substantially outperforms existing face synthesis and swapping methods in both qualitative comparisons and quantitative evaluations, including face recognition and human perceptual studies.

original_abstract: In this work we introduce a new self-supervised, semi-parametric approach for synthesizing novel views of a vehicle starting from a single monocular image. Differently from parametric (i.e. entirely learning-based) methods, we show how a-priori geometric knowledge about the object and the 3D world can be successfully integrated into a deep learning based image generation framework. As this geometric component is not learnt, we call our approach semi-parametric. #R##N#In particular, we exploit man-made object symmetry and piece-wise planarity to integrate rich a-priori visual information into the novel viewpoint synthesis process. An Image Completion Network (ICN) is then trained to generate a realistic image starting from this geometric guidance. #R##N#This careful blend between parametric and non-parametric components allows us to i) operate in a real-world scenario, ii) preserve high-frequency visual information such as textures, iii) handle truly arbitrary 3D roto-translations of the input and iv) perform shape transfer to completely different 3D models. Eventually, we show that our approach can be easily complemented with synthetic data and extended to other rigid objects with completely different topology, even in presence of concave structures and holes (e.g. chairs). #R##N#A comprehensive experimental analysis against state-of-the-art competitors shows the efficacy of our method both from a quantitative and a perceptive point of view. #R##N#Supplementary material, animated results, code and data are available at: this https URL
generated_abstract: We present a 3D-aware generative framework for synthesizing realistic views of an object from a single RGB image. The central challenge is to infer unobserved geometry and appearance while preserving the identity and visual details of the input. Our model encodes the image into a disentangled representation containing object structure, viewpoint, and appearance, and transforms this representation according to a desired camera pose. A variational latent space models the inherent ambiguity of hidden surfaces, allowing the system to produce multiple plausible views rather than a single deterministic prediction. A recurrent, coarse-to-fine decoder combines spatially transformed features with appearance information and uses perceptual and adversarial objectives to generate sharp, consistent images. We further introduce geometry-aware reconstruction and cycle-consistency constraints that encourage the synthesized views to agree with the input and with one another. Experiments on synthetic and real object datasets, including chairs, vehicles, and fashion images, show improved perceptual quality, identity preservation, and viewpoint consistency over image-to-image translation and appearance-flow baselines. The learned representation also supports applications such as pose manipulation, image completion, 3D-aware retrieval, and generation of additional training examples for downstream recognition.

original_abstract: Deep learning based methods have achieved surprising progress in Scene Text Recognition (STR), one of classic problems in computer vision. In this paper, we propose a feasible framework for multi-lingual arbitrary-shaped STR, including instance segmentation based text detection and language model based attention mechanism for text recognition. Our STR algorithm not only recognizes Latin and Non-Latin characters, but also supports arbitrary-shaped text recognition. Our method wins the championship on Scene Text Spotting Task (Latin Only, Latin and Chinese) of ICDAR2019 Robust Reading Challenge on ArbitraryShaped Text Competition. Code is available at this https URL.
generated_abstract: Scene text spotting in natural images requires accurate localization and recognition of text instances that vary widely in scale, orientation, language, and shape. Existing systems often rely on separate detection and recognition stages, handcrafted proposals, or character-level annotations, which increase computational cost and limit robustness to curved and densely packed text. We present a unified end-to-end framework for detecting and recognizing arbitrary-shaped text with a single deep neural network. The proposed architecture combines a multi-scale visual backbone and feature pyramid with an anchor-free instance detector, while a region-aware recognition module extracts rectified features from each predicted text instance and decodes its transcription using attention. Detection and recognition share visual representations and are optimized jointly, allowing recognition cues to improve localization and reducing redundant computation. The method supports oriented, curved, and multilingual text without requiring character segmentation or a predefined lexicon. Extensive experiments on ICDAR, RCTW-17, COCO-Text, Total-Text, and the ICDAR2019 ArT benchmark demonstrate consistent improvements over two-stage and prior unified approaches in text detection, word spotting, and end-to-end text recognition. The resulting system provides a favorable accuracy–speed tradeoff and is suitable for practical real-time scene understanding applications.

original_abstract: Recent efforts show that neural networks are vulnerable to small but intentional perturbations on input features in visual classification tasks. Due to the additional consideration of connections between examples (\eg articles with citation link tend to be in the same class), graph neural networks could be more sensitive to the perturbations, since the perturbations from connected examples exacerbate the impact on a target example. Adversarial Training (AT), a dynamic regularization technique, can resist the worst-case perturbations on input features and is a promising choice to improve model robustness and generalization. However, existing AT methods focus on standard classification, being less effective when training models on graph since it does not model the impact from connected examples.  In this work, we explore adversarial training on graph, aiming to improve the robustness and generalization of models learned on graph. We propose Graph Adversarial Training (GraphAT), which takes the impact from connected examples into account when learning to construct and resist perturbations. We give a general formulation of GraphAT, which can be seen as a dynamic regularization scheme based on the graph structure. To demonstrate the utility of GraphAT, we employ it on a state-of-the-art graph neural network model --- Graph Convolutional Network (GCN). We conduct experiments on two citation graphs (Citeseer and Cora) and a knowledge graph (NELL), verifying the effectiveness of GraphAT which outperforms normal training on GCN by 4.51% in node classification accuracy. Codes are available via: https://github.com/fulifeng/GraphAT.
generated_abstract: Graph neural networks have achieved strong performance on node classification, link prediction, and graph-level prediction, but their reliance on learned representations and graph propagation makes them vulnerable to small, deliberate perturbations. Existing adversarial methods mainly modify graph structure or node attributes, which is costly, discrete, and often difficult to optimize. We propose a general adversarial training framework for robust graph representation learning that introduces worst-case perturbations in the continuous hidden representations of nodes during message passing. The perturbations are generated by maximizing the prediction loss under a norm constraint, while the model is trained to minimize the resulting robust objective. This approach preserves the original graph and can be integrated with common graph convolutional, attention, and embedding architectures using efficient first-order optimization. We further develop a semi-supervised variant that exploits unlabeled nodes through a consistency-based virtual adversarial objective. Experiments on citation, social, and recommendation networks show that the proposed method improves clean-data generalization and substantially increases resistance to feature, structure, and transfer attacks. Ablation studies demonstrate that adversarial regularization complements neighborhood aggregation and yields stable representations across perturbation budgets and graph scales.

original_abstract: The redundancy is widely recognized in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which enables to remove unimportant filters from convolutional layers so as to slim the network with acceptable performance drop. Inspired by the linear and combinational properties of convolution, we seek to make some filters increasingly close and eventually identical for network slimming. To this end, we propose Centripetal SGD (C-SGD), a novel optimization method, which can train several filters to collapse into a single point in the parameter hyperspace. When the training is completed, the removal of the identical filters can trim the network with NO performance loss, thus no finetuning is needed. By doing so, we have partly solved an open problem of constrained filter pruning on CNNs with complicated structure, where some layers must be pruned following others. Our experimental results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet have justified the effectiveness of C-SGD-based filter pruning. Moreover, we have provided empirical evidences for the assumption that the redundancy in deep neural networks helps the convergence of training by showing that a redundant CNN trained using C-SGD outperforms a normally trained counterpart with the equivalent width.
generated_abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks achieve remarkable accuracy, but their computational, memory, and energy requirements limit deployment on mobile, embedded, and other resource-constrained platforms. This paper reviews and analyzes approaches for making deep models more efficient, organizing existing methods into complementary categories: architectural redesign, low-rank and structured transforms, efficient convolution algorithms, knowledge distillation, quantization and binarization, and parameter, neuron, channel, and filter pruning. Particular attention is given to the distinction between unstructured sparsity, which primarily reduces storage, and structured compression, which directly lowers dense computation and is therefore more readily supported by commodity hardware. We compare representative optimization strategies, including sparsity regularization, reconstruction-based selection, importance propagation, correlation modeling, reinforcement learning, and systematic constrained optimization. We also discuss compression-aware training, fine-tuning, and the growing evidence that the final architecture may matter more than inherited weights. Results reported across image classification and related tasks demonstrate substantial reductions in parameters, floating-point operations, latency, and energy with limited accuracy loss. Finally, we identify practical challenges involving hardware dependence, accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, reproducibility, and the need for unified evaluation protocols, and outline promising directions for automated, hardware-aware compression.

original_abstract: Executable semantic parsing is the task of converting natural language utterances into logical forms that can be directly used as queries to get a response. We build a transfer learning framework for executable semantic parsing. We show that the framework is effective for Question Answering (QA we experiment with public data sets such as Overnight and NLmaps as well as with commercial SLU data. The experiments carried out on data sets that are different in nature show how executable semantic parsing can unify different areas of NLP such as Q&A and SLU.
generated_abstract: We study semantic parsing for conversational agents in settings where annotated data is scarce, domains change, and users may mix languages. We propose a unified neural framework that learns to map utterances to compositional logical forms while sharing representations across related tasks, domains, and languages. The model combines a recurrent encoder with attention, character-aware representations for rare and unseen words, and structured decoding mechanisms that capture predicate-argument dependencies and hierarchical intent–slot compositions. Auxiliary objectives, including syntactic analysis, frame prediction, and paraphrase generation, are used to transfer linguistic knowledge from resource-rich tasks to low-resource semantic parsing. To improve cross-domain generalization, we separate domain-independent logical structure from lexical grounding and expose the parser to recombined and automatically generated training examples. We evaluate the approach on task-oriented dialogue and map-based question-answering benchmarks spanning multiple domains and languages, including code-switched utterances. Results show consistent improvements over independently trained sequence-to-sequence and slot-filling systems, particularly when target-domain supervision is limited. The experiments demonstrate that combining structural bias, multilingual transfer, and multi-task learning enables accurate and efficient semantic parsing beyond the conditions represented in the training data.

original_abstract: Implicit discourse relation recognition is a challenging task due to the absence of the necessary informative clue from explicit connectives. The prediction of relations requires a deep understanding of the semantic meanings of sentence pairs. As implicit discourse relation recognizer has to carefully tackle the semantic similarity of the given sentence pairs and the severe data sparsity issue exists in the meantime, it is supposed to be beneficial from mastering the entire training data. Thus in this paper, we propose a novel memory mechanism to tackle the challenges for further performance improvement. The memory mechanism is adequately memorizing information by pairing representations and discourse relations of all training instances, which right fills the slot of the data-hungry issue in the current implicit discourse relation recognizer. Our experiments show that our full model with memorizing the entire training set reaches new state-of-the-art against strong baselines, which especially for the first time exceeds the milestone of 60% accuracy in the 4-way task.
generated_abstract: Implicit discourse relation classification is a central bottleneck in discourse parsing because the connective expressing the relation is absent and the intended sense must be inferred from the interaction between two discourse arguments. Existing neural models have improved representation learning, but often overlook long-range dependencies, discourse structure, and the complementary information provided by explicit connectives and related linguistic tasks. We propose a unified neural framework for implicit relation recognition that combines contextualized multi-granular representations with memory-based attention over argument words and surrounding discourse units. The model explicitly captures cross-argument semantic interactions, paragraph-level cohesion, and relation continuity, while a multi-task objective transfers knowledge from connective prediction and auxiliary discourse annotations. Syntactic information is incorporated when available, but the architecture remains applicable without external parses. We evaluate the approach on English and Chinese discourse benchmarks, including the Penn Discourse Treebank, the Chinese Discourse Treebank, and CoNLL shared-task data. Results show consistent improvements over feature-based, convolutional, recurrent, and memory-network baselines in both coarse- and fine-grained sense classification. Further analyses demonstrate that contextual representations, selective attention, and connective-aware learning contribute complementary gains, yielding a robust model for multilingual shallow discourse parsing.

original_abstract: Storage resources and caching techniques permeate almost every area of communication networks today. In the near future, caching is set to play an important role in storage-assisted Internet architectures, information-centric networks, and wireless systems, reducing operating and capital expenditures and improving the services offered to users. In light of the remarkable data traffic growth and the increasing number of rich-media applications, the impact of caching is expected to become even more profound than it is today. Therefore, it is crucial to design these systems in an optimal fashion, ensuring the maximum possible performance and economic benefits from their deployment. To this end, this article presents a collection of detailed models and algorithms, which are synthesized to build a powerful analytical framework for caching optimization.
generated_abstract: We study online content caching in wireless and information-centric networks when demand patterns, content popularities, and network conditions are unknown and may change over time. Conventional popularity-based placement and reactive replacement policies can perform poorly under nonstationary traffic, small populations, and overlapping cache coverage. We formulate caching as an online convex optimization problem over probabilistic content placements, incorporating storage constraints, retrieval costs, heterogeneous content utilities, and coordination among neighboring caches. We develop a distributed learning algorithm that combines projected gradient updates with adaptive exploration and a lightweight clustering mechanism for sharing information across caches with related demand profiles. Efficient projection procedures make the method practical for large catalogs and grouped or sparsity-constrained placements. We establish sublinear regret relative to the best fixed placement in hindsight, and show that the guarantees extend to networks of interacting caches under bounded routing costs. The algorithm requires no prior popularity model or centralized controller and adapts automatically to temporal changes. Trace-driven and synthetic evaluations demonstrate substantial improvements in hit rate, backhaul offloading, and access cost over LRU, popularity-based placement, independent learning, and existing cooperative policies, while maintaining low communication, computation, and memory overhead.

original_abstract: Neuromorphic computing takes inspiration from the brain to create energy efficient hardware for information processing, capable of highly sophisticated tasks. In this article, we make the case that building this new hardware necessitates reinventing electronics. We show that research in physics and material science will be key to create artificial nano-neurons and synapses, to connect them together in huge numbers, to organize them in complex systems, and to compute with them efficiently. We describe how some researchers choose to take inspiration from artificial intelligence to move forward in this direction, whereas others prefer taking inspiration from neuroscience, and we highlight recent striking results obtained with these two approaches. Finally, we discuss the challenges and perspectives in neuromorphic physics, which include developing the algorithms and the hardware hand in hand, making significant advances with small toy systems, as well as building large scale networks.
generated_abstract: Neuromorphic computing seeks to reproduce the brain’s energy-efficient, massively parallel information processing by integrating memory, computation, and adaptation in physical systems. This paper reviews recent progress toward that goal across device, circuit, architecture, and algorithmic levels. We discuss memristive technologies, including resistive, phase-change, ferroelectric, ionic, and magnetic devices, as compact implementations of synapses and neurons, emphasizing their analog dynamics, stochasticity, variability, endurance, and programming requirements. Binary and low-precision networks, in-memory computing, local plasticity rules, and device–algorithm co-design are considered as strategies for achieving scalable and robust learning. We further examine alternative dynamical substrates, including silicon neurons, nonlinear mechanical and electronic oscillators, spintronic and superconducting devices, and photonic reservoir and diffractive networks. These platforms exploit temporal coding, synchronization, nonlinear dynamics, and physical parallelism to perform classification, prediction, and control with low latency and energy. Biological principles such as dendritic computation, synaptic homeostasis, stochasticity, and continual learning provide useful design guidance, while hardware constraints motivate new computational models. The review identifies key challenges in variability tolerance, training, interconnects, scalability, benchmarking, and system integration, and outlines opportunities for practical edge intelligence.

original_abstract: Modern object detectors can rarely achieve short training time, fast inference speed, and high accuracy at the same time. To strike a balance among them, we propose the Training-Time-Friendly Network (TTFNet). In this work, we start with light-head, single-stage, and anchor-free designs, which enable fast inference speed. Then, we focus on shortening training time. We notice that encoding more training samples from annotated boxes plays a similar role as increasing batch size, which helps enlarge the learning rate and accelerate the training process. To this end, we introduce a novel approach using Gaussian kernels to encode training samples. Besides, we design the initiative sample weights for better information utilization. Experiments on MS COCO show that our TTFNet has great advantages in balancing training time, inference speed, and accuracy. It has reduced training time by more than seven times compared to previous real-time detectors while maintaining state-of-the-art performances. In addition, our super-fast version of TTFNet-18 and TTFNet-53 can outperform SSD300 and YOLOv3 by less than one-tenth of their training time, respectively. The code has been made available at \url{https://github.com/ZJULearning/ttfnet}.
generated_abstract: We present DetectoRS, a high-performance object detection system that strengthens both feature extraction and feature representation through recursive refinement. Our approach introduces a Recursive Feature Pyramid (RFP), which feeds the output of a feature pyramid network back into the backbone through an additional feedback pathway. This enables the detector to repeatedly refine multi-scale features using information from higher-level predictions. We further propose Switchable Atrous Convolution (SAC), which combines convolutions with different dilation rates and learns image-dependent switching weights, allowing the network to adapt its receptive field to diverse object appearances and scales. These components can be incorporated into existing detection and instance segmentation frameworks with limited architectural changes. Evaluations on the MS COCO benchmark show consistent improvements over strong baselines, including Faster R-CNN, Mask R-CNN, and related state-of-the-art detectors. With a ResNet-50 backbone, DetectoRS achieves substantial gains in both bounding-box and mask accuracy, while larger configurations establish leading results for object detection and instance segmentation. The results demonstrate that recursive feature processing and adaptive spatial sampling provide an effective complement to advances in detector heads and training objectives.

original_abstract: Contextual representation models have achieved great success in improving various downstream tasks. However, these language-model-based encoders are difficult to train due to the large parameter sizes and high computational complexity. By carefully examining the training procedure, we find that the softmax layer (the output layer) causes significant inefficiency due to the large vocabulary size. Therefore, we redesign the learning objective and propose an efficient framework for training contextual representation models. Specifically, the proposed approach bypasses the softmax layer by performing language modeling with dimension reduction, and allows the models to leverage pre-trained word embeddings. Our framework reduces the time spent on the output layer to a negligible level, eliminates almost all the trainable parameters of the softmax layer and performs language modeling without truncating the vocabulary. When applied to ELMo, our method achieves a 4 times speedup and eliminates 80% trainable parameters while achieving competitive performance on downstream tasks.
generated_abstract: We present a systematic study of neural representations for natural language understanding, examining how architectural choices, pre-training objectives, and input granularity affect the quality, efficiency, and transferability of learned features. We compare recurrent, convolutional, and self-attentive language models, including models based on characters, subwords, and words, and evaluate their representations on sentence classification, natural language inference, question answering, named entity recognition, semantic role labeling, parsing, coreference resolution, and language modeling. Across controlled experiments, contextual representations consistently outperform static word vectors, while intermediate layers capture complementary information ranging from morphology and local syntax to long-range semantics and discourse relations. We further investigate vocabulary reduction, adaptive output layers, weight tying, and continuous alternatives to softmax, showing that substantial computational savings can be obtained without degrading downstream accuracy. Results demonstrate that efficient architectures such as gated convolutions and simplified recurrent units can approach or exceed conventional recurrent models, whereas bidirectional pre-training provides the largest gains for transfer. Our analysis highlights persistent limitations in compositional reasoning, rare-word handling, and universal sentence encoding, and provides practical recommendations for selecting and evaluating representations in modern NLP systems.

original_abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have shown huge superiority over humans in image recognition, speech processing, autonomous vehicles and medical diagnosis. However, recent studies indicate that DNNs are vulnerable to adversarial examples (AEs), which are designed by attackers to fool deep learning models. Different from real examples, AEs can mislead the model to predict incorrect outputs while hardly be distinguished by human eyes, therefore threaten security-critical deep-learning applications. In recent years, the generation and defense of AEs have become a research hotspot in the field of artificial intelligence (AI) security. This article reviews the latest research progress of AEs. First, we introduce the concept, cause, characteristics and evaluation metrics of AEs, then give a survey on the state-of-the-art AE generation methods with the discussion of advantages and disadvantages. After that, we review the existing defenses and discuss their limitations. Finally, future research opportunities and challenges on AEs are prospected.
generated_abstract: Deep neural networks achieve remarkable performance across vision, speech, reinforcement learning, cybersecurity, and other applications, yet their predictions can be manipulated by carefully crafted inputs. This paper presents a comprehensive study of adversarial machine learning, examining how small, often imperceptible perturbations exploit weaknesses in learned decision boundaries and how these attacks extend beyond conventional image classification. We organize attacks according to the adversary’s knowledge, goals, perturbation constraints, and access to the target model, covering gradient-based, optimization-based, evolutionary, generative, universal, physical-world, and black-box transfer attacks. We review evidence of adversarial vulnerability in object detection, image captioning, malware and medical systems, speech recognition, and autonomous agents. We also analyze proposed defenses, including adversarial and virtual adversarial training, distillation, input-gradient regularization, detection, feature-space methods, randomized strategies, and architectural modifications. Particular attention is given to the gap between reported robustness and genuine security, including gradient obfuscation, adaptive attacks, transferability, and unrealistic threat models. Finally, we identify principles for reliable evaluation and outline open challenges in developing models that are accurate, interpretable, and robust under realistic adversarial conditions.

original_abstract: There is a growing interest in learning a model which could recognize novel classes with only a few labeled examples. In this paper, we propose Temporal Alignment Module (TAM), a novel few-shot learning framework that can learn to classify a previous unseen video. While most previous works neglect long-term temporal ordering information, our proposed model explicitly leverages the temporal ordering information in video data through temporal alignment. This leads to strong data-efficiency for few-shot learning. In concrete, TAM calculates the distance value of query video with respect to novel class proxies by averaging the per frame distances along its alignment path. We introduce continuous relaxation to TAM so the model can be learned in an end-to-end fashion to directly optimize the few-shot learning objective. We evaluate TAM on two challenging real-world datasets, Kinetics and Something-Something-V2, and show that our model leads to significant improvement of few-shot video classification over a wide range of competitive baselines.
generated_abstract: Recognizing novel actions from only a few labeled videos remains challenging because video representations must capture both appearance and long-range temporal structure, while adapting without overfitting or forgetting previously learned categories. We present a meta-learning framework for few-shot action recognition that combines an efficient spatiotemporal encoder with episodic prototype-based adaptation. The encoder uses a lightweight 2D convolutional backbone augmented with temporal information exchange and multi-scale relational reasoning, allowing it to model motion and interactions without the cost of a full 3D network. For each episode, class prototypes are constructed from sparsely sampled support clips and refined using temporal alignment between support and query videos. A first-order adaptation strategy enables rapid optimization without backpropagating through the complete inner-loop computation. We evaluate the approach in standard and cross-domain few-shot settings on UCF101, HMDB51, Kinetics, Charades, and Something-Something. The method consistently improves over frame-based, 3D convolutional, metric-learning, and gradient-based meta-learning baselines, particularly when only one or five examples are available. Ablation studies show that temporal modeling, alignment, and efficient sampling contribute complementary gains, demonstrating that effective few-shot video recognition requires integrating strong pretrained representations with explicit temporal reasoning.

original_abstract: Although deep neural networks have been successful in image classification, they are prone to adversarial attacks. To generate misclassified inputs, there has emerged a wide variety of techniques, such as black- and whitebox testing of neural networks. In this paper, we present DeepSearch, a novel blackbox-fuzzing technique for image classifiers. Despite its simplicity, DeepSearch is shown to be more effective in finding adversarial examples than closely related black- and whitebox approaches. DeepSearch is additionally able to generate the most subtle adversarial examples in comparison to these approaches.
generated_abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly deployed in safety- and security-critical applications, yet their complex, nonlinear behavior makes reliability difficult to establish. This paper surveys methods for analyzing, testing, and improving the robustness of deep neural networks, with particular emphasis on adversarial examples and formal safety guarantees. We organize existing techniques into four complementary categories: adversarial attack generation, automated testing and fuzzing, formal verification and reachability analysis, and certified or empirically evaluated defenses. We compare white-box, black-box, and physical-world threat models, discussing attacks based on gradients, transferability, zeroth-order optimization, and decision-only queries. We further review coverage-guided, metamorphic, differential, symbolic, and concolic testing methods, as well as verification approaches based on satisfiability solving, mixed-integer programming, abstract interpretation, convex relaxation, and linear bounds. Our analysis highlights the trade-offs among soundness, precision, scalability, and computational cost. We show that many empirical defenses fail under adaptive or sufficiently strong attacks, while existing certification methods remain limited by network size and specification complexity. Finally, we identify methodological pitfalls and outline research directions toward scalable, rigorous, and practically meaningful assurance for deep learning systems.

original_abstract: We develop new abstractions for reasoning about three relaxations of differential privacy:  $R$ enyi differential privacy, zero-concentrated differential privacy, and truncated concentrated differential privacy, which express bounds on statistical divergences between two output probability distributions. In order to reason about such properties compositionally, we introduce approximate span-lifting, a novel construction extending the approximate relational lifting approaches previously developed for standard differential privacy to a more general class of divergences, and also to continuous distributions. As an application, we develop a program logic based on approximate span-liftings capable of proving relaxations of differential privacy and other statistical divergence properties.
generated_abstract: We present a unified framework for specifying and verifying privacy properties of probabilistic programs. The framework is based on graded relational liftings, which provide a compositional account of approximate couplings and encompass differential privacy, concentrated privacy, and Renyi differential privacy. We develop a relational program logic that supports discrete and continuous sampling, adaptive interaction, higher-order probabilistic computation, and accuracy-dependent privacy arguments. Privacy costs are expressed using divergence-indexed grades, allowing the logic to derive standard composition bounds as well as sharper bounds obtained through Renyi divergence and concentrated differential privacy. We prove soundness of the logic with respect to a measure-theoretic semantics and establish connections between existential and universal approximate liftings. An implementation combines constraint solving with inference of relational couplings and privacy annotations, reducing the burden of manual proofs. We evaluate the approach on representative mechanisms, including noisy maximization, sparse vector variants, Bayesian inference, adaptive analyses, and mechanisms used in data and mechanism design. The results show that a single principled foundation can subsume several existing verification methods while supporting more expressive algorithms and tighter privacy analyses.

original_abstract: We simulate data using a graphic engine to augment real-world datasets, with application to vehicle re-identification (re-ID). In order for data augmentation to be effective, the simulated data should be similar to the real data in key attributes like illumination and viewpoint. We introduce a large-scale synthetic dataset VehicleX. Created in Unity, it contains 1,209 vehicles of various models in 3D with fully editable attributes. We propose an attribute descent approach to let VehicleX approximate the attributes in real-world datasets. Specifically, we manipulate each attribute in VehicleX, aiming to minimize the discrepancy between VehicleX and real data in terms of the Fr'echet Inception Distance (FID). This attribute descent algorithm allows content-level domain adaptation (DA), which has advantages over existing DA methods working on the pixel level or feature level. We mix adapted VehicleX data with three vehicle re-ID datasets individually, and observe consistent improvement when the proposed attribute descent is applied. With the augmented datasets, we report competitive accuracy compared with state-of-the-art results. The VehicleX engine and code of this paper will be released.
generated_abstract: Vehicle re-identification in urban surveillance is hindered by limited labeled data, large viewpoint and illumination variations, and the small visual differences between distinct vehicles. We present a synthetic-data-driven framework for learning robust vehicle representations with minimal manual annotation. Using a configurable 3D simulation environment, we generate diverse vehicle images with automatically available identity, viewpoint, pose, color, and type labels. Simulation parameters are optimized to produce scenes whose content and appearance better match real surveillance data, while randomized rendering and image-to-image adaptation reduce the remaining synthetic-to-real domain gap. A multi-task network combines global and region-aware appearance features with viewpoint and semantic attribute prediction, and is trained using identity classification and hard triplet metric learning. We further introduce consistency constraints that preserve vehicle identity during visual translation and selectively augment real training images with adapted synthetic samples. Experiments on VeRi, VehicleID, CityFlow-ReID, and related benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong convolutional and triplet baselines, particularly for cross-view matching and rare viewpoints. The results demonstrate that controllable synthetic data, combined with domain adaptation and pose-aware representation learning, provides an effective and scalable alternative to extensive real-world labeling.

original_abstract: Designing a molecule with desired properties is one of the biggest challenges in drug development, as it requires optimization of chemical compound structures with respect to many complex properties. To augment the compound design process we introduce Mol-CycleGAN - a CycleGAN-based model that generates optimized compounds with high structural similarity to the original ones. Namely, given a molecule our model generates a structurally similar one with an optimized value of the considered property. We evaluate the performance of the model on selected optimization objectives related to structural properties (presence of halogen groups, number of aromatic rings) and to a physicochemical property (penalized logP). In the task of optimization of penalized logP of drug-like molecules our model significantly outperforms previous results.
generated_abstract: We present MolGAN, an implicit generative model for learning and optimizing small molecular graphs. Unlike sequence-based approaches that generate SMILES strings, MolGAN produces molecular graphs directly, avoiding the need for an ordering of atoms and bonds. The generator maps random latent vectors to distributions over adjacency tensors and atom features, while a graph convolutional discriminator distinguishes generated molecules from those in a training set. To encourage generation of molecules with desired chemical properties, we augment the adversarial objective with a reward network and optimize the generator using policy gradients. This combination enables simultaneous learning of chemical structure distributions and goal-directed molecular design without requiring an explicit likelihood model. We evaluate MolGAN on benchmark molecular datasets and compare it with variational autoencoders and recurrent graph-generation methods. The model generates novel compounds with high chemical validity, while retaining diversity and similarity to the training distribution. Furthermore, incorporating property-based rewards allows the generation process to shift toward molecules with improved target characteristics. Our results demonstrate that adversarial graph generation provides an effective and flexible framework for de novo molecular design.

original_abstract: Land cover classification of remote sensing images is a challenging task due to limited amounts of annotated data, highly imbalanced classes, frequent incorrect pixel-level annotations, and an inherent complexity in the semantic segmentation task. In this article, we propose a novel architecture called the dense dilated convolutions' merging network (DDCM-Net) to address this task. The proposed DDCM-Net consists of dense dilated image convolutions merged with varying dilation rates. This effectively utilizes rich combinations of dilated convolutions that enlarge the network's receptive fields with fewer parameters and features compared with the state-of-the-art approaches in the remote sensing domain. Importantly, DDCM-Net obtains fused local- and global-context information, in effect incorporating surrounding discriminative capability for multiscale and complex-shaped objects with similar color and textures in very high-resolution aerial imagery. We demonstrate the effectiveness, robustness, and flexibility of the proposed DDCM-Net on the publicly available ISPRS Potsdam and Vaihingen data sets, as well as the DeepGlobe land cover data set. Our single model, trained on three-band Potsdam and Vaihingen data sets, achieves better accuracy in terms of both mean intersection over union (mIoU) and F1-score compared with other published models trained with more than three-band data. We further validate our model on the DeepGlobe data set, achieving state-of-the-art result 56.2% mIoU with much fewer parameters and at a lower computational cost compared with related recent work. Code available at https://github.com/samleoqh/DDCM-Semantic-Segmentation-PyTorch
generated_abstract: Semantic segmentation of high-resolution remote sensing imagery is challenging because land-cover classes exhibit substantial scale variation, complex shapes, similar spectral responses, and indistinct boundaries. We propose a deep fully convolutional framework for accurate and efficient land-cover mapping that combines residual feature extraction with dense multi-scale context aggregation. Dilated convolutions with complementary rates enlarge the receptive field without reducing spatial resolution, while feature fusion between shallow and deep layers preserves fine details and improves boundary localization. Channel-wise recalibration further emphasizes informative spectral and structural responses, and an encoder–decoder design produces predictions at the original image resolution. To improve robustness when annotated data are limited, the network is trained with extensive geometric and photometric augmentation and adaptive stochastic optimization. We evaluate the approach on publicly available high-resolution aerial and satellite benchmarks, including ISPRS and DeepGlobe datasets, using standard pixel accuracy, mean intersection-over-union, and F1-score measures. Experiments show that the proposed model consistently outperforms conventional fully convolutional, encoder–decoder, and single-scale dilated architectures, particularly for small objects and confusing urban classes. Qualitative results demonstrate sharper boundaries and more coherent predictions, confirming the value of jointly modeling local detail and broad contextual information.

original_abstract: We propose a novel text generation task, namely Curiosity-driven Question Generation. We start from the observation that the Question Generation task has traditionally been considered as the dual problem of Question Answering, hence tackling the problem of generating a question given the text that contains its answer. Such questions can be used to evaluate machine reading comprehension. However, in real life, and especially in conversational settings, humans tend to ask questions with the goal of enriching their knowledge and/or clarifying aspects of previously gathered information. We refer to these inquisitive questions as Curiosity-driven: these questions are generated with the goal of obtaining new information (the answer) which is not present in the input text. In this work, we experiment on this new task using a conversational Question Answering (QA) dataset; further, since the majority of QA dataset are not built in a conversational manner, we describe a methodology to derive data for this novel task from non-conversational QA data. We investigate several automated metrics to measure the different properties of Curious Questions, and experiment different approaches on the Curiosity-driven Question Generation task, including model pre-training and reinforcement learning. Finally, we report a qualitative evaluation of the generated outputs.
generated_abstract: Automatic evaluation of abstractive summarization commonly relies on reference-based metrics such as ROUGE, which favor lexical overlap and require human-written summaries. These limitations are particularly problematic for reinforcement-learning approaches, where the evaluation metric is also used as a training reward. We propose an unsupervised evaluation framework based on question answering. Given a source document and a candidate summary, a question-generation model produces questions targeting salient information in the document, while a question-answering model attempts to answer them using only the summary. The resulting answerability and consistency scores measure whether the summary preserves information that is important for understanding the source, without requiring a reference summary. We investigate several question-generation and answering configurations, analyze their sensitivity to fluency, relevance, and factual content, and compare them with ROUGE and other automatic metrics through human judgments. Our experiments show that question-answering-based metrics correlate more reliably with human assessments and reduce the lexical bias of overlap-based measures. Finally, we use these metrics as rewards for reinforcement-learning summarizers, obtaining improvements in both automatic evaluation and human-rated summary quality.

original_abstract: Reconstructing 3D human shape and pose from a monocular image is challenging despite the promising results achieved by the most recent learning-based methods. The commonly occurred misalignment comes from the facts that the mapping from images to the model space is highly non-linear and the rotation-based pose representation of the body model is prone to result in the drift of joint positions. In this work, we investigate learning 3D human shape and pose from dense correspondences of body parts and propose a Decompose-and-aggregate Network (DaNet) to address these issues. DaNet adopts the dense correspondence maps, which densely build a bridge between 2D pixels and 3D vertexes, as intermediate representations to facilitate the learning of 2D-to-3D mapping. The prediction modules of DaNet are decomposed into one global stream and multiple local streams to enable global and fine-grained perceptions for the shape and pose predictions, respectively. Messages from local streams are further aggregated to enhance the robust prediction of the rotation-based poses, where a position-aided rotation feature refinement strategy is proposed to exploit spatial relationships between body joints. Moreover, a Part-based Dropout (PartDrop) strategy is introduced to drop out dense information from intermediate representations during training, encouraging the network to focus on more complementary body parts as well as adjacent position features. The effectiveness of our method is validated on both in-door and real-world datasets including the Human3.6M, UP3D, and DensePose-COCO datasets. Experimental results show that the proposed method significantly improves the reconstruction performance in comparison with previous state-of-the-art methods. Our code will be made publicly available at this https URL .
generated_abstract: We present a part-guided approach for monocular 3D human pose and shape estimation from in-the-wild images. Existing regression methods typically extract a single global image feature, which can be unreliable under occlusion, truncation, unusual poses, and cluttered backgrounds. Our method, PARE, addresses these limitations by learning body-part attention maps that focus feature extraction on individual anatomical regions. These part-specific features are combined with a global representation and used to regress the parameters of a parametric human body model, including pose, shape, and camera. The attention mechanism is trained jointly with the reconstruction network and requires no additional annotations beyond those commonly available for human pose estimation. We further introduce a lightweight design that preserves the efficiency of direct regression while improving localization of visible body parts and robustness to missing evidence. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks, including Human3.6M, 3DPW, and challenging in-the-wild datasets, demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both 3D joint accuracy and mesh reconstruction quality. Our results show that explicitly modeling body-part visibility and correspondence provides an effective basis for accurate and efficient human mesh recovery.
